title: Superyacht Security: Here Are The Top Ways To Protect Your Voyage
text:
Despite lower-than-average piracy incidents this year, the shipping and yachting industry continues to pressure all vessels to remain vigilant as violent attacks remain a concern. The International Chamber of Commerce International Maritime Bureau’s Piracy Reporting Center (IMB) detailed that sixty incidents of piracy and armed robbery against commercial ships were recorded in the first half of 2024, a decrease from 65 incidents for the same period in 2023.
ICC Secretary General John W.H. Denton AO says, “While we are reassured to see a fall in the number of overall reported acts of piracy, the concerning rise in incidents of a violent nature underscores the need for continued vigilance from the international community to ensure the safety of all seafarers — especially at this time of heightened uncertainty for maritime transport.”
Of the 60 incidents reported this year, 46 vessels were boarded, eight reported attempted attacks, four were hijacked, and two were fired upon. Perpetrators successfully boarded 85% of targeted vessels.
Violence towards crew continues, with 85 taken hostage compared to 36 in the same period last year, with 11 kidnapped and two threatened. Guns and knives were reported in 34 of the 59 incidents, a worrying increase from the same period the previous year. While most reported pirate attacks are on commercial vessels, Yacht owners are advised to maintain strict anti-piracy watch and measures, especially at anchor.
The Caribbean Safety and Security Net (CSSN), notes the top destinations in 2024 for theft aboard a private boat are Grenada, St Martin, St Lucia, St Vincent, British Virgin Islands, and Antigua. In February, the catamaran Simplicity was found abandoned off a beach on the island of St. Vincent. According to reports, the bodies of the owners were likely thrown overboard after their yacht was hijacked.
I spoke with yacht owners about how they are spending millions setting up their large yachts with military-style technology while training their crews to avoid conflicts, as well as MARSS, the leading company providing security solutions. They provide protection for the maritime and yachting industry against airborne, surface, and subsurface threats. This includes enhancing surveillance capabilities with AI detection and verification, as well as connecting to onboard countermeasures and remote support.
MARSS recently delivered its advanced security and surveillance system, NiDAR, to a very famous billionaire who added to their 400+ foot yacht and 200+ foot support vessel with a revolutionary $4 million state-of-the-art security installation.
According to Frederik Giepmans, MD of Safety and Security with MARSS, “Developments in AI are transforming security on superyachts by improving accuracy and efficiency and reducing operator burden. In the case of securing yachts, AI can be used to rapidly analyze data from sensors, such as radio-frequency detection, cameras, radars, and sonar, and present key relevant information as specific targets and threats.”
“What may appear as a few pixels in the distance on your screen can be identified as a bird or drone threat with the help of AI,” he adds. “AI can also help determine whether something is a threat based on parameters such as course, direction, and speed, and will alert operators only when there is a real threat and action is required. Systems like MARSS’ NiDAR have been using AI for years to learn, constantly improve, and help operators to work better, faster, safer.”
Additionally, MARSS says “With the rise of intelligent, evolving, and more sophisticated threats around the globe—particularly with the proliferation of drones—superyachts need to have the correct safety systems in place to protect those on board. Yacht owners want seamless, unobtrusive protection so they and their guests can get on with life, knowing any incoming threats can be detected.”
NiDAR is the primary protection system, and offers long-range, multi-layer, 360° perimeter security for superyachts, tenders, toys, guests, and crew. The product uses the latest sensor technology connected via MARSS' proprietary command and control touch user interface with data fusion and machine learning capabilities. In real-time, NiDAR monitors, identifies, and tracks manned and unmanned air, surface, and underwater objects. The system utilizes AI-powered software algorithms to automatically analyze and rank threats, alerting captains and crew to take appropriate action.
There are countless protection devices on the market, but the most popular include the following from MARSS:
NiDAR X-COMPACT, an air surveillance system designed for use on mobile platforms, including superyachts. The system is equipped with radars, an IR camera, and Radio Frequency Monitoring to provide 360° surveillance for protection against drones and unmanned vehicles. The NiDAR CUAS Compact system (NiDAR Core is the company’s software-based AI platform, while CUAS means counter unmanned aerial systems) can detect and thwart up to 1,000 drones. The customizable system uses artificial intelligence and sensors for drone detection and optional electronic countermeasures.
CLiMBERguard: This unique high-accuracy climber detection system is an automatic climber detection system for the instant detection, classification and alert of onboarding activities on the side of a vessel or maritime structure.
RADiRguard: An intelligent all-in-one perimeter surveillance solution. Each self-contained RADiRguard unit combines built-in radar, CCTV and IR, plus intelligent threat classification to reliably detect and classify objects in advance of reaching a perimeter. RADiRguard is easily and rapidly deployable and is a cost effective, scalable solution that can be configured to a wide variety of surveillance areas.
Other protection additions for yacht owners include Long-Range Acoustic Devices (LRAD), which provide pain-inducing sound beams to invaders; Underwater Sonar Detection Systems, which detect movement below the surface; exterior lockdown systems, which provide total lockdown and are used on many yachts; and Safe Rooms, which act as fortified areas on a ship where the crew can take refuge in the event of a pirate attack.
Dutch superyacht builder Oceanco receives countless special security requests from clients as they fit their massive yachts. Among the requests are Citadel rooms, where owners can retreat to a hidden safe room to override access to the yacht's navigational and satellite communications systems. The rooms have ballistic-protected walls, an independent ventilation system, and water and food supplies.
Also requested are Emergency escape life pods that offer a rapid getaway, resist impact, and feature built-in GPS trackers, temperature and fire barrier controls, and air purification systems. Currently in development are Smart floors that track movement but can also be used to control lighting or heating.
There are certainly more lethal devices used aboard some superyachts. According to an eyewitness report in the Sunday Times, "The captain of a superyacht once deployed sonic weapons and 'pain rays' to fend off armed pirates in the Arabian Sea. The captain targeted ear-splitting, high-volume acoustics at the pirates using narrow beams of electromagnetic energy that trigger a burning sensation on the skin. The threat of pirate attacks is all too real. In some areas, such as along the coast of Africa in the Gulf of Aden, it's even expected. Any protective technology worth having will find its way aboard a yacht."

title: Council Post: 10 Essential Guidelines For Enterprise-Ready AI Solutions
text:
Isaac Madan is the co-founder and CEO of Nightfall AI, a comprehensive, AI-native data security platform.
AI-powered solutions are becoming increasingly prevalent in enterprise environments, leading to a new trend in procurement: the need for comprehensive AI governance frameworks. This shift reflects a growing awareness of AI-specific risks and the need for more granular controls.
As the founder of Nightfall AI, a startup building AI models for data security, I've navigated hundreds of procurement cycles and observed a rise in AI-specific requirements. I expect AI governance frameworks to become as ubiquitous as information security or privacy policies.
For AI startups selling their products to enterprises, demonstrating a commitment to responsible AI development is crucial. For enterprises adopting AI solutions, reviewing robust AI policies from vendors is essential to protect data and align with ethical and regulatory standards.
The goal of AI governance guidelines remains consistent: Build trust, ensure compliance and mitigate risks associated with AI-powered solutions.
1. Compliance With Laws And Regulations
All AI solutions must comply with existing data privacy regulations like GDPR and CCPA. However, the regulatory landscape for AI is rapidly changing, making it crucial to stay informed about developments in relevant jurisdictions.
For instance, California's Senate Bill 1047, if enacted, would significantly impact open-source model development by regulating AI at the model level. To understand these concerns, I've found it important to collaborate with our privacy counsel and AI research teams to anticipate and address the implications of impending AI-related laws and regulations.
2. Ethical AI Use
Ethical considerations should be central to AI development, requiring continuous evaluation of models to ensure fairness, transparency, accountability and safety. This is challenging, as it demands constant vigilance against unintentional biases or harmful outputs.
Companies like OpenAI and Anthropic prioritize ethical AI use throughout their development process. Anthropic has published its core views on AI safety, while OpenAI released a detailed System Card for GPT-4, describing its capabilities, limitations and risks.
When developing or reviewing AI solutions, consider how these leading AI companies employ gradual release approaches and robust content filtering to study and mitigate potential risks.
3. Alignment And Safety
AI providers can ensure alignment and safety through regular audits and robust testing protocols, such as:
• "Red teaming," which involves adversarial testing, helps evaluate and improve AI system safety.
• Establishing clear procedures for handling safety incidents is also critical.
• Continuous monitoring and testing of models helps prevent security risks and ensure technologies function as intended.
4. Data Privacy And Security Throughout The AI Life Cycle
Throughout the AI life cycle—from data collection to deployment—implementing robust safeguards ensures compliance with relevant privacy laws.
My company, for example, encrypts data in transit and at rest, and we employ strict access controls and user authentication to protect data and prevent unauthorized access. It's also essential to regularly review data handling procedures and conduct security assessments to maintain compliance. These measures ensure data is used only for its intended purpose, preserving customer trust.
5. Transparency
Be prepared to explain how your AI models work and the data they are trained on. This transparency builds trust and helps identify potential issues.
Citations enhance the transparency and verifiability of content generated by LLMs. Sharing performance metrics, such as accuracy on benchmark tasks, and discussing the limitations of these metrics in real-world applications can build credibility and long-term trust in AI.
6. Bias And Fairness
Proactively eliminate bias in AI models and demonstrate efforts to prevent discriminatory outcomes. This is crucial for maintaining fairness and avoiding legal and reputational risks. AI companies typically address this concern by:
1. Using diverse, representative training and evaluation datasets to reduce bias and ensure fair decisions across demographic groups.
2. Employing bias detection tools to identify and address unfairness in models.
3. Implementing regular testing to prevent discriminatory outcomes and maintain stakeholder trust.
7. Human Oversight
Maintain human oversight in AI workflows, especially for decisions with potential legal implications, while ensuring accountability and allowing necessary interventions.
Leading AI companies achieve this by clearly defining roles and responsibilities for AI system overseers. For example, Anthropic has established committees like Alignment and Trust & Safety teams for accountability and supervision.
Many top AI companies also implement training programs, equipping employees with skills to manage AI-related tasks and handle issues through proper escalation procedures.
8. Intellectual Property (IP) Protection
Respect and protect enterprise IP by sanitizing training data and implementing appropriate handling procedures. At Nightfall, we use synthetic data generation techniques to protect sensitive information during AI model training.
It's important to also establish clear guidelines for handling sensitive data, ensuring appropriate use and compliance. Regular audits of data usage help ensure IP protection and prevent unauthorized use of proprietary content.
9. Information Reporting
Be prepared to maintain detailed documentation of development and deployment processes.
Leading AI companies implement comprehensive logging and monitoring systems to track AI model performance and behavior. They develop standardized reporting templates for clear stakeholder communication and establish procedures for external audits.
10. Continuous Monitoring
Finally, stay informed about evolving ethical standards and regulatory changes. This vigilance is essential in the rapidly evolving AI landscape.
One way to do so is to subscribe to industry publications to track new developments. Anthropic's "Responsible Scaling Policy," for instance, exemplifies commitment to adapting to emerging government policies on responsible AI development in various geographies. They have a formal process for modifying safety levels and ensuring AI systems align with current ethical and regulatory standards.
The Future Of AI In The Enterprise
As AI technologies evolve, both AI providers and enterprise customers must prioritize robust AI governance frameworks. This approach helps navigate the complex landscape of AI adoption while maintaining compliance, security and ethical standards.
AI startups meeting these requirements will streamline procurement and demonstrate commitment to responsible development. Ultimately, organizations prioritizing AI governance will be better positioned to harness AI's power while mitigating risks and building stakeholder trust.

title: Council Post: AI And Biotech: How Companies Can Demonstrate Value To Investors
text:
Niven R. Narain, Ph.D., President & CEO, BPGbio.
For the past several years, investors have flocked to biotech on the promise of AI to accelerate drug development, reduce costs and enhance predictability. The math was a no-brainer: Shaving just 10% off the drug development timeline could translate to hundreds of millions saved.
Many of these companies, however, didn't deliver ROI as quickly as investors expected. Also, 56% of publically traded biotech companies had two or fewer years of cash in 2023, which also diminished investor expectations.
As the president and CEO of a biotech company that incorporates AI into every step of its drug development process, I have seen both the promise—and the limits—of AI. As I think about what separates hype from genuine opportunity in AI-driven drug discovery and development companies, five key elements stand out:
1. Proof
It’s no longer enough for companies to claim they have AI capabilities and expect investment. Companies should demonstrate to investors tangible progress in drug target discovery, validation or clinical trial development as proof that the company’s AI models can accurately reproduce biology.
As less investor money goes into companies with early-stage assets, these companies will need to demonstrate the role that AI modeling plays in the development of those assets. Companies entering human trials will also need to show how well those assets performed in the clinic and what, if any, translation errors impeded clinical success.
2. Transparency
Companies should be able to explain how their AI informed their identification and validation of drug targets. Some black-box AI models spit out targets but can’t show you how the model got from point A to point B. Such models leave researchers and doctors unable to explain the mechanism of action and potentially hinder regulatory processes.
Adopting a causal, hypothesis-free approach to AI can allow companies to trace the relationship between the biology and the drug and to validate the model with wet lab science.
3. Robust Underlying Data
The effectiveness of AI in drug development is largely dependent on the quality and size of the data sets used to feed the AI models. Small sample sizes, with just a handful of patients, are inadequate to identify causal relationships.
Companies that use large biobanks with hundreds of thousands of patient samples usually have much better AI output, especially when starting from unbiased, clinically annotated data from a multiethnic population.
4. Scalability
Scalability is vital for AI models in drug development. Key questions include: What size models can the AI manage? Can it manage billions of data points? Computer processing capabilities do play a role—faster computers mean faster outputs, of course—but it’s far more important that the AI model can handle a significant amount of data.
My company has gained access to the world’s fastest supercomputer, for example. We've found that while it speeds up our processes considerably, it would be useless without the AI capability to match.
5. De-Risking
Many savvy biotech investors consider the number of failed trials and whether the company used AI to mitigate these risks.
When used correctly, AI can guide trial design, optimize patient selection and refine dosing regimens, lowering the risk of trial failure. For example, AI showed my company that a drug was most effective against aggressive tumors. AI modeling also pointed the path toward other rare disease indications we plan to study further.
Using AI to optimize patients and dosing can help prevent clinical trial failures. All of these workstreams enable the de-risking of the asset before other dealmaking activities.
Final Thoughts
Proving value to investors in biotech requires distinguishing between potential and reality. Individual investors and family offices, who may lack the capacity to fully evaluate the technology, will likely consider looking at clinical trial evidence as the next best indicator.
By prioritizing proof, transparency, robust data, scalability and de-risking through AI, biotech companies can help investors make more informed decisions and show that their company is better positioned to leverage AI for meaningful advancements.

title: Council Post: Incorporating Responsible AI Into Your Knowledge Management Strategy
text:
Antti Nivala is Founder and CEO of M-Files, a leader in knowledge work automation.
Knowledge is power. It holds the context and insight required to drive business forward. However, knowledge is often trapped in data silos—stuck on a server or lost in a forgotten folder. That valuable information, such as a deep understanding of customer preferences or unique trends, holds enormous potential only AI can likely uncover.
AI can expose deep insights and information scattered across documents, emails and conversations. For many, it is the intelligence that powers problem-solving and enables knowledge workers to work more efficiently. However, with that intelligence comes responsibility.
Although many companies feel they need AI to keep up with the latest advancements and remain competitive, many don’t take the time to understand its impact on the business. As the pace of innovation increases, we must balance innovation and security effectively by assessing three aspects of that data: connectivity, curation and confidentiality.
Here are a few considerations to keep in mind when implementing AI across your information management strategy:
Connectivity
AI can help overcome the challenge of information overload head-on and unlock the value of unstructured data. But to be effective, we must ensure AI is working as intended and relaying accurate information.
When looking to advance AI capabilities, AI must have access to the right information resources to provide real value. Data should be integrated from all key storage systems and software solutions and connected with the right business processes. Ensuring a smooth flow of information allows the AI to analyze and interpret data effectively, leading to more informed decision-making.
It’s important to be aware of potential biases and risks so that businesses can implement mechanisms to uncover and prevent unintended consequences. AI hallucinations, for example, continue to be a real problem among large language models, where AI generates unrelated or incorrect information.
Vigilant knowledge management practices, such as metadata tagging, can help ensure that your AI solution avoids falling prey to the "garbage in, garbage out" scenario. Identifying vendors committed to deploying accurate tools to minimize AI hallucinations can also help your enterprise from falling victim.
Curation
With the influx of information generated across an organization, it’s important to understand what data AI models are trained on to ensure the information being leveraged is current, accurate and valuable. The data served to and accessed by AI models must be relevant to the topic, informative and not duplicative in a way that analyses are incorrectly skewed.
To ensure the insights your knowledge management system unlocks are accurate and valuable, a good place to start is to ensure your organization adheres to effective information governance protocols. In the same way that you may become confused in finding the latest version of a document, an AI solution can make similar mistakes if working from an unmanaged set of documents.
For example, content classification helps ensure AI models have access to the high-quality inputs required for accurate, unbiased results. The more that AI has access to data that has been classified and placed in context, the better it will be at extracting valuable information.
When considering curation as part of your document management strategy, ask yourself if your organization has data governance protocols in place and if you know whether you the AI can access the latest version of the data. Having a better understanding of how your data is curated and interacts with AI can ensure you are confident in the way you leverage the context of documents and interact with your organization's knowledge.
Confidentiality
Even though adopting AI has many benefits, it inevitably raises concerns about data privacy and confidentiality. Organizations need to understand how AI collects and uses data, who can access the data and whether the AI uses all the data collected to retrain its model platform-wide. Enterprises shouldn’t be afraid to examine vendor AI usage policies to make sure AI models can comply with their organization’s information security protocols and aren’t being trained on their data without their written consent.
Establishing information security and access management policies across your organization before deploying AI is essential to maintain data privacy and ensure that the AI only serves up information that the user is entitled to access. Adopting a metadata tagging structure in your knowledge management practices can also help apply granular access controls to your data.
By ensuring that the AI complies with these policies, you can be confident that the AI doesn’t have unauthorized access to personal information or confidential customer data. Transparently sharing these policies outside your organization can also demonstrate respect for your customers’ information security and go a long way in establishing trust.
Ensuring Guidelines
To get the most out of AI in your information management strategy, it’s important to establish clear guidelines and standards around AI’s usage while enabling successful AI deployment with capabilities for connectivity, curation and confidentiality. Establishing guidelines goes a step beyond simply considering the impact of accuracy and transparency. It provides the missing ingredient to make the value of your AI real—removing potential distrust to deliver on promises.
When developing guidelines, a good place to start is focusing on policies around how AI interacts with your data and your customers. For example, do customers maintain control in deciding how they want AI to interact with their data? Are there clear notices of AI integration and opt-in capabilities put in place? A metadata structure within your information management system also supports the need for data consistency and helps you identify, manage and enforce AI data policies as it provides an information model specific to each customer’s content. By taking responsibility for AI usage and evaluating current practices, businesses can have confidence that their systems and practices are aligned with their principles and values.
Forward-thinking organizations must harness their ability to absorb information and draw insights. AI has the potential to transform how we work, freeing employees from repetitive, time-consuming tasks and turning information into a growth driver. However, it's our responsibility to consider and monitor the impact of our AI or risk falling into pitfalls along the way.

title: Why Leaders Shouldn’t Wait To Adopt AI
text:
AI has been on everyone’s mind since ChatGPT burst onto the scene in fall of 2022. But it’s only in 2024 that businesses have really begun to use—and benefit from—the promises that generative AI holds. According to new research from McKinsey, the percentage of organizations employing generative AI has nearly doubled in just 10 months, rocketing from 33 to 65 percent. And expectations remain high: Three quarters of the survey’s respondents predict that gen AI will lead to “significant or disruptive” change in the coming years.
For leaders, the time to adopt AI is now. Here’s why.
AI Isn’t Just Hype
As a leader, it’s important to discern a passing fad from a major innovation that will fundamentally disrupt the way we live and work. A decade ago, it looked like Snapchat was going to change the landscape of social media, with “snaps” only viewable for a short time before they vanished forever. Lots of businesses paused before rushing to jump on board, biding their time to see if the model would actually stick. Ultimately it did, but the hesitation to jump on the bandwagon was sensible.
That “wait and see” model may have been prudent for a social media platform, but AI is not that. Like the internet before it, AI is completely transforming how work is done. With the AI market predicted to reach a value of more than $500 billion in 2024, leaders who are not actively integrating its services into their businesses are at serious risk of falling behind. If you’re holding out for a new development or ideal moment to get started, consider Google, which by 2015 already had more than 2,700 AI projects underway. There’s no reason to wait until technology advances further before making the leap.
Implementing AI Will Take Time
Adopting AI on a company-wide scale isn’t something that can be accomplished with a handful of training sessions. The reality is that creating a whole new system from the top down will take significant time and resources. As Vikram Mahidhar and Thomas H. Davenport point out at Harvard Business Review, businesses need to configure AI systems in a way that actually adds value, which can take months. Once the systems are built, they need to be integrated into the organization, which requires planning and adaptation. Lastly, the majority of AI systems are not fully autonomous—they require human input to be effective, which means hiring and retraining employees.
“Like any tool, it creates no value unless it’s used properly,” explains Barbara H. Wixom, a principal research scientist at the MIT Center for Information Systems Research. “AI is advanced data science, and you need to have the right capabilities in order to work with it and manage it properly.” Creating those capabilities is not an overnight project, but a whole institutional shift.
The Cost Of Haste
In addition to not adding value, hasty implementation of AI can be downright catastrophic. Perhaps you heard about the eating disorder hotline that had to be shut down after a chatbot offered dubious advice to callers. Or the lawyer who was sanctioned after submitting a legal brief containing six fictitious citations generated by a hallucinating ChatGPT.
This isn’t to say AI isn’t useful—it demonstrably is. Already, it’s regularly employed to help humans complete burdensome tasks like writing emails, managing workflows, analyzing data and much more. At Jotform, for example, we receive thousands of customer support requests and we use AI to detect anomalies. If a particular type of problem is recurring, an AI tool will send us an email and report the issue. This enables us to recognize and solve problems faster.
But what we didn’t do was rush to automate every aspect of our customer service framework—as the unfortunate hotline incident revealed, AI isn’t ready for that, and there’s no replacing an empathetic human when a customer is experiencing an issue. By implementing AI tools gradually, we’ve been able to take our time to see how they can add the most value. This also gives teams a chance to experiment, workshop new strategies, and generally test the limits of what AI can do—and what it can’t. Forcing teams to adopt new technology too quickly can inspire backlash, especially given the widespread fear that AI will eventually replace jobs. Early adoption positions AI as what it is—a tool to reduce dull, tedious tasks and free up more time for meaningful work.
Final Thoughts
We’re only at the beginning of undertanding the extent of AI’s impacts—on business, on society, on how we live. When the iPhone was released in 2007, we had no idea that it would change the way we thought of “cell phones” forever. The same will be true of AI.
As leaders, this is the moment to establish your philosophy toward AI. How does it fit into your business, both in its current form and as it evolves? What groundwork can you lay today to prepare for the future? By asking these questions now, you’ll both make yourself competitive in the present, and be ready for what comes next.

title: How AI Is Revolutionizing E-Mail Marketing
text:
E-mail newsletters are a mainstay of customer relationship management, but that doesn’t mean that they’ve been ideal. They’re both static and labor-intensive; the newsletters are often prepared weeks or months in advance of sending, then updated at the last minute with promotions and other tweaks that can cause substantial re-work and commotion. They’re adapted very little to the interests of unique customers, except perhaps with a few A/B tests that still result in little customization. And measurement of their performance tends to be in large-scale averages rather than through a nuanced view of what works with whom.
However, change is on the horizon. As Lindsay Massey, VP of Marketing at Victoria’s Secret, explained in an interview, “We wanted to move beyond a manual, one-size-fits-all content strategy and provide a 1:1 personalized experience at scale.” Victoria’s Secret used AI to do the job.
In its case, the firm partnered with a company called Movable Ink to provide the technology through a platform it calls Da Vinci. Movable Ink’s CEO, Vivek Sharma, explained the goal in an interview. “Think about what is the story I’m telling every single customer, so that it’s correlated with what imagery, with what creative. Think about the best time to deliver it so that they’re most likely to respond. What’s the right frequency of communication? What sales channel preference do they have? What tone should be used within the set brand voice, like whether there should be a sense of urgency or joy?”
This is a radically different approach to e-mail marketing than what’s predominated over the past decades. But AI is making it possible. Movable Ink is among a vanguard of companies enabling it, along with rivals such as Waxwing and OneSignal. Sharma explained that the company combines four types of AI to do it. First there is a vision model that uses deep learning to understand potential imagery and copy to use. Then generative AI writes copy based on customer preferences and past behavior. Third, a separate insights model gains that understanding, based on how creative is performing such as through driving people to new categories or higher levels of spend. Finally, the fourth element is a prediction model that deploys classic machine learning to hone the offerings. That classic approach is more observable and explainable than a neural network, which is important when significant money and customer relationships are at stake.
The results have been compelling. Massey says that it tested “AI-powered personalization against our ‘business as usual’ manual approach, measuring the impact to total e-mail performance, customer engagement, and to our internal operations workflow.” Based on that data, within a matter of weeks the company rolled out the technology to its total subscriber base and now includes AI personalization in nearly every campaign.
Massey claims the company has gone from “one version of an e-mail campaign on a given day to thousands, or even hundreds of thousands, of versions, with less setup time.”
Another company trying this approach is L.L.Bean, which is also a Movable Ink customer. Devon Phelan, L.L.Bean’s Senior Manager of Digital CRM Programs, says, “We were looking for a process and a toolset that enabled us to expose the right products to the right subscribers without the opportunity cost of exposing anything except our top-selling products.”
L.L.Bean says this personalization has been responsible for “$14 - $15 million in analyzed revenue last year.” Moreover, Phelan recounts, “This past Monday, we sent one campaign that had nearly 1.1 million unique content variations. That would have been inconceivable before.”
E-mail marketing may not be the first thing that consumers think of when they picture AI, but it may become a facet of AI that touches them on a very routine basis. Both Victoria’s Secret and L.L.Bean say that there’s no going back.

title: Council Post: How AI Is Upgrading Personalized Gifting For Business
text:
Archer Chiang, Founder/CEO at Giftpack.
Personalized gifting is immensely rewarding but often challenging due to the time and effort required. From selecting the right gift that resonates with the recipient to managing logistics, the process can be time-consuming and complex. In a corporate setting, these challenges become more pronounced, demanding efficiency and precision to ensure a meaningful impact.
This is where artificial intelligence (AI) can step in. AI's ability to analyze vast amounts of data and predict preferences makes it invaluable in creating a seamless and effective personalized gifting experience. By automating the selection and logistics of gifts, AI saves time and enhances the precision and personalization of each gift, ensuring recipients feel truly valued.
As a four-time startup founder since 2006 and an expert in corporate gifting and supply chain, I have witnessed firsthand how AI can streamline operations and boost success rates.
The Challenge Of Personalized Gifting
Personalized gifting is often perceived as tedious due to the time and effort required to select meaningful gifts for each recipient. Traditional gift selection processes involve manual research, extensive planning and coordination. These hurdles can lead to delays, increased costs and inconsistent satisfaction levels.
When done poorly, there can be a significant impact on employee or client satisfaction and engagement. Recipients may feel undervalued if they receive generic or inappropriate gifts, which can negatively affect morale and loyalty. Improving corporate gifting efficiency can significantly boost overall engagement and satisfaction.
How AI Transforms Personalized Gifting
The gift selection process has been transformed by leveraging data to make personalized choices more effective and efficient. By examining data points such as demographic details, cultural background, personal preferences, social media activity and purchase history (with the recipient’s consent), it’s possible to provide highly tailored gift recommendations. This approach not only streamlines the entire process but also ensures the gifts are meaningful and relevant to each individual.
Benefits Of Using AI In Corporate Gifting
• Efficiency: AI automates the time-consuming tasks of sorting through gift options and managing logistics. This reduces the workload on HR and administrative teams, allowing them to focus on more strategic initiatives.
• Personalization: By analyzing data such as social media activity, purchase history and personal preferences, AI ensures that each gift is tailored to the recipient's unique tastes and interests. This level of personalization enhances the emotional impact of the gift.
• Scalability: AI can handle large volumes of gifting tasks simultaneously, making it ideal for companies with a large number of employees or clients. This scalability ensures personalized gifting can be implemented across the organization without compromising quality.
Examples Of Successful AI Implementations In Gifting
Here are some ways we're seeing businesses, including clients of ours, leverage AI in gifting.
Employee Recognition Programs
A mid-sized tech company with 300 employees used an AI-driven solution to enhance its Employee Appreciation Day. The AI system gathered data from employees and recommended four gift options tailored to each individual's preferences. The result was a significant boost in morale and engagement.
Automated Year-Round Gifting
A large corporation with 4,000 employees utilized AI to manage its gifting program throughout the year. The AI system sent personalized gifts for company milestones, employee anniversaries and personal achievements. This continuous appreciation fostered a positive work culture and sustained high morale.
Customer Loyalty Programs
Businesses are also using AI to enhance customer loyalty by sending personalized gifts to loyal customers. By analyzing purchase history and preferences, companies can send gifts that resonate with their customers, strengthening brand loyalty and customer satisfaction.
Predictions For Future Trends In AI And Gifting
According to corporate gifting trends, AI’s role in corporate gifting is set to expand significantly. Predictions indicate AI will continue to enhance personalization, making it more efficient and precise. As AI technologies advance, they will increasingly leverage application programming interfaces (APIs) and microservices to create complex yet streamlined gifting solutions. These systems can analyze data such as customer behavior, inventory management and personalized marketing tools to provide tailored gifting experiences that align with individual preferences and cultural nuances.
Emerging Technologies And Innovations
Several emerging technologies are predicted to transform the corporate gifting landscape. Multimodal generative AI, which integrates text, speech and images, will allow for more contextually relevant and personalized interactions. This technology can analyze spoken requests, interpret financial documents and assess visual cues to provide more precise gift recommendations. Additionally, the increasing focus on AI safety and ethics will ensure responsible development and deployment of these technologies.
Potential Challenges (And How To Overcome Them)
Integrating AI into corporate gifting introduces several challenges, particularly around data privacy and ethical considerations. It’s crucial for companies to prioritize data security and ensure compliance with regulations like GDPR and SOC2 to protect recipient information. Additionally, incorporating AI systems into existing workflows can be daunting as these challenges require robust data management practices, continuous employee training and collaboration with AI experts to ensure effective implementation and operation.
AI technology revolutionizes personalized gifting by automating selection and logistics, ensuring tailored gifts that enhance their impact. Integrating AI into gifting strategies simplifies the process and boosts employee and client satisfaction, leading to improved engagement and productivity. Embracing these innovations helps businesses create more meaningful connections, ultimately driving success.

title: Council Post: From Chaos To Clarity: Preparing For GenAI's Patient Access Revolution
text:
Dr. Graham Gardner, Founder and CEO, Kyruus Health—a leading care access platform on a mission to connect people to the right care.
There’s a lot of excitement about what generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can do for healthcare. And for good reason—not only can AI help us more efficiently perform the myriad of administrative tasks required by the industry, but it also offers to help us translate the overwhelming amount of new knowledge produced every year into clinical practice much more quickly and effectively than ever before.
The healthcare industry, in general, and patient experiences, in particular, suffer from fragmentation across existing systems. GenAI-assisted patient engagements, clinical trial analyses and member personalization have all shown promising signs of reducing that friction and driving a much better experience.
That said, we, as an industry, are at the early stages of GenAI’s adoption curve. In fact, without significant improvements, the inaccessibility of raw data itself threatens to handicap what AI can deliver. GenAI needs data to learn and to return accurate results. This is especially true in a field like healthcare, where there are right and wrong decisions and where precision and specificity matter.
Today, too much of healthcare data isn’t accessible—instead siloed in different IT systems and saved in different formats. Data labels are not standardized, and despite years of progress, some important data elements are not even digitized. S,o while GenAI demonstrations can look magical, we can’t achieve the dream until we first organize our underlying data.
Thankfully, many organizations are beginning to understand this and have started assessing how well they are positioned from a data and infrastructure perspective to adopt new AI solutions. Technology investments in healthcare have long lagged behind other industries, so it is important to catalog how best to catch up. Across the board, organizations and solutions that are looking to rapidly innovate in this emerging space are taking the following steps.
1. Digitization Of Clinical Data And Workflows: Too much healthcare information today still exists on notes, clipboards and paper charts across the patient’s care journey. If GenAI is going to provide clinical workflow solutions, it will require data from medical records, office check-in procedures, insurance cards, symptom checkers and a multitude of other sources that are still often collected on paper today.
2. Interoperability Of Data Through Standardization And Simplification: We all know that healthcare data is siloed, restricted by access and permission limits or inaccessible altogether—e.g., the multicolored sticky notes that frame a physician practice manager’s computer screen, cut off from EHRs and clinical workflows. In addition, no single entity has all the data necessary to deliver both a high-quality patient experience and improve outcomes. Keeping privacy, trust and compliance as first principles, there remains a tremendous opportunity for the healthcare system of records to continue driving toward interoperability to provide synergetic value to patients, providers and payers.
3. Subject Matter Expertise To Build Secure And Scalable Solutions: The sophistication of large language models (LLMs) is growing at an exponential rate. However, in order to harness the real value and build the scalable, cost-effective and secure architecture that can be deployed at production scale, tech-enabled organizations will need to fund and support their workforce with expertise in data, analytics, machine learning, cloud computing and iterative development. Investments in human capital and skill set development are often overlooked, but an insufficiently trained workforce could stymie the ultimate performance of these solutions.
Done right, GenAI capabilities have tremendous potential to improve care access by optimizing appointment booking, minimizing wait times and maximizing resource utilization. These solutions and seamless integrations will hopefully one day ensure patients receive timely, personalized care while healthcare providers experience unparalleled efficiency, with actionable insights through data, enabling sophisticated care delivery. But in order to see that future, we must ensure that we structure, curate and share our data in a way that allows us to deliver on the promise.

title: Broadcom Cements VMware Cloud Foundation
text:
Tech firms love infrastructure. The ability to evidence a solid grasp of core infrastructure services is thought to validate a deep and expansive grasp of the lower layers of the “IT stack” and show completeness of vision. As a result, the marketing machines running the tech trade are fond of using the word “foundation” not to denote a charitable endeavor, but to express the positing of a given technology offering as a comprehensive base-layer substrate.
Microsoft famously did it with Microsoft Team Foundation Server (a product package now known as Microsoft Azure DevOps Server), a technology consisting of a set of collaborative cloud software development tools. Today we talk about artificial intelligence foundation models, an approach that AWS defines as that part of AI that is trained on massive datasets to provide large deep learning neural networks that have changed the way data scientists approach machine learning.
Then there is Broadcom and the VMware Cloud Foundation.
Come In Number 9
Again, not a registered charity, VMware Cloud Foundation (now in its version 9 iteration and known as VCF to its friends) is positioned as a unified and integrated private cloud platform that lowers cost and risk. Because cloud computing is still complicated as we have noted before, enterprises have a hard time managing all the tasks associated with the deployment, consumption and operation of a secure and cost-effective private cloud. The concept here hinges around the promise to tap into public cloud scale and agility (what the cloud evangelists call “elastic” computing and data services) with private cloud security, resilience and performance.
“To break infrastructure silos, reclaim control of public cloud sprawl and capture the opportunity for AI in the enterprise, our customers are shifting from best-of-breed siloed architectures to a modern private cloud platform,” said Krish Prasad, senior vice president and general manager, VCF division at Broadcom. “VMware Cloud Foundation 9 will redefine the landscape for private cloud by delivering a modern, integrated platform that will unify operations and automation to deliver a cloud experience that enables businesses to be more innovative, efficient, resilient and secure.”
Prasad and team point to a recent IDC Business Value study which suggested that users exposed to this technology are able to lower infrastructure costs and increase infrastructure and security team efficiencies i.e. while the cloud is still and always will be a very digital technical “thing”, business savings often come down to more accurate staff scheduling and payroll at the end of the day.
Why? Because IT teams can “spin up” cloud computing instances and bring new virtual machines to life faster and, in terms of crucial usability, when an IT system is achitected well (i.e. it’s not a clunky group of IT silos cobbled together) it delivers faster data storage performance and quite simply just works better. That’s what VMware is working on here.
VMware says Cloud Foundation 9 will deliver capabilities that enable an organization’s infrastructure to operate as a single unified and automated system, helping keep pace with modern app requirements. The technology has a self-service cloud portal for provisioning services and works with a single “management console” for operations and automation. New integrated workflows will simplify the transition between operations and automation tasks, while enhanced insights and analytics will enable more proactive management.
Complex Storage Topologies
Broadcom’s acquisition of VMware in November 2023 has created diverse opinions among the technology industry with predictable staff changes and product repositioning inevitably playing a central role in the consumption of VMware into the parent organization’s family. With some water now under the bridge, the integration of Broadcom and VMware technology results in capabilities to handle more complex storage topologies into existing VMware environments. A new memory tiering capability will enhance data-intensive applications, such as AI, databases and real-time analytics.
“AI workloads, especially those involving large datasets and complex models, demand rapid data retrieval and processing. Memory tiering using NVMe [nonvolatile memory express, a data storage access protocol for solid state drives] reduces latency and accelerates data throughput, which is crucial for training and inference tasks. Additionally, the cost-efficiency of tiering helps manage the high storage demands of AI applications, enabling scalable solutions that maintain performance without excessive expenses,” notes Broadcom, in a technical statement.
There is multi-tenancy, there is native networking-as-a-service experiences, there is the always-present inclusion of Nvidia chips for power, there is centralized security and compliance management and there is disaster recovery and certification too.
Easy-To-Consume Infrastructure
Put in the simplest terms, the concept behind VMware Cloud Foundation 9 is a technology service that exposes easy-to-consume infrastructure services that enable developers and application owners to deploy any application (virtual machine or containerized) without friction.
Over and above the huge list of features and functions in this foundational technology offering, there is that statement that this is easy-to-consume infrastructure that’s low fat (less cloud sprawl and so-called code bloat in the cloud management layer), high protein (extensive memory and processing power) and richly spiced (for complex storage topologies) for the cloud engineering dinner plate. As the Broadcom version of VMware now rises from the ashes of acquisition acrimony, it is good to see these developments happening in a tech brand that we’ve known now for a quarter century.

title: Cerebras Speeds AI By Putting Entire Foundation Model On Its Giant Chip
text:
AI is everywhere these days, and we’ve become accustomed to chatbots answering our questions like oracles or conjuring up magical images. Those responses are called inferences in the trade and the colossal computer programs from which they rain are housed in massive data centers referred to as ‘the cloud.’
Now, brace for a downpour.
Cerebras Systems, known for its revolutionary wafer-scale computer chip, big as a dinner plate, is about to unleash one of the top AI models—Meta’s open-source LLaMA 3.1—on its chip. Not beside it or above it or below it, but on it—a configuration that could blow away traditional inference.
What is more, Cerebras claims that its inference costs are one-third of those on Microsoft’s Azure cloud computing platform, while using one-sixth the power.
“With speeds that push the performance frontier and competitive pricing, Cerebras Inference is particularly compelling for developers of AI applications with real-time or high-volume requirements,” said Micah Hill-Smith, co-founder and CEO of Artificial Analysis Inc, which provides independent analysis of AI models.
Raindrops On The Water
This could create a ripple effect across the entire AI ecosystem. As inference becomes faster and more efficient, developers will be able to push the boundaries of what AI can do. Applications that were once bottlenecked by hardware limitations may now be able to flourish, leading to innovations that were previously thought impossible.
For example, in the realm of natural language processing, models could generate more accurate and coherent responses. This could revolutionize areas such as automated customer service, where understanding the full context of a conversation is crucial for providing helpful responses. Similarly, in fields like healthcare, AI models could process and analyze larger datasets more quickly, leading to faster diagnoses and more personalized treatment plans.
In the business world, the ability to run inference at unprecedented speeds opens new opportunities for real-time analytics and decision making. Companies could deploy AI systems that analyze market trends, customer behavior and operational data in real-time, allowing them to respond to changes in the market with agility and precision. This could lead to a new wave of AI-driven business strategies, where companies leverage real-time insights to gain a competitive edge.
But whether this will be a cloudburst, or a deluge remains to be seen.
As AI workloads move to inference and away from training operations, the need for more efficient processors becomes imperative. Many companies are working on this challenge.
“Wafer scale integration from Cerebras is a novel approach that eliminates some of the handicaps that generic GPUs have and shows much promise,” said Jack Gold, the founder of J. Gold Associates, a technology analyst firm. He cautions that Cerebras is still a startup in a room full of big players.
Inference As A Service
Cerebras’ AI inference service not only accelerates the pace of AI model execution but could also alter the way businesses think about deploying and interacting with AI in real-world applications.
In typical AI inference workflows, large language models such as Meta’s LLaMA or OpenAI’s GPT-4o are housed in data centers, where they are called upon by application programming interfaces (APIs) to generate responses to user queries. These models are enormous and require immense computational resources to operate efficiently. GPUs, the current workhorses of AI inference, are tasked with the heavy lifting, but they struggle under the weight of these models, particularly when it comes to moving data between the model’s memory and its compute cores.
But with Cerebras’ new inference service, all the layers of a model, currently the 8 billion parameter and 70 billion parameter versions of LLaMA 3.1, are stored right on the chip. When a prompt is sent to the model, the data can be processed almost instantaneously because it doesn’t have to travel long distances within the hardware.
The result? For example, while a state-of-the-art GPU might process about 260 tokens - pieces of data such as a word - per second for an 8-billion parameter LLaMA model, Cerebras claims it can handle 1,800 tokens per second. This level of performance, validated by Artificial Analysis, Inc., is unprecedented and sets a new standard for AI inference.
“Cerebras is delivering speeds an order of magnitude faster than GPU-based solutions for Meta’s Llama 3.1 8B and 70B AI models,” said Hill-Smith. “We are measuring speeds above 1,800 output tokens per second on Llama 3.1 8B, and above 446 output tokens per second on Llama 3.1 70B—a new record in these benchmarks.”
Cerebras is launching its inference service through an API, to its own cloud, but it is already talking to major cloud providers about deploying its model-loaded chips elsewhere. This opens a massive new market for the company, which has struggled to get users to adopt its chip, called a Wafer Scale Engine.
Breaking The Bottle
The speed of inference today is limited by bottlenecks in the network connecting GPUs to memory and storage. The electrical pathways connecting memory to cores can only carry a finite amount of data per unit of time. While electrons move rapidly in conductors, the actual data transfer rate is constrained by the frequency at which signals can be reliably sent and received, affected by signal degradation, electromagnetic interference, material properties and the length of wires over which the data must travel.
In traditional GPU setups, the model weights are stored in memory separate from the processing units. This separation means that during inference, there's a constant need to transfer large amounts of data between the memory and the compute cores through tiny wires. Nvidia and others have tried all sorts of configurations to minimize the distance that this data needs to travel—stacking memory vertically on top of the compute cores in a GPU package for example.
“10 times faster than anything else on the market”
Cerebras' new approach fundamentally changes this paradigm. Rather than etching transistor cores onto a silicon wafer and slicing it up into chips, Cerebras etches as many as 900,000 cores on a single wafer, eliminating the need for external wiring between separate chips. Each core on the WSE combines both computation (processing logic) and memory (static random access memory, or SRAM) to form a self-contained unit that can operate independently or in concert with other cores.
The model weights are distributed across these cores, with each core storing a portion of the total model. This means that no single core holds the entire model; instead, the model is split up and spread across the entire wafer.
"We actually load the model weights onto the wafer, so it's right there, next to the core," explains Andy Hock, Cerebras’ senior vice president of product and strategy.
This configuration allows for much faster data access and processing, as the system doesn't need to constantly shuttle data back and forth over relatively slow interfaces.
According to Cerebras, its architecture can deliver performance “10 times faster than anything else on the market” for inference on models like LLaMA 3.1, although this remains to be further validated. Importantly, Hock claims that due to the memory bandwidth limitations in GPU architectures, "there's actually no number of GPUs that you could stack up to be as fast as we are" for these inference tasks.
By optimizing for inference on large models, Cerebras is positioning itself to address a rapidly growing market need for fast, efficient AI inference capabilities.
Picking Nvidia’s Lock
One reason why Nvidia has had a virtual lock on the AI market is the dominance of Compute Unified Device Architecture, its parallel computing platform and programming system. CUDA provides a software layer that gives developers direct access to the GPU's virtual instruction set and parallel computational elements.
For years, Nvidia’s CUDA programming environment has been the de facto standard for AI development, with a vast ecosystem of tools and libraries built around it. This has created a situation where developers are often locked into the GPU ecosystem, even if alternative hardware solutions could offer better performance.
Cerebras' WSE is a fundamentally different architecture from traditional GPUs, requiring software to be adapted or rewritten to take full advantage of its capabilities. Developers and researchers need to learn new tools and potentially new programming paradigms to work with the WSE effectively.
Cerebras has tried to address this by supporting high-level frameworks like PyTorch, making it easier for developers to use its WSE without learning a new low-level programming model. It has also developed its own software development kit to allow for lower-level programming, potentially offering an alternative to CUDA for certain applications.
But by offering an inference service that is not only faster but also easier to use—developers can interact with it via a simple API, much like they would with any other cloud-based service—Cerebras is making it possible for organizations just entering the fray to bypass the complexities of CUDA and still achieve top-tier performance.
This is in line with an industry shift to open standards, where developers are free to choose the best tool for the job, rather than being constrained by the limitations of their existing infrastructure.
It’s All About Context
The implications of Cerebras’ breakthrough, if its claims are borne out and it can ramp up production, are profound. First and foremost, consumers will benefit from significantly faster responses. Whether it’s a chatbot answering customer inquiries, a search engine retrieving information, or an AI-powered assistant generating content, the reduction in latency will lead to a smoother, more instantaneous user experience.
But the benefits could extend far beyond just faster responses. One of the biggest challenges in AI today is the so-called “context window”—the amount of text or data that a model can consider at once when generating an inference. Inference processes that require a large context, such as summarizing lengthy documents or analyzing complex datasets.
Larger context windows require more model parameters to be actively accessed, increasing memory bandwidth demands. As the model processes each token in the context, it needs to quickly retrieve and manipulate relevant parameters stored in memory.
In high-inference applications with many simultaneous users, the system needs to handle multiple inference requests concurrently. This multiplies the memory bandwidth requirements, as each user's request needs access to the model weights and intermediate computations.
Even the most advanced GPUs like Nvidia's H100 can move only around 3 terabytes of data per second between the high bandwidth memory and the compute cores. That's far below the 140 terabytes per second needed to efficiently run a large language model at high throughput without encountering significant bottlenecks.
"Our effective bandwidth between memory and compute isn't just 140 terabytes, it's 21 petabytes per second," Hock claims.
Of course, it’s hard to judge a company statement without industry benchmarks, and independent testing will be key to confirming this performance.
By eliminating the memory bottleneck, Cerebras’ system can handle much larger context windows and increase token throughput. If the performance claims hold true, this could be a game-changer for applications that require the analysis of extensive information, such as legal document review, medical research or large-scale data analytics. With the ability to process more data in less time, these applications can operate more effectively.
More Models To Come
Hock said that the company will soon offer the larger LLaMA 405 billion parameter model on its WSE, followed by Mistral’s models and Cohere's Command-R model. Companies with proprietary models (hello, OpenAI) can approach Cerebras to load their models onto the chips as well.
Moreover, the fact that Cerebras’ solution is delivered as an API-based service means that it can be easily integrated into existing workflows. Organizations that have already invested in AI development can simply switch to Cerebras’ service without having to overhaul their entire infrastructure. This ease of adoption, if paired with the promised performance gains, could make Cerebras a formidable competitor in the AI market.
“But until we have more concrete real-world benchmarks and operations at scale,” cautioned analyst Gold, “it’s premature to estimate just how superior it will be.”

title: Ready Or Not, IT Automation Is Going Through Some Big Changes
text:
IT automation is a challenging product category to evaluate. For instance, for every big technology vendor that has a suite of tools, there are multiple massively popular point solutions that do their task remarkably well. This high degree of fragmentation often means that end users select solutions based on cross-product integration as much as functionality or cost.
This approach often works, because enterprises typically like the ability to assemble their own bespoke tooling stacks. That said, a best-of-breed approach, whether integrated or not, does raise its own challenges. For instance, when a problem arises, different interpretations of the issue coming from different automation tools can lead to slower diagnosis—and, in the worst case, ignite the blame game between teams.
But in the bigger picture, the whole category is changing as vendor consolidation and AI integration begin to alter the IT automation landscape. I predict that the IT automation market will look quite different two years from now—and I believe that’s a good thing for enterprise customers.
The Downsides Of The Status Quo In IT Automation
Let’s start with the challenges that IT automation has had to face:
- Multiple versions of the truth — Automation tools are often targeted at a specific IT role such as DevOps or a specific layer of the stack such as containers. So, we often see a DevOps person using one toolset and an SRE using something else. This can create challenges when a crisis arises. A single event can kick off multiple alarms that may trigger an uncoordinated response. Additionally, it can be a challenge for teams to develop the right path to achieve issue resolution because of different interpretations of the problem. So while you may be getting great visibility and analytics, you may not be getting great diagnosis and remediation.
- Event-driven approaches — IT automation tools are often event-driven. Events can be something routine like initiating a software update, or ad hoc, such as rebooting a hung server when a specific trigger is tripped. These types of robotic actions can be very helpful in enabling IT resources to better scale their efforts. However, this approach can also present the issue of programmability versus exception handling. Developing event-driven workflows can be hard to program in heterogeneous environments, given the number of exceptions that can be generated. Also, it’s a challenge to create enough workflows to handle all of the different possibilities. And none of these things are great for black-swan events such as the recent Crowdstrike BSOD incident.
- Tech-centricity versus business-centricity — IT automation tools historically have come from the perspective of reducing IT costs by increasing the capacity of existing IT resources. And while that has indeed happened, there are other aspects of operating IT such as forecasting capacity, optimizing cloud deployments and enforcing business compliance rules that are not automated. We are starting to see IT automation vendors take some of these elements into account. Some of the more visionary vendors are actually leveraging ideas from supply chain management to provide a more holistic and business-driven approach to IT. (More on that in a minute.) But there is a long way to go on this.
The Upsides Of The New Wave Of IT Automation
As I touched on earlier, there are many changes reshaping the IT automation market, and I believe they will end up being for the best over the next couple of years. Here are some of the positive trends driving a behind-the-scenes revolution in how enterprises will manage almost every aspect of delivering IT services in the years to come.
- Market consolidation — Large tech vendors have been making big moves in the IT automation space. For example, while many think about Broadcom’s acquisition of VMware as a virtualization play, VMware’s IT automation stack was also quite robust and was able to manage a lot more than VMs for a long time, so the IT automation aspect of that deal should not be overlooked. Meanwhile, IBM has spent the last few years building an IT automation stack based upon organic development for solutions such as IBM Concert as well as multiple acquisitions including Apptio, Turbonomic, Instana and now HashiCorp. These big vendors are all intent on providing a more unified and coordinated approach to IT automation. And it’s not just the big players: we are also seeing smaller companies in the space adding assets via acquisition to improve their stance in security or AI.
- AI and observability — Like most technologies, IT automation is going to get a big boost from AI. In the case of IT automation, that boost comes from both machine learning and generative AI. Machine learning will greatly enhance observability and create predictive patterns to set triggers and automatically create the right workflows. Also, we are seeing GenAI used to help relay suggestions to IT for resolving issues as they happen. But what is most important is that the underlying data models driving the AI will also help unify the disparate silos of information across enterprises. Take Dynatrace: while it’s a good example of a company that has touted the effectiveness of a single IT automation platform for years, it has also introduced its own AI solution to enhance how it predicts issues and builds workflows to mitigate them. Long term, you will also see AI used more actively in the optimization of the application. For example, there may be a performance advantage in changing to a different storage model or database. A well-trained AI may keep an eye on an enterprise's approved vendors to find the most effective technology—and even the best business deal—as the market changes.
- A supply-chain-based mentality — IT automation’s evolution is starting to resemble how companies have evolved to manage physical supply chains. One of the biggest similarities is that supply chain management is no longer an isolated function but a cross-functional team effort. When a new application is planned, it’s not just the technology requirements that are important for selecting components and services; business factors such as supportability and budgeting also need to come to the fore. And given the highly distributed nature of application services and infrastructure, regular reviews are mandatory, not just from an operational viewpoint but also from the standpoints of human capacity, costing and compliance. Many smart IT operations are following these practices now, but the tooling has not always caught up. Two companies that are really starting to dig into this supply-chain concept are IBM and JFrog. While their products are targeted at individual practitioners, each product portfolio works holistically to address the end-to-end application lifecycle. These solutions are a good analogue to how physical supply chains work in the real world.
Further Evolution Required
The big question remains whether all of this change will actually live up to the potential. I believe it will, but there are a couple of caveats that need to be addressed. First, the ROI model will need to evolve. These solutions can become expensive, and if the value proposition is simply IT cost reduction, it may not be enough. Other considerations such as the time to deliver a compliance audit or the value of higher-quality software—in other words, the delivery of business outcomes—will need to be considered.
Complexity and overlap must also be addressed. Larger vendors have quickly updated their IT automation stacks via acquisition, so there will need to be some refactoring efforts. Also, third-party integrations will still be necessary. As I said at the beginning of this piece, there are some tools out there that are best-of-breed for what they do, and customers using them will likely be reluctant to move away from them. Future winners in this market will need to be able to showcase both innovation and integration.
That said, the potential for more holistic, predictable and automated IT operations has not been this high since the pre-cloud days of large monolithic systems management suites. This is good news.
