title: Council Post: The Perils Of Generic Generative AI: Why Customization Is Key In IT Operations
text:
Assaf Resnick is the Founder and CEO of BigPanda, an automated AIOps platform empowering the teams that keep the digital world running.
Generative AI (GenAI) has sparked both excitement and skepticism in the world of IT operations. A few questions emerge as enterprises look to integrate AI into their operations. For instance:
• How will GenAI impact my business?
• Will it improve observability and speed incident management?
• Do I need pristine data to take advantage of GenAI?
• What are the risks?
There's a misconception today that to get started with AIOps or GenAI in IT, you must have pristine data. We at BigPanda believe it's the purpose of an AIOps platform to expect that there will be gaps, that there's no such thing as a “golden” configuration management database (CMDB) and to provide an AI-driven experience that creates and identifies good data versus garbage. Still, IT teams face the daunting task of wrangling inconsistent and disparate data sources. Good data is central to successful machine learning processes.
It seems like every tool in IT lately has been adding a GenAI co-pilot capability. However, it's become apparent that the accuracy and usability of these features have suffered. Without the ability to pragmatically explain, train and affect the role the co-pilot is performing, these generic GenAI experiences are often shelved.
Every step of the AI development process should focus on data quality, explainability and accuracy. Generic AI models run the risk of "hallucinating" and producing inaccurate or irrelevant insights. Instead of streamlining processes, you increase IT staff workload, decrease trust in the system and elevate risk. For example, suppose a generic AI model provided inaccurate information about an outage or error. In that case, IT staff may deploy an ineffective resolution that could increase downtime, harmful outages and customer frustration—and the model would never be trusted again for advice.
It’s vital to build trust and foster collaboration between AI-driven systems and human operators. AI can help you make informed decisions that align with business objectives and empower your team—if it has access to your data. You want your AI to function as an embedded employee who knows your company and its data as well as you do. You invest a lot of time onboarding an employee for one purpose: to instill a sense of culture and accountability. Would you allow a consultant with no idea of what your organization does to give unchecked advice to your employees? This is why generic GenAI could be dangerous if left unchecked.
It’s essential to avoid deploying AI solutions in a vacuum, siloed from the organizational data and operational workflows. Instead, take a holistic approach that accounts for your company's unique challenges, tools and approach to IT operations.
In the early stages of developing large language model (LLM)-based AI, we questioned the accuracy of our inferences from the training dataset. Our AI typically produced correct results, but its accuracy was suspect, as it relied on broad, generalized information from the internet. The breakthrough came when we partnered with customers to allow our AI to work alongside their workforce in production. You simply can't develop AI in siloes from synthetic information. Instead, our collaboration with customers produces relevant, accurate insights into common ITOps challenges.
It’s no secret the key to explainability and accuracy when utilizing GenAI is controlling the data. The recommended approach is to utilize retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). The latest AI “it” word, RAG is crucial for ensuring your LLM presents accurate information. RAG allows you to train multiple datasets and models to override the parent LLM model to avoid using external information for a question that could only be answered with your unique data.
If you want your AI to know art, feed it art data. The same goes for ITOps. When training AI for incident resolution, using your own incident-specific data and process helps ensure that the outputs are accurate and actionable. RAG is an effective way to prevent AI from making inferences outside the scope of what you’re trying to do. This blend of foundational knowledge gained from external sources combined with internal processes, data and insights is what makes GenAI so powerful. For example, you wouldn’t train the model on how to write a script to restart a service—it’s seen this in vendor and online documentation thousands of times. You would, however, want to train it on your application names, purposes and deployment topology to answer the question based on your unique environment.
GenAI has already become an integral part of IT operations, empowering teams to navigate complex challenges confidently. By embracing high-quality, data-driven decision-making and fostering collaboration between people and AI, your IT teams can unlock new levels of efficiency and innovation for your organization.

title: Council Post: Who Is A Data Scientist: GenAI's Impact On The AI Workforce
text:
Ambica Rajagopal, Group Chief Data and AI Officer @ Michelin. Global expert on AI and Data Transformation.
Since November 2022, it has become obvious that generative AI is going to impact most knowledge worker roles. An unexpected outcome was the disruption that GenAI has brought to the role of data scientists themselves.
Data scientists' niche role in developing AI applications has always been highly specialized, requiring a combination of mathematics, statistics, machine learning and software development. With generative AI making the technology highly accessible, millions of people worldwide are now incorporating AI into their work, without the help of data scientists.
The evolution we will see in the AI workforce is twofold: (1) The role of data scientists will evolve to focus on expertise and responsible AI, and (2) citizen data scientists will lead a widespread AI adoption.
Evolving Role Of Data Scientists
A telling line is from a 2024 key trend identified by MIT professor Thomas Davenport and thought leader Randy Bean: "Data scientists, who have been called 'unicorns' and the holders of the 'sexiest job of the 21st century' because of their ability to make all aspects of data science projects successful, have seen their star power recede."
For a data scientist, who has spent years training natural language processing models to do sentiment detection and topic classification, it can be quite disconcerting to see LLMs perform the same tasks with minimal extra effort or training.
The question raised is: "Post-LLMs, what is the role of expertise in AI?"
In this moving landscape of AI, leaders of data science teams need to contextualize these changes and evolutions to inspire data scientists to leverage the rapid evolution in AI to further develop their roles and expertise. Here are a few ways to do this.
1. Leveraging LLMs For Increased Accuracy
With LLMs, in areas of vision and natural language processing, data scientists now have advanced capabilities in image recognition, image classification, sentiment classification and topic detection available from LLMs like GPT-4, Claude and Mistral. These out-of-the-box capabilities allow task-specific models to benefit from the wider context in which the LLMs are trained.
Data scientists can use methods like RAG and few/zero-shot learning to train foundational LLMs for specific tasks. This can be quite successful—building an employee-facing application that leverages a foundational LLM like GPT-4 to provide question-and-answer capabilities specific to a company's HR policies is more efficient and accurate than traditional methods.
However, this approach might fail in the aspects where very high precision is required. It is central to the role of data scientists to experiment and test the accuracy of various such approaches to choose the right one for the use case.
2. Ambassadors Of Responsible AI
The capabilities of generative AI, the widespread use of AI and legislation like the EU AI Act have made ethical concerns around AI a central topic for all users and developers of AI. Identifying and addressing issues of bias, transparency and accountability often require deep technical knowledge.
Data scientists need to be ambassadors of the responsible AI approach to citizen data scientists and knowledge workers. The democratization of AI places a greater burden on the experts of the technology to advocate and facilitate its responsible usage. For example, data scientists can develop tools like identification of model bias or model drift that can be utilized by citizen data scientists.
The use of LLMs has brought to the forefront the trade-off between interpretability and accuracy—the more complex the system being modeled at high accuracy, the less interpretable the model becomes. Data scientists need to educate themselves and contribute to research on local and global interpretability techniques.
Rise Of Citizen Data Scientists
Millions around the world are now using LLMs for individual productivity tasks, while others are moving toward building AI applications with LLMs. Many of these "citizen data scientists" come to this field with little formal education in the field of AI, unlike their data scientist colleagues. Yet they are finding remarkable results and leading the global AI adoption wave. The transformation that AI will bring to the nature of our work is being created and molded by these citizen data scientists.
Think of accountants 100 years ago: The epitome of excellence in the field of accounting was the ability to do arithmetic accurately. Then, we as humans automated this facility (through calculators and Excel), which has led to the field of accounting becoming more sophisticated, with accountants focused on conceptual understanding/insights versus computation.
This same process has occurred many times in human working history. Citizen data scientists will lead a similar transformation of roles and jobs in all fields through AI and GenAI.
According to the International Labour Organization's 2024 report "Generative AI and Jobs," "The social and economic impacts of Generative AI will largely depend on the management of its integration. It [the report] highlights the necessity of policies that facilitate a fair and consultative transition, emphasizing the importance of workers' input, skills training, and adequate social protection."
Here are a couple of ways enterprises can help their workforce participate and grow with the AI revolution.
1. Internalizing GenAI
Enterprises need to take into account the natural reticence of individuals to explore unknown areas—and therefore make it very easy and secure for their employees to explore generative AI capabilities. Workers need to be empowered with training to leverage these tools to innovate in their day-to-day roles.
2. Data Scientists As Mentors
As the onboarding of knowledge workers to AI is about thinking about tasks in a new way, having access to a "guru" to show the way can help. Enterprises can consider setting up avenues for their emerging citizen data scientists to interact with expert data scientists. A few avenues could be training sessions, hands-on interactions with tools and proposing and working side by side on use cases.
Building Empowered Workforces
GenAI is evolving the way we all work. Thoughtful interventions and structured empowerment of various roles will result in a net positive outcome from this new wave of technology. Enterprises are in the driver's seat to direct this change.

title: Council Post: Why The SEC's Four-Day Disclosure Rule Raises The Bar For Security
text:
Kevin Pierce is VikingCloud’s CPO. During his 30 years in the technology space he has designed and built several scalable cloud systems.
Seventy-four percent of cybersecurity leaders are confident in their ability to detect and respond to cyberattacks in real time, according to new research. Confidence rises the closer you get to the corner office when comparing C-suite leaders (81%) to front-line managers (66%). Yet 68% also say their company could not meet the Security and Exchange Commission's (SEC) four-day disclosure deadline.
Whether poor incident response stems from a lack of technology, resources or talent, it should have leaders questioning their confidence. And although the SEC’s rule adds pressure to already-strained cyber teams, it spurs the action needed to drive a more robust cybersecurity program.
Many leaders are turning to artificial intelligence (AI) to mitigate cyber risk, enable swift reporting and build a more realistic level of confidence.
What The SEC's Ruling Means For Security Teams
Security leaders today must comply with evolving regulations, including the SEC’s new final rule, requiring public companies to disclose material cybersecurity incidents within four days, or 30 days for financial institutions with disclosures involving customer information.
Failure to properly disclose can result in serious penalties. The SEC charged the chief information security officer (CISO) of SolarWinds for allegedly "understating or failing to disclose known risks." The former CISO of Uber was convicted on charges that he tried to cover up a hack in 2016.
But these regulations aren’t just a forcing mechanism. They set a new standard in the industry around fast reporting. Customers, stakeholders, partners and the government now expect all companies to quickly disclose any incidents or data breaches—especially those with compromised customer data. Fast reporting will become a best practice that sets a company apart, demonstrating a robust and efficient security program. However, organizations are struggling to do just that.
Why Cyber Teams Struggle With Quick Disclosure
Despite the SEC's mandate, many companies can’t meet the four-day disclosure deadline. Fifty-two percent of companies don’t have a formal incident response plan in place, and 58% of those that do only conduct drills quarterly or annually, creating severe delays when minutes matter.
Additionally, for 63% of companies, false positives take up four or more hours per week, causing 33% to be late in responding to a cyberattack. This problem is further compounded by the talent shortage. Four million security professionals are needed worldwide, making it difficult for teams to thoroughly respond to every incident.
Even if a threat is identified, 40% of cyber teams are staying silent out of fear of losing their jobs. Thirteen percent of C-Suite respondents have personally or had someone on their team intentionally not report a cyber incident. For managers, that number balloons to 58%. Those with a more direct connection to a cyber incident are far more likely to hide the impacts, potentially leading to cascading effects.
It’s borderline impossible for humans to predict and prevent—or respond to—all cyber risks, but a healthy business needs always-on protection. With a combination of strategy, technology and culture, security teams can respond faster.
Five Ways Security Teams Can Speed Up Detection, Response And Reporting
Cyberattacks are rising; there were 3,205 compromises in 2023 with over 353 million victims, a 72% increase from 2021. Here’s how security teams can be more proactive in responding to inevitable breaches while ensuring resilience, compliance and overall excellence.
1. Create an incident response plan—and practice often.
Develop an incident response playbook of who's taking what action when, and practice it through monthly tabletop exercises.
Regular penetration testing can identify unknown entry points and vulnerabilities so teams can strengthen their responses before a real attack happens.
2. Use generative AI to enhance monitoring, response and more.
Generative AI (GenAI) can monitor the attack surface for threats, automate tasks to free teams up for incident response and scan for vulnerabilities so weaknesses can be patched before they're exploited.
In fact, 24% of security leaders said GenAI has the potential to create more efficient incident response plans.
3. Let regulations guide your cybersecurity growth.
Organizations must be aware of and comply with the regulatory landscape in which they function. Yet simply meeting that requirement doesn’t guarantee security. Start with compliance as a baseline, then build security practices and strategies on top of it. Companies can use these widespread regulations to guide their security programs to the cutting edge of protection and industry demand.
4. Create a culture of transparency.
Encourage team members to communicate about incidents or vulnerabilities they see without fear of penalty or punishment.
Then, assess any skills or technology gaps that may result in less-than-optimal security coverage and provide your team with training and tools to help them perform more confidently—like using AI to reduce alert fatigue.
Additionally, create a culture of security across the organization to increase awareness around good security habits.
5. Partner with a managed security service provider
Managed security service providers (MSSPs) can augment the staff of organizations that are having difficulty hiring cyber workers. MSSPs have the industry knowledge, tools and workforce to help internal teams develop robust incident response plans and speed up cyberattack response and remediation.
Preparing For The Future Of Cyber Response Today
The SEC’s rulings, and ever evolving requirements, are raising the bar for security teams. While data shows only 32% of companies could meet the SEC’s 4-day cyber incident reporting requirement, with the new 30-day reporting requirement for financial institutions, potential compliance skyrockets to 93%. This may reflect the challenges security teams face around faster incident response, which will continue to be an important metric for regulators.
As the regulatory landscape shifts, shoring up your incident response plans, adopting AI in your security practices and creating a culture where everyone contributes to better security is essential.
Cyber regulations will only get more stringent. Align your internal plans and strategies to meet these requirements as a baseline, then build your security program upon them so that when there’s an incident, you will quickly respond.

title: The Best Questions To Ask ChatGPT When Building Your Personal Brand
text:
Building your personal brand requires moving through a sequential, three-step process. The first step, Know, focuses on brand discovery, uncovering your unique promise of value. Once you’ve defined your brand, you can articulate your story in the Show phase. Then, you can expand your brand's visibility and connections in the third step, called Grow. Leveraging the power of AI in all three steps can transform your personal branding efforts. The key lies in knowing which AI prompts to use so you can glean the most meaningful and actionable insights.
Using AI ensures that every step of your personal branding journey is informed by data-driven decisions, maximizing your potential for success. Before beginning, gather the content about yourself that you can share with ChatGPT. Then, use these prompts:
Know: Personal Brand Discovery
What are my unique strengths and how can they benefit others?
Starting with this prompt allows AI to help you identify and articulate your core strengths. AI tools can analyze your professional experiences, skills, and feedback from colleagues to provide a clear picture of your unique capabilities. By understanding how these strengths benefit others, you can craft a narrative that positions you as an invaluable asset in your field.
What do others think are my greatest strengths and differentiation using this feedback (paste in content from your LinkedIn recommendations, performance reviews, testimonials, 360 assessments, etc.)?
Your brand is held in the hearts and minds of those who know you. To validate your self-perceptions, make sense of the feedback you have received over time. There is likely too much data for you to synthesize yourself. That’s where the power of AI can help.
Show: Telling Your Brand Story
How can I effectively communicate my personal brand story?
Your personal brand story is the backbone of your brand identity. This prompt helps AI generate a cohesive and compelling narrative by pulling together key elements of your career journey, personal values, and professional milestones. A well-crafted brand story not only humanizes your brand but also resonates deeply with your audience, making your message more memorable and impactful.
What personal anecdotes and experiences should I highlight to build trust and authenticity?
Authenticity is the cornerstone of a strong personal brand. This prompt helps AI sift through your professional journey to find personal anecdotes and experiences that highlight your authenticity. Sharing these stories can build trust with your audience, making your brand relatable and trustworthy. AI can help identify the most impactful stories and suggest ways to present them compellingly.
Grow: Expanding Your Brand
What are the best practices for networking and relationship-building in my industry?
Networking is essential to career success and a critical component of personal branding. Use this prompt to get AI-driven advice on best practices for networking and relationship-building specific to your industry. ChatGPT can offer tips on where to connect with industry leaders, how to approach networking events, and ways to maintain meaningful professional relationships.
What are the most relevant keywords and phrases to include in my professional profiles?
SEO isn’t just for websites. It’s crucial for personal branding as well. By asking ChatGPT to identify the most relevant keywords and phrases, you can optimize your LinkedIn profile, resume, and personal website to ensure you appear in search results for your desired roles and industries. This prompt helps you stay current with industry trends and ensures your profiles are aligned with what your stakeholders are looking for.
How can I enhance my online presence and engagement?
In today’s digital-first environment, your online presence is often the first impression you make. Use this prompt to get AI-generated strategies for enhancing your visibility and engagement on social media platforms. GhatGPT can provide tailored recommendations on content types, posting frequencies, and engagement techniques that will help you build a rich and interactive online presence.
What are the potential gaps in my current personal branding strategy?
Use this prompt to have AI analyze your existing branding efforts and identify any gaps or areas for improvement. Whether it’s inconsistencies in your messaging, a lack of engagement, or missing elements in your brand story, AI can provide actionable insights to help you refine and enhance your strategy.
How can I leverage multimedia to strengthen my personal brand?
Incorporating multimedia elements like videos, podcasts, and infographics can significantly enhance your brand’s appeal. This prompt guides AI to suggest the best multimedia formats for your brand and how to effectively use them. By diversifying your content, you can reach a broader audience and keep your brand fresh and engaging.
Leveraging AI in personal branding isn’t about replacing your unique human touch, it’s about enhancing it. These AI prompts can help you uncover insights, optimize your strategies, and ensure your personal brand stands out in a crowded marketplace. The essence of personal branding lies in authenticity, relevance, consistency, and continuous improvement. By embracing these AI tools, you can elevate your personal branding efforts and achieve greater professional success.

title: Council Post: How AI Could Change Development
text:
Luke Wallace is VP of Engineering at Bottle Rocket, building great teams to help our clients deliver their digital products.
Intellisense was the Microsoft version that I first used extensively, but similar tools have existed since the 1990s. Intellisense allowed developers to get in-line assistance as they were typing code, akin to the autocomplete tools that people first used on mobile devices. It greatly accelerated development by suggesting functions, methods and variable names that you were likely to need. Developers stopped having to memorize exact names for things and only needed to remember how something started. It also became an easy way to see available options, with pop-up documentation snippets that helped developers learn about new options.
I believe AI tools will have analogous benefits to the code completion tools of the past, but at a 10-times or 100-times impact. Instead of autocompleting a variable name, the tools can autocomplete an entire line of code. Instead of showing you what functions are available, it will suggest the block of code based on your desired functionality. Pseudocode will be enough for the tools to write the code needed, and it will be based on the code it already sees in the project.
Junior developers can learn to explain their problems better.
Going from an academic setting into a more structured environment always results in huge amounts of technical growth. Having teams that rely on you for results, and with tasks you didn’t imagine on deadlines you didn’t always dictate, creates a sink-or-swim mentality that I have seen people succeed in time and time again.
The challenge with current AI coding tools is that they still require a lot of context to be useful, and this will likely be the case for quite a while. The better the prompts, and the more thorough the context, the better the results I’ve seen. For junior engineers joining existing teams, this means the tools can be given the context of the current project, so even a mediocre prompt will probably return decent results. But a fundamental understanding of architecture, data types and structures and design patterns will still be beneficial. Being able to use the right language in creating a prompt will result in higher quality results faster.
Great developers could get even better.
Developers who have more experience will likely benefit even more from AI tools than junior devs. Much like being able to use Intellisense-like tools even faster once they know the framework they’re working in, they will be able to give more specific prompts about their needs, even generating large blocks of functionality that can be quickly tweaked when analyzed. A few more minutes explaining the need will result in results practically equivalent to a senior developer in a fraction of the time.
As the tools mature and become more integrated into their workflow, I can imagine senior developers treating their AI tool as a pair programmer, asking it to code simple blocks and only making minor suggestions. Over time, and as a project grows, the AI tools will have more context and be able to take on larger tasks with more sophisticated prompts. And with newer tools being able to translate UI into code given some guidelines and guardrails, a senior engineer could spend their time mostly editing AI code instead of writing it new from scratch.
All developers may go up in value due to these changes.
With the advancement of AI tools, I think teams will be able to do much more in the same amount of time. Some companies will think about this in a cost-saving way and reduce the number of engineers they need, but the more forward-thinking ones will see this as a way to improve velocity and code quality. Even non-developers may be able to jump into code more confidently and make edits where needed, using AI assistants to guide them on how to make changes. I think this makes all developers more valuable, able to get more done in less time and providing value that must be rewarded by companies.
The future of AI-assisted development is bright, and it should not be seen as a threat to engineers but as a benefit that could transform the speed and quality at which we’re able to innovate and produce new ideas across every industry.

title: Council Post: Small Businesses Must Bolster Cybersecurity With Actionable AI
text:
Dor Eisner is the CEO & Co-Founder of Guardz, the company creating a safer digital world for SMBs.
AI is certainly a boon for business productivity.
Unfortunately, it is also being weaponized on the digital battlefield as hackers leverage AI to bypass preventative security mechanisms and outmaneuver humans. Close to half (43%) of all cyberattacks are already directed at SMBs—organizations often without the means to thwart or recover from such security breaches.
But here is where it’s best to fight fire with fire: Although AI is being used offensively by hackers, it has also bolstered cybersecurity thanks to its unparalleled threat detection, predictive analytics and automated incident response mechanisms.
Often tasked with managing SMBs’ IT and cybersecurity needs, MSPs (managed service providers) must adopt actionable, AI-powered security approaches to beat hackers at their own game. Not only will it bolster their ability to safeguard clients against attacks, but it will also empower them to scale their services.
Offensive AI: Hacker Strategies
One way hackers exploit AI is with customizable Attack as a Service (AaaS) tools—their malicious take on SaaS products that increasingly utilize highly sophisticated AI-driven capabilities. Our company, Guardz, has identified numerous new AaaS tools on the dark web in the past year, including advanced hVNC and info-stealing malware designed to infiltrate macOS devices.
Threats like these have recently spiked, with 85% of security professionals saying that the use of generative AI was used to bolster such attacks. After all, large language models can help create convincing phishing campaigns and fake websites tailored to any target and realistically impersonating various organizations, whether a bank, utility company, internet service provider, or tech giant.
Threat actors also take advantage of data leakage, an indirect risk of GenAI (generative AI) that many users aren’t even aware of. More than half of all U.S. employees have already incorporated external GenAI services into their workflow, unaware that sensitive financial data or personally identifiable information may be inadvertently leaked to such services. In the wrong hands, this data can be used to extort individuals and vulnerable businesses, especially SMBs.
Defensive AI: The Role MSPs Play
As they say, the best offense is a good defense: Companies that shy away from AI for defensive purposes undermine their own cybersecurity posture.
Not only can AI be used to run phishing and various breach simulations for employee training, but GenAI in particular can help pinpoint and neutralize threats and anomalies in real time that analysts might otherwise miss. GenAI helps security tools accurately assess threats and prioritize the most critical remediations, helping alleviate burnout among security personnel and lower the financial cost required to facilitate remediation.
AI technology grants MSPs a twofold advantage: For one, it enables them to continuously monitor potential attack surfaces and reduce the time it takes to detect and respond to incidents; second, it allows them to efficiently manage all their clients’ security needs at once, a critical advantage given that MSPs often serve hundreds of clients. MSPs that integrate GenAI can streamline and scale their services, expediting notoriously labor-intensive tasks like quoting cyber insurance, completing compliance reports, and assessing risk.
By leveraging predictive models and GenAI, MSPs can be better equipped to provide SMBs with enterprise-quality cybersecurity, while benefiting from enhanced and streamlined cybersecurity management themselves.
Where AI Meets Ethics
AI adoption is not a cure-all for business or security needs, and it comes with its own set of concerns that must be considered. One primary issue is the ongoing tug of war between privacy and security. Indeed, while AI can capture and monitor large swaths of data, it can also sweep up private user data and activity while monitoring network activity.
Other issues arise around algorithmic biases, which can inadvertently be introduced into an AI algorithm depending on the way it was trained or the type of data it was trained on. This could mean over-favoring detection of a less dire threat, while underestimating the extent or potential danger of another, for example.
AI can also create an accountability issue—if AI-powered systems are making decisions on their own, they can make mistakes that seemingly no one is responsible for, or that no one understands enough to solve, especially if deep learning is involved.
Without accommodating these concerns, MSPs hoping to leverage AI to handle the cybersecurity needs of SMBs will be no better off than without it and may end up putting their clients at even greater risk.
AI Versus AI
AI has ushered in a new wave of cyber-warfare. And while the technology has empowered malicious actors with new ways of circumventing firewalls and stealing sensitive data, it is simultaneously the key to nullifying those very same attacks.
SMBs must adopt AI-powered cybersecurity solutions that thwart even the subtlest AI trickery—or outsource to an MSP that does.
Sometimes, all it takes is giving your adversaries a taste of their own medicine.

title: How Nvidia Stock Could Jump 2.5x To Reach $300
text:
Could Nvidia stock reach $300 in the next few years? Does this sound ridiculous? Consider this, less than nine months ago, at the end of December 2023, Nvidia stock was trading at around $50 levels. This year the stock has grown over 2.5x and trades at close to $128 presently. Nvidia stock trades at about 75x trailing earnings. Is this pricey? Not at all. Especially if you consider the fact that the company’s earnings could be about 4x the current level in the next few years.
How is that?
If Nvidia grows its sales at an average annual rate of over 60% for the next 3 years - its revenues could move from around $61 billion in FY’24 to around $250 billion by FY’27 or over 4x. For context, Nvidia’s revenues grew by close to 3x over the last 12 months, while notching an average annual growth rate of about 55% over the last three years. These growth rates could hold up, given the surge of demand for Nvidia’s high-end graphics chips, which have emerged as the defacto silicon for running artificial intelligence applications. The lure of AI is growing each day, and the demand for chips isn’t fading yet.
Why?
While initial AI models unveiled by the likes of OpenAI were largely text-based, models are increasingly multimodal, working with speech, images, video, and 3D calling for higher computing power and a larger number of GPU shipments. Moreover, sectors as diverse as energy to real estate, healthcare and medical equipment, and industrial robots are looking to leverage AI tech as an input that can help these companies win.
NVidia has already done it in the past
To put things in perspective, NVDA stock swelled 900% from levels of $13 in early January 2021 to around $130 now, vs. an increase of about 50% for the S&P 500 over this roughly 4-year period. It was a bumpy ride, with returns for the stock being 125% in 2021, -50% in 2022, and 239% in 2023. The underperformance in NVDA’s stock vs. the S&P 500 in 2022 stands out in particular - as the benchmark index had returns of -19% that year. Notably, the Trefis High Quality Portfolio, with a collection of 30 stocks, has outperformed the S&P 500 each year over the same period. Why is that? As a group, HQ Portfolio stocks provided better returns with less risk versus the benchmark index; less of a roller-coaster ride as evident in HQ Portfolio performance metrics.
But there is more to the story this time around
Let’s take the case of Eli Lilly - the maker of the weight loss drug Wegovy. Like all companies, Lilly uses electricity as an input in its factories and offices. Clearly, Lilly doesn’t expect to win against a rival such as Pfizer because it uses more electricity. Now AI is fast becoming a core input for companies across sectors, just like electricity. But with an important difference. Lilly believes that leveraging AI in its R&D will help develop better products, faster than the competition. Unlike more electricity, more AI will help Lilly win in the marketplace. This changes everything. It implies Lilly will want to invest in AI. Aggressively. With little concern about price, it will be willing to pay for better, faster chips from companies like Nvidia. Nvidia is in a rare position of producing something where the demand seems limitless. Limitless, across sectors and industries. And this isn’t going away soon.
Combine this solid revenue growth with the fact that Nvidia’s margins (net income, or profits after all expenses and taxes, calculated as a percent of revenues) are on an improving trajectory - they grew from levels of about 25% in FY’19 to about 49% in FY’24 as the company sees better economies of scale and a more favorable product mix skewed toward complex data center products. Software-related sales are also trending higher. We can assume that margins will remain flat at current levels as Nvidia’s launch of pricier higher-end products such as the Blackwell chips are offset by potential competitive pressures.
So is 4x growth in earnings possible?
Sure. Looks quite reasonable when you combine 4x revenue growth with potentially flat margins over the next few years. Now if earnings grow 4x, the PE multiple will shrink by 4 times, assuming the stock price stays the same! But that’s exactly what Nvidia investors are betting will not happen. If earnings expand 4-fold over the next few years, instead of PE shrinking from a figure around 75x now to about 19x, a scenario where the PE metric stays at about 40x to 45x looks quite likely. This would make a 2.5x growth in Nvidia stock price to levels of about $300 a real possibility.
What about the time horizon for this high-return scenario? In practice, it won’t make much difference whether it takes 3 years or 5, as long as Nvidia is on this revenue expansion trajectory, with margins holding up, the stock price could respond similarly.
And it could be a bumpy ride yet again. While there is definitely a case to be made for large long-term gains from NVDA stock, the Trefis High Quality Portfolio could be right up your alley if consistent outperformance is at the top of your list.

title: 2024 FMS Storage And Memory Announcements, Part 2
text:
This second article discusses announcements by Samsung, Trendforce, IDC and Neo Semiconductor as well as a combined talk by Western Digital, Meta and Fadu, at the 2024 FMS, gave further insights into the latest developments in NAND flash and DRAM as well as memory controllers.
Jim Elliott, EVP of US Memory Business, Hwaseok Oh, EVP of Solution Prouction Engineering Team and Taeksang Song, CVP of DRAM Solution Development spoke about how the AI revolution is fueling new demands for memory and storage. AI will require memory and storage which is faster, vaster and require less power. This slide was shown to emphasize the growing use of some AI technologies. Using AI users can create large file with images or video more easily than ever before—helping to drive demand for storage capacity.
According to Samsung, each GenAI text-to-image requires the same energy as charging your phone 577 times! This power demand is leading to new energy solutions, such as the use of small modular reactors in data centers (in the US).
Samsung talked about their 9th generation 3D NAND TLC (three bits per cell) product which increases bit density and IO speed by 50% while reducing read by 40% over the prior generation product. The company’s QLC (four bits per cell) product increases bit density by 86% and IO speed by 60% with a 30% read power reduction. The company believes both TLC and QLC products will be needed for AI applications. The image below shows Samsung projections for storage capacities with various form factor server SSDs out to 2025.
Samsung’s 32GB TLC PM9D3a U.2 SSD will be available in the 4th quarter of 2024. Likewise the TLC PM1753 32TB U.2 and E3.S SSD will also be available then. QLC SSDs BM1743 (64/128TB in U.2 and E1.L form factors) are now available. QLC BM1753 32/64/128TB SSDs in U.2, E3.S and E1.L form factors will be available in Q4 2024. Samsung’s 128TB QLC BM1743 has 128% higher sequential writing performance than the prior generation.
Samsung’s PM9D3a 8-channel SSD running on PCIe 5.0 has a 1.9X higher throughput, 40% lower latency, 1.5X higher power efficiency and 2.7X higher performance than the prior generation product in a U.2/E1.L or E3.S FDP/OCP form factor and permits immersion cooling. Samsung also introduced a 16-channel SSD for generative AI server application, the PM1753.
This product saturates the sequential read capability of PCIe Gen 5 and increases sequential writing by 1.6X over the PM1743. Random read performance increases 1.3X and random write performance by 1.7X. Power efficiency is increased up to 1.7X. This product also features post-quantum cryptography and supports SPDM v1.2 and PCIE IDE. Samsung said that idle power for this product is reduced to 5W, with plans for further reductions in coming product generations as shown below.
Reducing the thermal contributions from storage is another important element in data centers and Samsung is addressing this with immersive cooling solutions and materials optimization.
In addition to the impact of AI on storage, Samsung also made announcements on their DRAM to support AI, in particular expanding the memory hierarchy to include near memory, memory expanders and tiered memory to add to main memory, cache and core.
The figure below shows Samsungs projections for HBM and DDR memory advances through 2027. The company’s HBM4 and future solutions will be custom products with a standard core die and customized buffer die. DDR5 RDIMMs will increase from 128GB without TSV (through silicon vias) to 256GB with TSV. Overcoating will be added to reduce damage to die. DDR5 MRDIMM solutions with 8.8Gbps bandwidth and 512GB capacity (with TSVs) are also available.
Samsung also talked about scaling memory capacity and bandwidth using CXL memory pooling. CMM-D memory expansion modules with CXL 2.0 Type 3 interfaces are available with up to 1TB capacity and 36GB/s bandwidth. The companies CMM-H products create new persistent tiered memory options. The companies BMM-B module box provides a pooled memory option with up to 24TB (using CMM-D modules) capacity and hundreds of TB (with CMM-H). The company said that it is seeking a total cost of ownership (TCO) optimized memory expansion solution to enable AI platforms with scalable memory.
Avril Wu from Trendforce said that tight DRAM supplies will persist into 2025. With profit improvements, all the major DRAM companies are increasing their Capex spending by 305% or more. Because of AI he said that 2025 new fab spending is prioritizing HBM supply, with TSV solutions are dominant. AI server bit growth is significantly higher than other applications. Jeff Janucowicz, from IDC, showed that revenues from memory and storage technologies (including HDDs) will undergo significant growth, due to the impact of AI.
Neo Semiconductor CEO Andy Hsu talked about new 3D chip technology to accelerate neural network AI. He saw the company’s 3D memory architecture (3D X-DRAM) in an HBM configuration (3D-XAI) combined with GPUs to provide enhanced AI computational capabilities. 300 memory layers could provide weighting training repositories (synapses) bonded with a neuron chip could provide a faster and more efficient processing architecture. He projected that 120TB/s processing throughput with a 12 die 3D X-DRAM HBM would be possible while consuming much less power than with traditional HBM AI processing
A presentation by Eric Spanneut, VP Marketing, from Western Digital, Ross Stenfort. HW System Storage Engineer at Meta and Anu Murthy, VP of Marketing at Fadu talked about flash memory and AI applications. They pointed out that demand for SSD capacity has increased significantly since 2022, partly due to AI data demands. SSD demand for enterprise applications is driving two different approaches, one involves various type of compute in storage and the other is large object storage as shown in the figure below. AI uses these approaches for disaggregated training and inference and faster access to large curated data repositories. They estimate that over 150EBs of additional storage will be needed by 2028 to support AI (from 2024 demand).
AI with SSDs will lead to increasing use of E1.S form factors (which scales at least to 128TB). Flexible data placement in NVMe will also be important and this will improve endurance, performance and quality of service. Software is being updated to support this feature. The OCP Datacenter NVME SSD V2.6 specification will be released soon with an increased number of hyperscale datacenter and enterprise partners, which enables data management at scale and with open-source tooling support. Open-source SSD storage qualification test cases are available from Meta.
Fadu talked about SSD controller challenges to provide AI performance needs with reduced power and replacing HDDs with high-capacity SSDs. The company says that their SSDs are 36-49% more power efficient that leading competitors, leading to lower total cost of ownership (TCO). Fadu talked about their GEN5 controller, shipping since 2023 14GB/s sequential read and 10GB/s sequential write and 3.3M IOPS random read and 500k IOPS random write using less than 6W of power and built to OCP standards. Fadu also introduced its PCIe Gen6 Sierra controller available in late 2025, which will enable greater than 28GB/s read and write and 6.8M IOPS and supporting up to 256TB SSD capacities.
Samsung, NEO Semicondutor, Meta, Fadu and Western Digital announced major developments and grown of NAND flash, SSDs and DRAM to support AI workloads at the 2024 FMS. High-capacity SSDs with over 500TB capacities could be available before the end of the decade.

title: Council Post: Fixing Your Personal Brand When AI And Search Results Misrepresent You
text:
Jason Barnard is an entrepreneur, writer and CEO of Kalicube, a groundbreaking digital marketing agency.
Does Google think you’re someone you’re not? How do you fix the results for your name when Google is getting it wrong?
Google is getting it wrong more than you think.
My company found that much of the time, Google relies on third-party sources for information about you instead of what you say about yourself. We found this by using data from Google’s Knowledge Graph on our site; we are tracking 42,000 person entries, and the web page associated with the person is not under the control of the person in over 50% of cases.
Google does this because it has a little black book of trusted sources it uses to verify facts about people. When the little black book has the wrong information about you, search engines like Google can misrepresent your personal brand, overlooking the most accurate and authoritative source about you, which is yourself.
You can fix Google’s mistakes by taking proactive steps to add your own content to Google’s little black book as the definitive source of facts about your personal brand.
These mistakes have a huge impact on your personal brand narrative.
By far the most widely used search engine globally, Google's interpretation of your personal brand significantly influences how the world perceives you. Misrepresentations lead to confusion among your audience, potential partners and peers. Furthermore, this misalignment can affect your credibility and even impact business opportunities and relationships.
You can actively guide Google and other search engines by providing clear, consistent information that aligns with your intended brand message across your digital footprint. An intentional and targeted personal brand communication strategy ensures you are presented how you want to be presented and helps safeguard your online brand integrity.
When Google is getting it wrong, ChatGPT probably is, too.
If Google is getting your personal brand wrong, it’s very likely the AI machines are, too. And I foresee mistakes in AI today getting a lot worse tomorrow.
AI systems rely heavily on existing web data to generate responses. If the foundational data contains contradictions, confusion or errors, popular search engines will perpetuate these inaccuracies in AI tools' outputs.
You can stop a "spinning wheel of mistakes" about your brand by creating a clear, accurate and consistent digital footprint everywhere you are online at the outset. In this way, you can retrain the machines, remove the risk of misrepresentation and present a trustworthy, revenue-generating personal brand online.
Here's how to take control of how online sources understand and represent you.
Create a single source of truth for the AI algorithms: You.
Your personal website is the cornerstone of your online presence for your audience and the primary source of truth for AI algorithms used by systems like Google, Bing and ChatGPT. By meticulously curating the content on your website, the algorithms receive accurate, consistent and authoritative information about your personal brand.
I recommend you start by creating an "About" page on your website that clearly outlines who you are, what you do, your target audience, your history and why you are credible within your industry. This page, known as the entity home, provides a comprehensive version of the facts about you. The details on this page will define how well Google and AI algorithms understand and represent your brand. Make sure to regularly update this page to reflect changes in your business or offerings to maintain relevance.
If you can, also add structured data markup to help search engines understand the context of each piece of information more effectively. Structured data talks to machines in their native language, meaning it is easier for Google and chat-based search interfaces like ChatGPT to provide people with accurate representations of your personal brand based on trusted sources—with your personal website at the forefront.
Control the fundamental facts about yourself by getting the web to corroborate what you say.
You’ve created the fundamental facts on your website's entity home. Controlling these facts across the web is step two.
Align all other website pages that talk about you with the information presented on your entity home. Use the bio on your entity home for all podcast appearances, interviews and board position descriptions, as well as articles published on third-party websites and in directories relevant to your niche.
Communicating consistently about your personal brand across the web helps reinforce the credibility of the data you provide on your entity home to AI systems. When Google sees your fundamental facts corroborated by independent third-party sources across the web, it will add your website to its little black book as the trusted source about your brand.
When authoritative sites echo and validate the fundamental facts, they create a network of consistent information. Consistency helps Google recognize and trust your identity, message and purpose. You can control the foundational narrative about yourself in Google because the web’s corroboration of your facts solidifies your brand narrative in Google's eyes.
Controlling your online representation is key to preventing inaccuracies.
Taking control of how you are represented in search engines is vital for your reputation and safeguards against future inaccuracies perpetuated by AI systems like Google Gemini, ChatGPT, Copilot, etc.
Maintaining a clear, consistent digital footprint is a huge undertaking, though. You will be mentioned on dozens, hundreds or perhaps thousands of platforms. If you want to have any level of control over how the machines understand and represent you to their users (who are your target audience, remember), you must track each and every mention of you and communicate to search engines and other AI algorithms which ones they should focus on.
That is a tremendous and always-on task. So I urge you not to wait until next year (or the year after). The longer you leave mistakes about you in Google and AI, the more difficult it will become for you to retrain the algorithms. Fix this issue now.
Seeking professional help can provide the expertise needed to correct Google's mistakes and take definitive control of your personal brand narrative in search today and AI tomorrow.

title: Council Post: Existing Legal Frameworks And Gaps In Generative AI
text:
Dr. Suresh Rajappa, Global Data / Tax Leader at KPMG LLP.
This post is the fourth in a series exploring the privacy and legal concerns of generative AI. If you haven't already, you can catch up on the previous posts here.
As generative AI technologies continue to evolve and integrate into various sectors, the legal landscape faces significant challenges. The existing legal frameworks, designed for earlier technological paradigms, often fall short in addressing the unique issues posed by generative AI. This post explores these gaps and proposes areas for legal reform to ensure the responsible and ethical use of generative AI.
The Legal Landscape
Generative AI, with its ability to create realistic content, from images and text to deepfake videos, presents unique legal challenges. The technology’s rapid advancement has outpaced the development of regulatory frameworks, leaving significant gaps that need urgent attention. These gaps can be broadly categorized into intellectual property, data protection and liability laws.
Intellectual Property Challenges
One of the primary legal concerns with generative AI is its impact on intellectual property (IP) rights. Traditional IP laws are ill-equipped to handle the complexities introduced by AI-generated content. For instance, who owns the copyright to an image or piece of music created by an AI? Current laws typically grant copyright to human creators, leaving AI-generated works in a legal grey area.
Moreover, generative AI can replicate existing works so closely that it raises issues of copyright infringement. The line between inspiration and replication becomes blurred, making it challenging to enforce IP rights effectively. Legal reforms are needed to clarify ownership and ensure that creators are adequately protected in the age of AI.
Data Protection And Privacy
Generative AI systems often require vast amounts of data for training, which can include sensitive personal information. This raises significant privacy concerns. Existing data protection laws, such as the GDPR in Europe, provide a framework for data privacy, but they were not designed with AI in mind.
One major issue is the potential for generative AI to produce outputs that inadvertently reveal personal information from the training data, known as inference attacks. These attacks can lead to privacy breaches, even if the data was anonymized. Enhancing data protection laws to address these risks is crucial. This could involve stricter controls on data usage, improved anonymization techniques, and greater transparency in how AI systems use and process data.
The proposed EU AI Act aims to address some of these concerns by categorizing AI systems into different risk levels and imposing stricter requirements on high-risk AI applications. This includes robust data governance frameworks to ensure the protection of fundamental rights and the safety of AI systems.
Liability And Accountability
The question of liability is another critical gap in the current legal frameworks. When an AI system generates harmful or misleading content, it can be challenging to determine who is responsible. Is it the developer, the user or the AI system itself?
Existing laws generally hold developers and users accountable, but as AI systems become more autonomous, this approach may become untenable. The EU AI Act introduces the concept of an AI liability regime, which aims to establish clearer guidelines for responsibility and redress in case of AI-induced harm.
Legal reforms could include establishing clearer guidelines for liability and developing new legal entities for AI systems, similar to corporate personhood.
The Need For Legal Reforms
To address these gaps, comprehensive legal reforms are necessary. These reforms should aim to balance innovation with the protection of individual rights. Here are some key areas for reform:
• Clarifying IP rights: Establish clear guidelines for the ownership of AI-generated content and refine copyright laws to address the nuances of AI creativity.
• Strengthening data protection: Enhance existing data protection laws to specifically address the challenges posed by AI, including the risks of inference attacks and data misuse.
• Defining liability: Develop new frameworks for liability that consider the unique nature of AI systems, potentially including the concept of AI legal personhood.
• Promoting ethical AI: Encourage the development and use of ethical AI through regulatory incentives and public awareness campaigns. This could include requiring AI systems to be transparent and explainable, ensuring that users understand how and why decisions are made.
• EU AI Act implementation: Support the implementation and refinement of the EU AI Act and similar regulatory frameworks globally. These laws should evolve to keep pace with technological advancements and address emerging challenges.
Conclusion
Generative AI holds tremendous potential, but its rapid development has outstripped the existing legal frameworks designed to regulate technology. Addressing the gaps in intellectual property, data protection, and liability laws is crucial to harnessing the benefits of AI while safeguarding individual rights. By promoting legal reforms and encouraging ethical practices, we can navigate the complex landscape of generative AI and ensure its responsible and beneficial use.

title: Council Post: How The Ancient Art Of Spinning Can Help Your AI Decision-Making
text:
Erik Åsberg is the CTO of eSmart Systems. He is also recognized as a Microsoft Regional Director.
When making clothes before the 19th century, one important tool was the spinning wheel. The spinning wheel helped improve the task of turning fabric into thread that, again, would be used to make clothes.
The spinning wheel’s exact origins are unclear, but it is widely believed to have been invented in India between 500 and 1000 A.D., with other theories suggesting earlier origins in ancient Egypt or China. The technology then spread to Iran, India and eventually Europe during the late Middle Ages. Incremental improvements over the years made the spinning wheel more efficient, with the most important improvement being the introduction of pedals—to free up both hands.
Before you start operating a spinning wheel, you have to first prepare the fabric: Shearing the wool from the sheep. Skirting the wool to ensure quality. Washing and drying the wool. Carding the wool to intermix the wool fibers and prepare them for spinning. After the spinning, there is plying, if you want stronger yarn. Then you're washing again, before winding the yard into skeins. As you see, there were numerous upstream and downstream processes.
The cool thing about this is that all of this could be operated by one person, all the way from the raw material to the final stages. That one person had all the skills and full end-to-end control of the process.
Let's look at a hypothetical example. Alice Smith was one person like this. Let's say she was a person living in the English countryside around 1770, and she was famous for her spinning skills. Her yarn had exceptional quality. The word spread around about her excellent yarn. She worked as hard as she could, spinning out as much yarn as possible. She tried to think of ways to produce more yarn, but the only way for her to scale was to hire one more person to operate another spinning wheel. Her operation could only scale linearly.
When you think of it, operating a spinning wheel is quite similar to running an AI proof of concept (PoC). As a data scientist, you have access to the raw material—the data. You need to wash your data and make sure they are of high quality. You have your own infrastructure that you will use to run your PoC on. You have prepared your dataset, and you start training your AI model, that you might also have developed yourself. You get your result, and you produce a report that presents how AI could support your company. As a data scientist, you have all the skills and full control end to end. You are a skilled data scientist, so naturally the result of the PoC is successful.
In 1764, James Hargreaves invented the Spinning Jenny, a spinning machine that could do the same work as 20–30 people operating spinning wheels. With the industrial revolution, these machines quickly developed into large-scale spinning factories.
Operating a spinning factory is different from operating a spinning wheel. You need a completely different set of skills. You need textile experts, engineers, mechanics, quality assurers, planners and logistic experts—skills and knowledge that are unheard of when you are operating a spinning wheel. The machine must operate 24/7, so you must have people on call, also knowing what to do if things fail. And all these people with different skill sets must cooperate closely. Running factories is not cheap, so you need to ensure you run with as low cost and maintenance as possible, with focus on efficiency.
In order for a factory to be efficient, you also need to professionalize and scale all upstream and downstream processes. All processes must be equally efficient as the machine’s production. The raw material must be available at all times for the washing and drying and carding, as well as the plying and winding. If one of the sub-processes fails, then your machine will start delivering poor quality before it eventually comes to a halt. Running a machine requires large investments in not only the machine, but all upstream and downstream processes. In addition to investments in skills and knowledge needed.
Running AI at industrial scale is a very similar challenge. As mentioned, operating AI consists of many upstream and downstream processes: data collection, data verification, metadata verification, infrastructure administration, configuration, testing and more. For your AI to scale, all of these must also scale. This will require more specialized skills than running a PoC. Like in the spinning factory, you will need experts on the industry domain, data annotators, data engineers, infrastructure, software development, UX, monitoring and more.
Unlike a PoC, you will need to continuously make sure your AI is performing when processing new, unseen data 24/7. You have to establish solid processes for monitoring and feedback, as well as data extraction and updates of datasets based on that feedback. These new datasets will then have to be used to retrain your model before verifying performance and then deploy back in production. This cycle must be done for all your models in parallel. Continuously. Each new model increases the complexity.
You must also remember that when you do a PoC, you have done your PoC for a problem that had enough data. Your more difficult problems often have less data. But you will eventually have to solve those, too. And as your testing dataset usually comes from the same source as your training and validation datasets, you are likely to meet performance challenges when running your model on new, unseen data.
Very few people reflect on this, in the happiness of their PoC success.
This is why having a rock star data scientist, the Alice Smith of data science, with a newly performed AI PoC with stellar, blinding results, will have you thinking that you should invest in in-house AI, when what you eventually need is industrial scale AI, something that will require investments way beyond your current digitalization budget.
Most AI projects today fail when scaling—because running a spinning factory is different from running a spinning wheel.
