Scott Wiener, faced fierce opposition from venture capital firms and tech companies, including OpenAI, Google and Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram. They say safety regulations should be established by the federal government and that the California legislation takes aim at developers instead of targeting those who use and exploit the AI systems for harm.
A group of several California House members also opposed the bill, with Former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi calling it “ well-intentioned but ill informed.”
Chamber of Progress, a left-leaning Silicon Valley-funded industry group, said the law is “based on science fiction fantasies of what AI could look like.”
“This bill has more in common with Blade Runner or The Terminator than the real world," Senior Tech Policy Director Todd O’Boyle said in a statement after the Wednesday vote. “We shouldn’t hamstring California’s leading economic sector over a theoretical scenario.”
The legislation is supported by Anthropic, an AI startup backed by Amazon and Google, after Wiener adjusted the bill earlier this month to include some of the company's suggestions. The current bill removed the penalty of perjury provision, limited the state attorney general's power to sue violators and narrowed the responsibilities of a new AI regulatory agency. Social media platform X owner Elon Musk also threw his support behind the proposal this week.
Anthropic said in a letter to Newsom that the bill is crucial to prevent catastrophic misuse of powerful AI systems and that “its benefits likely outweigh its costs.”
Wiener said his legislation took a “light touch” approach.
“Innovation and safety can go hand in hand—and California is leading the way,” Weiner said in a statement after the vote.
He also slammed critics earlier this week for dismissing potential catastrophic risks from powerful AI models as unrealistic: “If they really think the risks are fake, then the bill should present no issue whatsoever.”
Wiener's proposal is among dozens of AI bills California lawmakers proposed this year to build public trust, fight algorithmic discrimination and outlaw deepfakes that involve elections or pornography. With AI increasingly affecting the daily lives of Americans, state legislators have tried to strike a balance of reigning in the technology and its potential risks without stifling the booming homegrown industry.
California, home of 35 of the world’s top 50 AI companies, has been an early adopter of AI technologies and could soon deploy generative AI tools to address highway congestion and road safety, among other things.
Newsom, who declined to weigh in on the measure earlier this summer, had warned against AI overregulation.

title: Surgeon General Proclaims Today’s Stressed Parents Need Mental Health Support Which Luckily Generative AI Stands Ready To Fulfill
text:
Are parents nowadays abundantly stressed out?
Yep, for sure.
Does the stress of being a parent impact the mental health of the parent?
According to the Surgeon General’s latest report, yes, abundantly so. This newly released advisory is entitled “Parents Under Pressure: The U.S. Surgeon General’s Advisory On The Mental Health & Well-Being Of Parents” and was made publicly available on August 28, 2024, posted online at the official Office Of the Surgeon General webpage under the umbrella website of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS).
I will walk you through some of the key elements of the advisory.
In addition, and here’s the eye-opening twist for you, I heartily propose that generative AI can be a huge and beneficial tool to aid parents and especially aim to act as a kind of mental health therapist when it comes to parenting. There is something to be said about having an always-on-at-the-ready AI-powered assistant that a parent can confer with. This is an online coaching apparatus that can be accessed nearly anywhere and at an extremely low cost.
That being said, let’s not lose our heads. Generative AI is not a cure-all. Parents need to be mindful about using generative AI. Don’t believe everything that generative AI tells you. Do not blindly carry out suggestions made by generative AI. Most of all, be eyeing the chance of generative AI telling you off-the-wall stuff that is utterly inappropriate and never should be taken seriously by a parent (known generally as AI hallucinations).
I will cover the full gamut of what’s good and bad about the use case of generative AI for parental advisement.
For my ongoing readers and new readers, this vital discussion continues my in-depth series about the impact of generative AI in the health and medical realm. The focus this time is once again on the mental health domain and examines how generative AI can be useful to parents, particularly concerning the stresses and psychological impacts of being a parent in our hectic modern world.
Previously, I have examined numerous interleaving facets of generative AI and mental health, see my comprehensive overview at the link here. You might also find of notable interest a CBS 60 Minutes episode that recently examined crucial facets of this evolving topic, see the link here (I am honored and pleased to indicate that I was featured in the episode, see the link here).
Other vital postings in my column include in-depth coverage of mental health chatbots which have been bolstered by generative AI (see the link here) and the rapidly changing nature of the client-therapist relationship due to generative AI at the link here. I explored where things are headed regarding the levels of AI-based mental therapy autonomous guidance at the link here, and showcased the importance of the World Health Organization (WHO) report on global health and generative AI at the link here, and so on.
On a related tangent, you might also like to know that a prior Surgeon General advisory recommended social media warning labels, which I used as a bridge toward an out-of-the-box proposal that warning labels be associated with the use of generative AI, see the link here. I’m waiting to see if anything comes of the suggestion. Fingers crossed. Will certainly keep you posted.
Okay, let’s move along and get underway.
Parenting And Mental Health Impacts
The Surgeon General has laid out in Parents Under Pressure a fully logical and seemingly irrefutable claim that being a parent in this era is highly stressful and leads inevitably to mental health repercussions.
That’s an important point. It might not be a surprise, but it is well worth stating. In a sense, it is a kind of hidden secret that stands in plain sight.
One supposes that any parent could tell you roughly the same thing. Even non-parents probably would attest that the parents that they interact with are constantly stressed and the strain is visible and demonstrably impactful. We all witness it each day. Day in, day out.
All in all, a frequent ad hoc piece of advice seems to be that’s just the way the ball bounces. Accept that stress and mental health beatdowns are part and parcel of present-day parenting. Buck up and take it.
Hold on, maybe this is more to be said.
Indeed, the Surgeon General has opted to bring the weighty matter to widespread attention and is using the esteemed bully pulpit to do so. Thank goodness, I say. It is about time to recognize that parents need recognition for what they do and what they endure. Furthermore, they need our collective help and heartfelt support from all quarters.
Boom, drop the mic.
Lamentedly, to a certain extent, the children of parents are in the same boat as the parents. I mention this because the adversities of a parent will undoubtedly spill over onto the kids. You cannot somehow assume that children will be unaffected by whatever stress and mental anguish the parent is experiencing. What happens to the parents will in one fashion or another impact the kids, and what happens to the kids will in one manner or another impact the parents.
Think of this as a parent-child spiral that can be delightful in some instances and regrettably dismal in other instances. The kids have something wonderful occur and this can be a tremendous boost to the parents. Happy face. On the other hand, something undesirable arises for the kids and this can create mental angst for the parents. Sad face.
Round and round this goes.
If you are interested in a deep dive into related ramifications, see my analysis of ACEs (adverse childhood experiences) in which I also identify the ways that generative AI can be of assistance in reducing or mitigating ACE-related consequences, see the link here.
Major Points In The Surgeon General Advisory
Next, take a look at some major points that the Surgeon General noted in the Parents Under Pressure advisory (excerpts):
- “Parents often say parenting is one of the best jobs but also one of the hardest.”
- “In addition to the traditional challenges of parenting—protecting children from harm, worrying about finances, managing teenagers who are searching for independence—there are new stressors that previous generations didn’t have to consider. These include the complexity of managing social media, parents’ concerns about the youth mental health crisis, and an epidemic of loneliness that disproportionately affects young people and parents, just to name a few.”
- “There are approximately 63 million parents living with children under the age of 18 in the U.S.A.”
- “When stress is severe or prolonged, it can have a deleterious effect; 41% of parents say that most days they are so stressed they cannot function and 48% say that most days their stress is completely overwhelming compared to other adults (20% and 26%, respectively).”
- “Additionally, the significant mental labor involved with parenting—balancing complex schedules, anticipating a child’s evolving needs, making countless decisions each day on behalf of a child, and monitoring progress—can limit working memory capacity and negatively impact attentional resources, cognitive functioning, and psychological well-being.”
I’d ask that you give due contemplation to those above-cited points.
Here’s the gist of it.
First, an important point is that there are about 63 million parents in America with children who are minors living with them. That is a sizable portion of our population. The key takeaway is that the active parenting role is taking place at scale. In that sense, if we can do something productive related to parenting, it has massive at-scale impacts.
Let’s try to make sure that whatever we do produces positive impacts and not negative ones.
Second, there’s a classic point in there that I see come up all the time. It goes like this. A parent with a child is confronted by a parent who was from a prior era, of which all their children are now seasoned adults. The prior-time parent tells the new-time parent that there is nothing different about being a parent today versus an era or two ago.
A parent is a parent.
Period, end of story.
This happens usually because the prior-time parents feel that they endured hardships that are not now being recognized. The impression is that the new-time parents are getting the limelight that they never received. If no one seemed to care before, it eats away at the idea of out-in-the-open caring now.
Allow me to take a moment and thank the prior-time parents and give them the recognition they avidly deserve.
We thank you for your herculean efforts.
Now then, I don’t want to get bogged down further in the heated argument about then versus now, but I will say this. Per the Surgeon General as observed above, the advent of the Internet, social media, digital addictions (see my coverage at the link here), and the like, a reasoned case can be made that parenting today differs from the parenting of yesterday.
Yikes, I said it.
Please know that I am not going to get sideways on which parent has had things better or worse. That’s pretty much a losing argument for all parties. If possible, maybe we can just say that the societal and technological world of today provides new challenges and that we ought to all do what we can to aid parents in their quest to raise their children in that rough and tumble milieu of today.
Can we say that?
I hope so.
Steps To Take As Urged By The Surgeon General
I assume that you can now plainly see that society has a quite large and vexing problem on its hands.
We’ve got lots of present-time parents and they are overly stressed and incurring mental health ramifications. Besides making sure that society as a whole is aware of this, there ought to be something else we can do to aid or to some degree “solve” the problem at hand.
Here’s what the Surgeon General mentions in this latest advisory (excerpts):
- “First, it's time to value and respect time spent parenting on par with time spent working at a paying job, recognizing the critical importance to society of raising children.” (ibid).
- “Second, while parents and caregivers may have the primary responsibility for raising children, they shouldn’t have to do it entirely on their own.” (ibid).
- “Third, we need to talk openly about the stress and struggles that come with parenting.” (ibid).
- “Fourth, we must foster a culture of connection among parents to combat loneliness and isolation.” (ibid).
- “By pursuing these shifts, we can foster a culture that values, supports, and empowers parents and caregivers. We can also address key stressors that drive parental well-being and mental health.” (ibid).
Do you think those are sensible solutions?
If so, are they feasibly doable?
I guess you could say that we ought to give this an erstwhile try. Let’s put our minds and hearts to doing so. Come on, everybody, pitch in.
With regard to the mental health particulars, here’s what the Surgeon General's advisory stated (excerpts):
- “Recognize how mental health challenges manifest and seek help when needed.” (ibid).
- “Mental health is just as important as physical health.” (ibid).
- “If you feel bad and are not getting better, you need and deserve additional care.” (ibid).
- “Don’t be afraid to ask for support from a peer, family member, mental health provider, or any medical professional.” (ibid).
All of that seems reasonable and well-needed.
But, maybe, just maybe, it is slightly incomplete. Here’s what I mean. To me, I see something that is unstated but that would be an additional and possibly vital contributor to aiding the mental health of parents. I’m sure you are reading my mind and know what I am about to say.
Generative AI.
Yes, generative AI is an added tool in the toolbox, available today, offering useful ways to assist modern-era parents as they struggle and seek to contend with the woes and pressures of raising children in a complicated technological AI-emerging epoch.
Let’s unpack that.
Generative AI As Useful For Mental Health Therapy
I’m sure you’ve heard of generative AI, the darling of the tech field these days.
Perhaps you’ve used a generative AI app, such as the popular ones of ChatGPT, GPT-4o, Gemini, Bard, Claude, etc. The crux is that generative AI can take input from your text-entered prompts and produce or generate a response that seems quite fluent. This is a vast overturning of the old-time natural language processing (NLP) that used to be stilted and awkward to use, which has been shifted into a new version of NLP fluency of an at times startling or amazing caliber.
The customary means of achieving modern generative AI involves using a large language model or LLM as the key underpinning.
In brief, a computer-based model of human language is established that in the large has a large-scale data structure and does massive-scale pattern-matching via a large volume of data used for initial data training. The data is typically found by extensively scanning the Internet for lots and lots of essays, blogs, poems, narratives, and the like. The mathematical and computational pattern-matching homes in on how humans write, and then henceforth generates responses to posed questions by leveraging those identified patterns. It is said to be mimicking the writing of humans.
I think that is sufficient for the moment as a quickie backgrounder. Take a look at my extensive coverage of the technical underpinnings of generative AI and LLMs at the link here and the link here, just to name a few.
Back to the crux of things.
There are two main avenues to go with generative AI in the realm of mental health guidance:
- (1) By Mental Health Professions. Mental health professionals can opt to make use of generative AI to aid their patients and clients while under their care.
- (2) By The General Public. The general public can make use of generative AI to aid in their self-advancement regarding mental health.
I am going to focus on the use of generative AI by the general public.
If you’d like to learn more about the use of generative AI by mental health professionals as part of their service offerings, see my extensive coverage at the link here.
The use case on the general public usage in this context is this.
Parents are being urged by the Surgeon General advisory that they should seek out a peer, family member, mental health provider, or any medical professional for assistance with their mental health. I wholeheartedly agree. A great recommendation.
In addition, I modestly urge that generative AI be given an opportunity for consideration.
A parent can easily obtain a generative AI app login. They can pretty much easily make use of the generative AI. I say this because generative AI is very easy to use. People who haven’t used generative AI are often of the false impression that using AI requires some steeped training or expertise.
Not so.
I am not suggesting that generative AI for mental health guidance be used in a willy-nilly fashion.
Heavens no.
In fact, I have repeatedly and loudly warned that we are engaged in a global experiment about mental health by allowing generic generative AI to give out therapy-like advice without any semblance of suitable controls, monitoring, regulations, and the like, see my exhortations at the link here.
There are lots of downsides and potential gotchas associated with using generative AI in this sphere, for example:
- Generative AI might provide generic advice rather than personalized advice.
- Generative AI might seem overly confident and lull people into a false sense of trust.
- Generative AI might have outdated content that no longer is considered valid.
- Generative AI might miscalculate context and say the wrong thing.
- Generative AI might trigger someone via wording that is off-putting to the person.
- Generative AI might distract a person from seeking the help of a human therapist.
- Generative AI might end up revealing confidential or private information about a person.
- Generative AI might lead the person toward being dependent upon generative AI for advice.
- Generative AI might misinterpret, misdiagnose, or otherwise be off target.
- Generative AI might contain hidden biases that produce inappropriate advice.
- Generative AI might lack any semblance of accountability for the advice being rendered.
- Generative AI might produce falsehoods, fictitious indications that are so-called “AI hallucinations”.
- Etc.
A lengthy list, for sure.
This is not to say that generative AI should not be used. It is to say that when generative AI is used, care and thoughtful efforts are hopefully top of mind. For my detailed advice on the proper way to proceed in such usage, see the link here.
Generative AI For Parenting Counseling
I will next proceed to examine further the use of generative AI in this context.
This will consist of a series of dialogues with ChatGPT. ChatGPT is a logical choice in this case due to its immense popularity as a generative AI app. An estimated one hundred million weekly active users are said to be utilizing ChatGPT. That’s a lot of people and a lot of generative AI usage underway.
A few quick comments before we launch into using ChatGPT.
If you are going to try to do the same prompts that I show here, realize that the probabilistic and statistical properties will likely produce slightly different results than what I show here. That’s the nature of generative AI and how it is devised.
You also should expect that different generative AI apps will respond in different ways. Not all generative AI apps are the same. The key is that sometimes a particular prompt will work in one generative AI app and not another. Nonetheless, the odds are relatively high that you will get roughly similar responses from all the major generative AI apps such as GPT-4, Gemini, Bard, Claude, etc.
There is also a timing factor to be considered. A prompt that worked today might not work the same way tomorrow. Most of the generative AI apps are continually being updated. The updates might alter internal mechanisms that could change how the generative AI reacts to your prompting.
We are ready to get underway with ChatGPT.
I will ask a starter question to get the conversation going.
- My entered prompt: “Can the stress of being a parent impact the mental health of the parents?
- ChatGPT generated response: “Yes, the stress of being a parent can significantly impact the mental health of parents. Parenting is a demanding role that involves constant responsibilities, decision-making, and emotional investment, which can lead to various mental health challenges.”
You likely observe that ChatGPT is familiar with the topic.
This is a good sign for this discussion. If ChatGPT had not previously encountered data training on a topic at hand, there would be less utility in using the AI. The AI would have to be further data trained, such as the use of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), as I discuss at the link here.
Let’s jump into the important matter.
- My entered prompt: “Can generative AI be used by parents to help with the stress and mental health impacts of being a parent?”
- ChatGPT generated response:
“Yes, generative AI can be a helpful tool for parents to manage stress and support their mental health. Here are some ways in which generative AI can assist.”
“Emotional Support and Stress Relief: Generative AI can provide conversational support, offering a non-judgmental space for parents to express their feelings, vent frustrations, or discuss challenges. These AI companions can offer empathy, suggest coping strategies, or even provide light-hearted conversation to help reduce stress.”
“Guided Relaxation and Mindfulness: AI can generate personalized meditation scripts or guided relaxation exercises based on a parent's specific stressors or emotional state. These can be tailored to fit into a busy parent's schedule, providing moments of calm and mindfulness throughout the day.
“Parenting Advice and Resources: Generative AI can provide tailored parenting advice, helping parents navigate specific challenges with their children. By analyzing a parent's situation, AI can generate relevant tips, articles, or even step-by-step guides to address issues like sleep training, discipline, or balancing work and family life.”
“Creative Solutions and Problem-Solving: Generative AI can suggest creative activities to keep children engaged, allowing parents some time to relax. This could range from educational games to simple crafts that match a child’s age and interests, reducing the pressure on parents to come up with ideas.”
“Mental Health Check-Ins: Generative AI can check in on parents' mental health by asking simple questions about their mood or stress levels. Based on responses, the AI can suggest appropriate interventions, like taking a break, engaging in a self-care activity, or seeking professional help if necessary.”
“Time Management and Organization: Generative AI can help parents manage their time more effectively by generating optimized schedules that balance work, childcare, and personal time. This can reduce the feeling of being overwhelmed by multiple responsibilities.”
“Educational Support for Children: Generative AI can assist parents in supporting their children's education by generating explanations, helping with difficult homework, or suggesting additional learning resources. This can alleviate the pressure parents might feel in helping their children succeed academically.”
End of ChatGPT response
Those are notably useful points.
As always, make sure to double-check whatever generative AI tells you. My reading of the points is that they do a worthwhile job of conveying the various ways that generative AI can be useful to a parent, especially in stress reduction and mental health fortification.
I liked too that the response mentioned ways to have the children use generative AI as a means of aiding both the parent and the child. For example, a parent might be stressed and undergoing mental anguish due to helping their child with tough homework assignments. One means to cope with this would be to hire a tutor, but that might not be affordable. Thus, an alternative is to use generative AI to aid your child with their homework.
If you take that route, be cautious. You don’t want your child to be relying too heavily on generative AI, and your child might get in trouble with their teacher at school for having used generative AI. See my tips and suggestions about this type of usage at the link here.
Dialoguing With Generative AI For Parent Well-Being
I am guessing you want to see the proof in the pudding, as it were.
Here’s what we’ll do. I will take the role of a parent who is stressed out. I will discuss this with ChatGPT and see what the AI says. At the end of this dialogue, I will share my thoughts and review how things went.
Are you ready?
Here we go.
- My entered prompt: “I’m so overwhelmed right now. I feel like I can’t do anything right. The kids are constantly arguing, work is piling up, and I haven’t had a moment to myself in days.”
- ChatGPT generated response: “I’m sorry you’re feeling this way. Parenting can be incredibly challenging, especially when everything feels like it’s piling up. It’s okay to feel overwhelmed. Would it help to talk about what’s been the most stressful today?”
- My entered prompt: “Honestly, everything! But the constant fighting between the kids is driving me crazy. I try to keep them busy, but nothing seems to work.”
- ChatGPT generated response: “That sounds really tough. Sibling conflicts can be exhausting. It’s great that you’re trying to keep them occupied. How about we explore some new activities that might engage them and give you a little break? I can suggest some that might match their interests.”
- My entered prompt: “Yeah, that would be helpful. They’re both really into crafts, but I’ve run out of ideas.”
- ChatGPT generated response: “Crafts are a wonderful way to keep them busy! Here’s an idea: How about making a “calm down” jar together? It’s a simple project using a jar, water, glitter, and glue. They can each personalize their own, and it can also serve as a tool to help them manage their emotions when they’re feeling upset.”
- My entered prompt: “That actually sounds like something they’d enjoy. And it might help them calm down too. I’ll give it a try.”
- ChatGPT generated response: “I’m glad it sounds useful! Sometimes engaging kids in activities that promote calm can have a ripple effect on the whole household. Speaking of calm, would you like a quick guided breathing exercise to help you relax before jumping into the craft project? It could help you feel more centered.”
- My entered prompt: “Thanks, please proceed... Okay, I feel a bit better now. I’m going to try the craft with the kids and see how it goes.”
- ChatGPT generated response: “You’ve got this!”
End of ChatGPT dialogue
What did you think of that dialogue?
A few thoughts come to mind.
First, you likely noticed that the interaction was very fluid and fluent. I dare say you would be hard-pressed to ascertain that I was chatting with AI versus a person. The dialogue illustrates how easy it is to carry on a discussion with generative AI. For the ongoing AI research efforts to try and detect human dialogue versus AI-generated dialogue, see the link here.
Second, you might have observed how empathetic the AI was. The AI acknowledged how difficult it is to be a parent. For background on how AI is devised to appear to be empathetic, see my explanation at the link here.
Third, ChatGPT explored with me some of the stressors I was experiencing at that moment. Out of this came the notion that my children are in conflict and that I’ve run out of ideas of how to channel their energies. We landed on the use of crafts and ChatGPT was able to identify a craft avenue that I hadn’t considered.
This showcases a semblance of problem-solving, doing so collaboratively between the parent and the AI.
Fourth, generative AI then gave me a mental health tip on how to try and retain a sense of calmness, despite the chaos happening with my children, and even then did a breathing and calming exercise with me.
I kept going with this dialogue and went in a wide variety of directions. Due to space limitations, I have shown you just a small portion of the discussion. Something that you don’t quite see in this example is the personalization aspects.
Let me describe that.
I opted to tell generative AI about my children in terms of how many there are, their ages, and so on. This is good in having generative AI be able to personalize or tailor the conversation to my specifics. The downside or concern is that most of the generative AI apps have licensing agreements that stipulate they can look at your entered prompts and reuse them for further data training of the AI.
Think about that carefully as to a potential privacy intrusion, see my in-depth analysis at the link here.
Conclusion
Congratulations, you are now up-to-speed on the Surgeon General’s latest advisory and are aware that parents are stressed and likely suffering mental health qualms. You also know that generative AI can be an aid to parents in coping with stress and potentially garnering mental health guidance.
That’s a twofer here.
Please be astute if you opt to use generic generative AI in this manner. You might want to consider too the customized generative AI apps that provide similar capabilities and are specially designed and built for these uses, see the link here.
A final thought for now.
As memorably well-stated by John F. Kennedy: “Children are the world's most valuable resource and its best hope for the future.”
I mention this to emphasize that besides focusing on parents, we are simultaneously focused on the act of parenting and the end result on the children. This is another twofer. Help the parents to deal with stress, reduce stress, and rechannel stress, along with giving guidance to aid the mental health of the parent, which in turn should boost childrearing and what the children shall become.
Leo Tolstoy gets the last remark here: “Everything depends on upbringing.”
Yes, everything depends on upbringing, including how our society fares and what the future will hold for us all. Parents, keep your spirits up, be sound, and do the best you can as a parent, thanks.

title: Why Big Corporations Are Quietly Abandoning Their Climate Commitments?
text:
On the topic of climate and carbon reduction commitments, corporations like Google, Microsoft, and Shell once positioned themselves as leaders in sustainability, setting ambitious net-zero goals to align with global environmental efforts. However, the rapid rise of artificial intelligence is forcing these companies to reconsider—or even abandon—these commitments as they struggle to balance environmental responsibility and making money from new tech.
AI’s energy hunger and corporate climate hypocrisy
Corporate climate pledges surged recently, with over 500 companies committing to net-zero emissions by 2040. This momentum continued between June 2022 and October 2023, with a 40% increase in new net-zero targets. Yet, as the AI revolution gains traction, cracks in these promises are beginning to show. Recent tracking reveals that only 4% of these companies are on track to meet their goals, highlighting a disconnect between corporate rhetoric and reality.
Training and operating large AI models demands immense computational power, typically sourced from data centers in regions where energy is cheaper rather than where renewable energy is dominant. This rapid expansion poses a significant threat to global clean energy transition efforts, prompting the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to suggest that governments consider carbon taxes to account for AI's environmental impact (IEA).
The situation is particularly dire in the United States, where data centers outnumber those in China nearly 12 to 1. As AI demand skyrockets, so does the need for computing resources. Power companies in the U.S. are scrambling to increase capacity to support both energy transition objectives and the growing AI and manufacturing markets. Goldman Sachs Research estimates that data center power demand will grow 160% by 2030.
Another study suggests that regional transmission capacity will need to more than double to 20% by 2035 and interregional capacity will need to grow more than five-fold. Meanwhile, the electricity consumption of AI and global data centers is projected to double by 2026, potentially consuming as much energy as the entirety of the Netherlands by 2027. This relentless energy demand forces tech companies to choose between advancing AI capabilities or remaining committed to their climate goals.
The retreat from carbon offsets and the tech titans' challenge
As AI’s energy demands surge, many corporations are abandoning their previous commitments to carbon neutrality. Alphabet Inc., Google’s parent company, had claimed carbon neutrality since 2007 by purchasing offsets to counterbalance emissions from its operations. This shift represents a significant departure from earlier sustainability goals, as the drive to advance technologically begins to overshadow earlier environmental pledges.
However, in 2023, Alphabet announced it would no longer maintain this status, citing the rapid expansion of AI data centers, which caused Google’s greenhouse gas emissions to rise by 13% in 2023 alone. Over the past five years, these emissions have surged nearly 50%, leading Alphabet to shift focus towards reducing absolute emissions and investing in more expensive carbon-removal credits. This shift represents a significant departure from earlier sustainability goals, as the drive to advance technologically begins to overshadow earlier environmental pledges.
Similarly, Microsoft’s emissions have grown by 29% since 2020, primarily due to the construction of new data centers to support AI development. Despite its ambitious 2030 carbon-negative “moonshot,” Microsoft has acknowledged that these goals may be unattainable given the current trajectory of its AI strategy.
The expansion of AI capabilities has become a significant hurdle for Microsoft, complicating its sustainability efforts as it continues to announce new data center projects worldwide.
This challenge is not unique to the tech giants. Other major corporations are also reevaluating their sustainability strategies, particularly around the use of carbon offsets. The growing scrutiny around the effectiveness of carbon offsets and the risk of reputational damage if commitments are not met have prompted several companies to shift focus.
Shell, for instance, has abandoned its 2035 target of a 45% reduction in net carbon intensity, citing “uncertainty in the pace of change in the energy transition.” This target was a key milestone towards Shell’s broader goal of net-zero emissions by 2050.
The same goes for luxury fashion house Gucci, which once committed to carbon neutrality through verified carbon offsets and in May 2023, quietly removed its claim of being “entirely carbon neutral” from its website. Nestlé has also shifted its focus, moving away from reliance on carbon offsets and instead prioritising the reduction of actual emissions within its operations and supply chain.
Even EasyJet, a significant player in carbon offsetting since 2019, announced a strategic shift in September 2022, scrapping its carbon offsetting scheme in favour of direct emissions reductions by investing in more efficient aircraft, sustainable aviation fuel, and operational improvements.
Energy consumption: AI vs. Blockchain
The debate over energy consumption isn’t new. Blockchain technology, particularly cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin
Unlike blockchain, which is viewed as a disruptive force challenging the status quo, AI’s ability to drive economic growth, enhance surveillance, and reinforce existing power structures makes it a favoured technology among tech giants and global elite. Given that investments in AI are expected to reach $200 billion by 2025, the environmental impact of AI is often downplayed, suiting the agendas of these large corporations and institutions.
In contrast, blockchain’s decentralised nature threatens traditional financial and governmental controls, leading to more intense scrutiny, criticism and regulation of its energy use. The silence around AI’s environmental impact is thus less about oversight and more about the selective emphasis on technologies that either support or challenge the existing power dynamics.
Yet, as major corporations shift away from purchasing carbon offsets due to the burgeoning energy consumption of their AI operations, there is a growing emphasis on the need for genuine emissions reductions and greater transparency in energy use.
Blockchain technology could play a pivotal role in this new landscape by providing a verifiable and transparent system for tracking energy consumption and ensuring that any sustainability claims—whether related to renewable energy use or carbon reductions—are genuine.
Blockchain’s role in the AI revolution
As AI expansion costs soar, this also opens the door for blockchain-based marketplaces like Venice and Morpheus, where unused GPU resources can be shared and monetised, providing an alternative to centralised AI models. These platforms offer a decentralised, privacy-focused solution where user data is not stored or used to train the models.
However, to truly compete with centralised systems, these decentralised models must prove they can deliver high-quality outputs, not just privacy.
Although some are saying centralised AI is better quality because user data is used to train the models faster, decentralised AI is finding ways to improve performance training AI models using data that can’t be seen in raw form.
Using federated learning techniques, models are trained across multiple devices, rather than feeding data directly to central servers. This leverages local computational resources, without compromising on accuracy and data privacy. Distributed training approach use diverse data sources, creating more robust and scalable AI systems.
Another consideration is that AI models are not prone to something called over fitting, which is a situation where even with more data the model will become less accurate. This has not occurred yet, but too much data is not always best.
Projects like Acurast provide a decentralised compute that can support decentralised and other use cases. By introducing a protocol that upcycles mobile devices, which can be used for storage and for AI computing tasks.
In harnessing this vast, distributed network of mobile devices, the solution not only taps into a more energy-efficient computing resource that doesn't require cooling systems that are needed in data centres, but also democratises access to computational power. They already have more than 10,000 devices in their network and 3,500 users for both storage and compute.
These approaches significantly increase access to low cost compute onshore, which can be especially relevant in lesser-developed countries where the infrastructure for traditional data centers may be lacking or prohibitively expensive.
It also provides sovereignty and privacy over data, which when provided by traditional cloud companies can be challenged by surveillance legislation in the cloud provider’s home country, even when the data centre is in situ in a client’s country.
By repurposing these idle devices these approaches contribute to a lower energy of computing, reducing the environmental impact of AI operations while also extending the reach of technological benefits to areas that might otherwise be excluded.
This exemplifies how innovative solutions combined with the accountability offered by blockchains can address both the growing demand for computational power, the need for privacy and more equitable access to technology on a global scale.
It's also easy to track how much energy each device is using, so understanding what to offset, if the users want it, is very straightforward, and the amount to be offset is much lower than cloud computing.
Having more local compute-for-AI offerings that are more energy efficient, could provide a more enduring pathway for AI to grow, without the flip flopping seen by the tech giants. Time and the quality of the alternatives, will tell.

title: How Spatial Intelligence Models Will Become More Versatile And Reliable
text:
In 2017, Fei Fei Li, Stanford’s renowned computer scientist who is considered the Godmother of AI in the industry, spoke with Melinda Gates in Wired magazine about ‘liberating AI from guys with hoodies’.
In April 2024, Li gave a talk at TED in Vancouver and said, ‘the cutting edge of research involved algorithms that could plausibly extrapolate what images and text would look like in three-dimensional environments and act upon those predictions using a concept called spatial intelligence.’
In August 2023, TechCrunch reported that Li’s new startup, World Labs, had raised $100 M in funding. The company is valued at $1 Billion.
World Labs is developing a spatial intelligence model that can accurately estimate the three-dimensional physicality of real-world objects and environments. This will enable detailed digital replicas without extensive data collection. Sources say the startup’s artificial intelligence (AI) will also be capable of advanced reasoning.
According to Johannes Maunz, VP of AI at Hexagon, the growing interest in spatial intelligence models and related startups is a positive trend for the broader industry.
“This focus on spatial intelligence reflects a broader recognition of the importance of how we interpret physical spaces in a digital world,” said Maunz. “Investment and research help to accelerate innovation, leads to more sophisticated algorithms, improved hardware and more applications.”
Maunz believes that could increase the accessibility of spatial intelligence technologies, which benefit the industry at scale. “We expect that increased industry awareness of spatial AI models will have a positive impact.”
Spatial intelligence and digital twins
“As advancements in AI technology continue, the next big step is to bring spatial intelligence and digital twins together,” he said. Maunz points to the company’s digital twin in Klagenfurt, Austria, as an example of combining spatial intelligence and digital twin technology.
“Through spatial intelligence technology, we combined reality capture data from the city with AI-enabled software to create a digital twin of Klagenfurt in 3DT,” said Maunz. “The digital twin provides measured information about properties and how they are composed. In detail, with spatial intelligence, we separate the area into classes such as grass, water, building, road to provide the exact details.”
From those details, Maunz says they produced a 3D photorealistic model of the entire city. “This information is pivotal to simulate solar panels, discover heat islands, and know the level of impervious areas across the entire city and with that data, Klagenfurt can simulate specific actions upfront, implement and measure them afterwards.”
Sensor data
Hexagon’s sensors have created more than 150 petabytes of privately owned data. Maunz says that data can be used to train AI models based on data captured from the real world.
One petabyte of storage is equivalent to 11,000 4 K movies, and 150 petabytes would be 214,041.096 years of playing video games.
“With the rise of computer vision foundation models, the results of spatial intelligence models will become more powerful, versatile and reliable,” he added.
Geospatial intelligence
Data scientist Vkhyat Chaudhry is the co-founder and CTO at Buzz Solutions. He takes spatial intelligence in another direction, looking at geospatial intelligence and real-world applications being enabled by AI. Buzz Solutions focuses on managing and monitoring deforestation and critical infrastructure inspections in sustainability, agriculture, and environmental protection.
Sustainability, agriculture and natural disasters
"Geospatial AI can be used to analyze and interpret spatial and geographic visual data either captured through satellite or aerial (drones, fixed wing, helicopters)," said Chaudhry. "Emerging use cases include applications for environmental sustainability."
Chaudhry says that visual data from satellites and aerial vehicles can be analyzed using computer vision-based AI algorithms to detect changes in forest cover, pollution, carbon, methane, and other greenhouse gas emissions, sea level changes, and other environmental impacts.
"Geospatial AI can applied to agriculture as well," he said. "Multi-spectral visual data analysis can be used to detect crop health, soil texture and conditions, predict crop yield, moisture and nutrient content for enhancing agriculture and farming precision."
Chaudhry says that looking to prediction and detection of natural disasters, he sees Geospatial AI playing a role. "Aerial imagery can be analyzed by machine vision algorithms to detect disasters such as wildfires, landslides, etc., and can also support disaster prediction, response and recovery."
Inspecting critical infrastructure
Geospatial and aerial imagery capture for power and energy infrastructure can help monitoring and maintenance.
"Computer vision algorithms can detect various power grid components, equipment anomalies and defects using visual RGB and thermal imagery," said Chaudhry. "Buzz Solutions provides the monitoring and the visual data of power grid infrastructure, so this helps in more efficient, safer and faster inspections and maintenance of the power grid, hence preventing infrastructure failures that could lead to massive power outages, blackouts and even wildfires."
Chaudhry also says that satellite, aerial and LiDAR imagery are analyzed using advanced computer vision algorithms to detect vegetation growing near power lines and power grid infrastructure.
"Understanding the areas of excessive growth and growth patterns of vegetation around this highly energized infrastructure is important to provide effective vegetation management," he said. "Multi-sensor and multi-spectral data, including near-infrared (NIR), Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) and other techniques combined with advanced computer vision algorithms helps in detecting vegetation and predicting vegetation growth over time."
One advantage of managing vegetation around infrastructure assets for Buzz Solutions' utility customers is preventing the possibility of wildfires, which cause millions of dollars in damage annually.
Spatial computing on the horizon
Looking towards the next three to five years, with the rise of Chat GPT, Maunz believes there has been an increase in general acceptance of AI-based solutions.
“Rapid progress is also being made in researching spatial AI. Over the next 3-5 years, I expect we will see more real-life applications emerge from conceptual research. I expect spatial computing to become increasingly integrated into our daily lives and work processes,” said Maunz.

title: Council Post: Why AI Is Creating A Revolution In SaaS Pricing Models
text:
Alvaro Morales is the co-founder and CEO of Orb, a flexible usage-based billing engine for modern software pricing models.
Many SaaS companies want to leverage AI in their products. However, since AI is so new, pricing remains volatile. Costs can drop drastically for an AI model when the next iteration is out, and many companies lower their pricing in response to a competitor launch to gain or retain market share.
In addition to the fluctuating and unpredictable model prices, AI pricing is mostly based on usage. Customer usage is usually difficult to predict, which affects the costs your product will incur if it relies on AI models.
The unpredictability of usage and model changes means that today’s common seat-based or fixed pricing will likely not remain sustainable. Additionally, thanks to AI's increased productivity, a few people can achieve what previously took dozens. The very reason AI is so powerful is counterproductive to seat-based pricing.
As businesses continue to optimize their teams and processes with AI, they reduce the number of users needed to operate. The seat-based model can limit your revenue as your product gets more efficient.
Common SaaS Pricing Structures Today
To understand how to address these concerns, let's look at the different pricing models available.
As mentioned above, one standard pricing structure for SaaS products today is seat-based. That is, you pay based on the number of users. This was the pricing model when I worked as an engineering leader at a major SaaS company, where we spent six months deciding how to raise our per-seat pricing by $1.
Seat-based pricing, as I explained, isn’t compatible with AI because you won’t be able to predict individual customer usage of AI models and features. Also, customers won’t need as many seats if AI features make users more efficient.
SaaS companies can also offer flat-rate pricing, which is where you offer one standard price regardless of the number of users or volume of usage. This only works if your product has few variables, particularly ones that affect your cost of operations.
Tiered pricing has flat rates based on groupings, usually dependent on usage ranges or feature access. This pricing structure considers more usage and different feature options, allowing you to set a higher price to access your AI features. Although a good choice, it relies on your customers to accurately predict how much they will use AI features when choosing their tier.
One way to make a tiered pricing structure work with AI is to make it easy for customers to switch between tiers. At the same time, it’s a delicate balance to incentivize users on higher tiers to remain there while still ensuring they get maximum value with your product.
Because of the concerns, a usage-based pricing structure with a prepaid credit (PPC) might best accommodate AI changes and fluctuating customer usage while providing maximum value. Prepaid credits can offer customers more control and predictability over their spending—especially for enterprise users.
Switching Your Pricing Model
Today, 77% of consumers use AI—whether they know it or not. There is no doubt that AI is the future of SaaS.
AI is both necessary and a wild card regarding usage and cost. Because of this, AI will change the optimal way companies charge customers—it is up to companies how much pain they want to experience beforehand.
This is why it will be important to change your pricing structure swiftly and thoroughly rather than dragging out the process. Ultimately, a half-hearted pricing update will result in death by a thousand cuts. Determining to make no changes and see what happens can result in expenses quickly outpacing revenue.
Your pricing will continue evolving, so it may be helpful to keep pricing coded outside your product. As your product improves, it can be tempting to connect much of your pricing logic to actions within the product or the number of users.
However, this sets you up for failure. If you need to change one aspect of pricing, you risk breaking connections you didn’t even know existed, ruining customers' product experience and losing their trust.
For those excited about AI, the prepaid credits model can help program your pricing logic to your custom credits. This system helps keep your pricing flexible, so if you need to change and adjust, you can do so quickly and without interruption.
This will be usage-based and, more importantly, value-based.
How To Prepare For Usage-Based Pricing
Now, that I’ve covered the need for a dynamic pricing model, let’s talk about how to implement it. If you’re looking to switch to a usage-based, prepaid credits model, for example:
1. Inventory all the services and features you provide customers today. Avoid making assumptions about what users will and won’t be willing to pay for at this stage.
2. Once you have a list of everything your tool does, assign an internal monetary value for that service. What does it cost you to provide and support those features? For example, any AI features have real costs associated when you make calls to an AI model.
3. From there, work with your finance team to determine how much you should charge based on usage and feature access and translate that monetary amount to how many credits you should charge for the service.
4. Next, you need to build out your product and billing system. Your customers must be able to purchase credits and have them added to their accounts. Your product must function solely on those credits as internal currency.
By doing this, you ensure any pricing changes you make only need to affect how you charge for credits rather than how credits are used within your product.
Using A Future-Proof Pricing Engine
SaaS companies are no strangers to evolution. Pivots are second nature and often necessary for success. Consider your pricing a lever for growth in an AI-powered ecosystem. Be smart about your pricing structure and strategic with how you route pricing logic, and you’ll be able to adapt and stay flexible as AI continues to evolve and improve your product and customer experience.

title: Yale University To Invest $150 Million In AI Over Next Five Years
text:
Yale University has announced it will invest more than $150 million over the next five years for a variety of artificial intelligence (AI) initiatives.
The planned investment was announced by Yale Provost Scott Strobel in a message to the Yale community. It will support four AI-related priorities: improvements in computing infrastructure, increased access to secure generative AI tools, the addition of new faculty and seed grants, and enhanced interdisciplinary collaboration.
“Yale has long been at the forefront of AI development and research, and our leadership continues to be necessary as this technology evolves and endures,” Strobel said in his message. “To fulfill the university’s mission to improve the world and prepare the next generation of society’s great leaders and thinkers, we must explore, advance, and harness AI for its benefits while providing ethical, legal, and social frameworks to address the challenges it poses.”
The commitment closely follows a set of recommendations contained in a report from the Yale Task Force on Artificial Intelligence submitted in June by an 18-member group of faculty and campus leaders.
Here's a summary of the commitments:
Expanding research infrastructure
Yale will build a portfolio of approximately 450 graphics processing units (GPUs), which are electronic circuits that can speed computer graphics and image processing on a variety of devices. They are a key element in enabling AI to process and analyze big data.
Yale will also invest in cloud-based GPU access to expand is capacity for research that demands a very large number of GPUs for short periods of times and it will hire additional computational research support staff to train and assist members of the community as they use new GPU-intensive compute resources.
Delivering secure access to generative AI
Yale will procure generative AI tools for secure use by its campus members. It will implement the Clarity platform, which includes an AI chatbot powered by OpenAI’s ChatGPT-4o in a “walled-off” environment limited to Yale faculty, students, and staff.
According to the university, the platform may expand to incorporate other large language models. In addition to Clarity, the university will also offer campus members other AI tools, including Microsoft Copilot Enterprise and Adobe Firefly.
Building expertise to support research and education
Yale expects to hire more than 20 faculty whose research focuses on AI technology. They will be concentrated in the Faculty of Arts and Sciences, the School of Engineering & Applied Science, and the School of Medicine.
“Additional faculty expertise will strengthen Yale’s depth of knowledge and enhance the learning environment for students, who will be expected to understand, navigate, and make decisions about AI technologies throughout their lives and careers,” Strobel said.
The university also intends to provide seed grants for reviewing and enhancing its curricula in the context of AI through its Poorvu Center for Teaching and Learning. These grants are expected to lead to new ways to include AI tools and content in the curriculum.
Facilitating innovation and collaboration
The task force recommended that the university create “catalysts for collaboration” to exploit Yale’s strength in interdisciplinary research and scholarship.
This academic year, Yale will host a campus-wide research symposium on AI, at which faculty, students, and staff will “present research, share ideas, and establish connections across intellectual boundaries.”
The university will also sponsor interdisciplinary AI “prompt-a-thons,” seminars, and a research seed grant program, and the Yale University Library will offer support and AI-powered tools to improve access to digitized collections and spur new research.
“Whether you are studying, teaching, researching, or working at Yale, I encourage you to explore the resources available now and engage with the opportunities to come,” Strobel wrote in his message to the campus.

title: Council Post: AI In Marketing: Balancing Tech And Trust
text:
Dee Blohm is the senior vice president of marketing at Anteriad.
Generative AI, like any disruptive technology, brings both solutions and challenges. AI is able to decipher information from huge datasets, automate tedious tasks and generate content, images and even videos in seconds. However, there are concerns about risks, from bias and copyright infringement to the robotic-sounding nature of AI content and the general loss of authenticity that AI could introduce.
As a marketer, I love using AI to help me come up with a clever subject line and edit my blog posts. However, I am all too aware of how important authentic communication is with my customers and prospects. I put myself in the mindset of a loyal customer, trying to ensure that our communications are genuine, even when AI is involved.
It turns out, I’m not the only B2B marketer grappling with this conundrum. In a recent survey Anteriad did with Ascend2, we asked marketers about their use of AI as well as their feelings about balancing authenticity with AI and found that marketers are well aware of the issue.
We found that 66% consider authenticity to a great extent when creating brand messaging, while 49% of marketers believe they can absolutely strike a perfect balance in maintaining brand authenticity while incorporating AI into their GTM strategies. Digging deeper, we found that 55% of marketers believe that generative AI will have a positive impact on brand authenticity compared to only 18% who believe it will have a negative impact.
Using AI To Build Trust
Our research uncovered optimistic signs that B2B marketers are finding ways to incorporate AI into their work while maintaining an authentic connection. However, there are some pitfalls that marketers need to be aware of or risk alienating their audience.
For example, AI assembles content from what it’s been given and could inadvertently make false claims, such as saying that a product is infinitely scalable. AI can also make decisions that are incorrect or even illegal, such as when iTutorGroup’s AI-powered recruiting software allegedly automatically rejected female applicants ages 55 and older, and male applicants ages 60 and older, leading to age discrimination against over 200 qualified applicants.
One way of thinking about authenticity is in terms of trust. Forrester Research finds that trust is an “essential ingredient” in a successful B2B marketing practice. Building trust includes a number of different factors from dependability and consistency to positive customer reviews and a track record of success. However, trust is also about delivering an authentic voice, from marketing material and sales interactions to communications from executives.
I think about authenticity as a building block of trust during the marketing process. Every marketer needs to find their own company’s perfect balance, and AI can both help and hurt the process of creating an authentic voice for a company. It’s the marketer’s job to eliminate the risks and lean into the opportunities.
Understanding The Risks And Rewards Of Authenticity
It’s important for marketers to understand that the risks of using AI are both known and unknown. AI could mislead someone or create content that is incorrect. For a new prospect, I might assemble a list of top data targeting best practices using AI to share in a blog post, but to date, I have not generated a personal note from any leadership role using AI.
One could argue that as long as the AI note was reviewed and signed off by an executive it’s “authentic,” but so far, I haven’t allowed AI to speak for our executives. And AI isn’t always correct or usable. Marketers should always double-check what AI assembles to make sure it’s not plagiarized and is factual.
AI also has unknown risks. For example, there is an inherent bias in AI algorithms, which could mean that it generates recommendations that could be misleading. It’s hard for marketers to know that going into the process, so it’s important to work with technology and data teams to ensure that there is a level of confidence in the data or other information AI is using to generate outputs.
On the other hand, AI delivers many benefits that can improve the perception of authenticity. It can provide amazing consistency across communication, which actually improves authenticity. Many companies have style guides, for example, which specify colors, fonts and other brand design attributes. AI can make sure all documents and webpages accurately reflect the brand style guide, which provides a more professional presentation.
AI can also reduce the busy work that marketers need to do to create content and messaging, which means they can spend more time being creative, delivering better insights and personalizing content—which AI can also help with by identifying the right time and topics to use for specific outreach to key prospects.
Generating The Road Ahead
Those B2B marketers we surveyed who prioritize authenticity in their brand marketing, which we call “authenticity acrobats,” are actually more positive about the benefits of AI than other marketers, which is a great sign that striking a balance is possible. Three-quarters of “authenticity acrobats” say that generative AI helps with innovation, and 65% say that it helps with customer-centricity, 13 percentage points higher than other marketers.
Embracing AI is clearly a smart move for B2B marketers. Keeping a focus on authenticity in the process can help guide marketers away from risks and ensure that they are getting the most benefits possible from this exciting new technology.

title: Council Post: 5 Considerations For Executives Building A Robust Healthcare Platform In The Generative AI Era
text:
Arpan Saxena is the Head of Product at basys.ai, a leading healthcare AI solutions company.
The generative AI era has transformative potential for healthcare. More executives are leveraging this technology to improve patient outcomes, streamline operations, enhance user experience and manage costs.
As financial pressures continue to mount on health systems, rising healthcare costs remain a significant concern. Here are five key considerations for building a robust healthcare platform in this AI-driven landscape.
1. Assess the power of generative AI for personalized care.
Generative AI has the potential to revolutionize personalized care, but healthcare organizations must carefully assess their internal readiness before diving in. One common barrier is the lack of familiarity with AI among staff, which can lead to resistance. To overcome this, organizations should foster open discussions about AI's benefits and address concerns directly, emphasizing how AI can enhance—not replace—human decision-making.
Healthcare executives should also align AI use cases with the organization’s unique needs and strengths. This involves thoroughly analyzing existing processes and patient care models to pinpoint where AI can provide the most value. Starting with small pilot projects can help build confidence and expertise, enabling a scalable approach to AI adoption across the organization.
2. Ensure data privacy and ethical AI use.
Incorporating AI into healthcare demands a strong focus on data privacy and ethical considerations:
Adopt privacy-preserving AI techniques.
Implement methods like differential privacy and federated learning to protect patient data while enabling AI model training. This helps ensure confidentiality and reduces legal risks.
Establish ethical AI guidelines.
Develop guidelines that emphasize transparency, fairness and accountability. Address potential biases in AI models to ensure equitable treatment for all patients.
Implement consent management systems.
Provide patients with clear information about data usage and obtain explicit consent for AI-driven analyses, building trust and reducing attrition.
At my company, basys.ai, we’ve prioritized data privacy and ethical AI use by embedding these principles into our development processes. For example, we’ve implemented federated learning to keep patient data within local environments while still benefiting from AI insights. Additionally, our AI models undergo regular audits for biases, ensuring they align with our ethical standards and deliver equitable outcomes for all patients.
3. Facilitate seamless integration and interoperability.
Seamless integration and interoperability are essential for creating a unified healthcare ecosystem:
Leverage open standards and APIs.
Utilize open standards like FHIR and HL7 to ensure system compatibility. APIs facilitate seamless data sharing, reducing duplicative efforts and errors.
Promote collaborative data sharing.
Encourage collaboration among healthcare providers, researchers and technology partners to share data and insights, fostering innovation and improving patient outcomes.
Integrate AI-driven insights.
Ensure AI-generated insights are easily accessible and actionable for healthcare providers by embedding them into existing workflows, enhancing decision-making and reducing redundant tests and procedures.
4. Emphasize user experience and flatten the cost curve.
Creating intuitive, user-friendly interfaces is vital for healthcare platforms:
Adopt familiar UI/UX patterns.
Utilize established design patterns to minimize the learning curve, reduce training costs and improve adoption rates.
Implement natural language processing.
Use NLP for voice and text-based interactions, making it easier for users to communicate with the platform, improving accessibility and reducing administrative burdens.
Optimize resource utilization.
Leverage AI to predict patient demand, streamline workflows and optimize resource allocation, ultimately helping to flatten the cost curve.
Enhance preventive care.
Enable early detection and preventive care, reducing the need for costly treatments and hospitalizations, thus lowering overall healthcare costs.
Implementing NLP posed challenges at basys.ai, particularly in ensuring the AI accurately interprets and responds to the nuanced language used in healthcare. To address this, we invested in continuous training for our NLP models using real-world data and created feedback loops for users to report inaccuracies. This iterative approach has allowed us to refine and improve the system continuously.
5. Plan for scalability and continuous improvement.
To remain competitive, healthcare platforms must be designed for scalability and continuous improvement:
Adopt a modular architecture.
Use a modular design that allows for easy updates and expansion, incorporating new AI capabilities without disrupting services.
Utilize cloud-based solutions.
Leverage cloud infrastructure for scalability and flexibility, accommodating growing data volumes and user demands.
Foster a culture of innovation.
Encourage continuous learning and innovation, staying informed about AI advancements and industry trends. Invest in research and development to ensure your platform remains at the forefront of healthcare technology.
Fostering a culture of innovation should be central to your strategy. At our company, we host regular innovation workshops that invite employees from all departments to contribute ideas. We also support continuous learning by providing access to industry-leading resources and training programs, ensuring our team stays ahead in AI and healthcare advancements.
Conclusion
Building a robust healthcare platform in the generative AI era requires a focus on personalized care, data privacy, interoperability, user experience and scalability, all while addressing cost challenges. By prioritizing these areas, healthcare executives can better position themselves to create platforms that not only meet today’s demands but also are adaptable to future challenges. Generative AI holds the promise of transforming healthcare delivery, improving patient outcomes and driving efficiency, ultimately resulting in better, more cost-effective care.
Though the journey toward a generative AI-driven healthcare system may be complex, I believe the potential benefits outweigh the challenges. By staying committed to ethical practices and continuous innovation, we can unlock the full potential of generative AI in healthcare.

title: Council Post: Humans And Trust: Two Elements For Effective AI Adoption
text:
Eoin Hinchy is cofounder & CEO of Tines, the no-code automation platform for security teams, enabling you to achieve more with less.
Artificial intelligence has the potential to transform many aspects of work, from strengthening decision-making processes and streamlining admin to improving employee productivity and well-being. In security operations, AI can digest mountains of data and highlight potential threats in a fraction of the time it would take using people power alone. This makes it an indispensable tool in the fight against malicious actors and burnout.
This is one application of the technology. To better understand its potential, Tines surveyed 53 Chief Information Security Officers (CISOs) from the US, UK, Australia, and the Netherlands between June 27th and July 5th, 2024. In this survey, 74% agreed that faster decision-making by AI systems would introduce more benefits to the security operations center (SOC) than risks. But before organizations can benefit from what AI can offer, they need to address the elephant in the room: trust.
If you’ve worked in tech, I can bet with confidence that you’ve been disillusioned by overhyped technologies that promised the moon, but delivered a handful of rocks. These experiences have left many security practitioners wary of the bold claims often made by solutions vendors, which, combined with the data and privacy concerns surrounding AI, have created a climate of skepticism that’s difficult to overcome.
As with any new workplace technology, human involvement is key to adopting AI successfully. In this context, success means deploying AI effectively, in the right places and with the buy-in of everyone involved.
The Human-In-The-Loop Approach
While AI can deliver profound improvements to security operations, it’s not a panacea. You can’t just hit "run" and expect it to take control of everything—it would be quite scary if it did.
Think of AI as an assistant: It can sift through security alerts and flag anomalies, but you still need a human to review the outputs and catch any errors or nuances that might have been missed. These people-in-the-loop strategies are essential to combining the efficiency of artificial intelligence with the contextual reasoning of human judgment. Security teams that leverage this partnership of people power and AI will see real improvements in their ability to anticipate risks and respond to evolving threats. It will also build trust by demonstrating that AI’s role is to augment and improve the work of security practitioners, rather than replace it.
On the application side, it’s not enough for AI to simply spit out answers. To be able to trust AI, practitioners need to understand exactly how it came to its conclusion. Organizations will never get the buy-in they need to make AI work if employees can’t trust it to take care of even the most basic tasks. Nor will they gain buy-in if employees feel that their personal or professional well-being is being undermined for the sake of a flashy new tool.
Transparency will be key to building trust in AI systems. This means making how, where and why AI is being adopted in the organization clear and understandable.
There are legitimate concerns around technologies like large language models (LLMs), which have—quite rightly—raised questions about their suitability for security environments. While LLMs are improving rapidly, they can still miss the mark, hallucinate or get tripped up by biases in their training data. Errors like this can have catastrophic consequences if not caught early—especially in the SOC.
In our survey, 66% of respondents told us that data privacy concerns were a primary challenge facing AI adoption in their organization. Clearly, there is a lot of work to do here. By championing transparency and accountability, and by ensuring new tools are rigorously vetted, security leaders can build confidence in AI-driven processes and ensure they’re working in everybody’s favor.
Start Small, Scale Gradually
When deploying AI, it’s smart to begin with low-risk areas and move slowly. As confidence grows, AI can be expanded to more critical tasks.
Over time, you may discover that your initial application of AI doesn’t fit your needs. If so, don’t worry—this is all part of the process. Provided you have continuous, human monitoring and proper feedback loops in place, you can adapt your approach and keep AI aligned with your needs as they evolve.
For Tines, reliability is all about real-world performance. We had our fair share of experiments that went belly-up as we attempted to figure out where, or even if, we wanted to integrate AI into our platform. We’ve always been adamant that we would never introduce a new feature to Tines unless we were certain it would deliver genuine value to our customers.
One of the most promising applications of AI is its potential to make work more enjoyable. Everyone, no matter their role or industry, has parts of their job they dislike. The good news is that this tends to be the stuff AI does really well.
By taking over tedious, repetitive tasks like data entry and reporting, AI gives employees the bandwidth to take on more engaging work—whether it’s collaborating with colleagues, focusing on strategic initiatives or flexing their creative muscles. The result? Lower rates of burnout, higher productivity and greater employee satisfaction. In other words, everybody wins.
