title: 8 Tips To Optimize Your Resume For Applicant Tracking Systems
text:
Have you been working hard to update your resume but haven't received any interviews? More employers are using Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS) to filter resumes. Yours could quickly be sorted away if the right keywords or format are not there.
As International Update Your Resume Month is celebrated in September, it's time to re-think your resume with AI in mind. As companies are relying on Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS) to streamline their hiring processes, these systems scan resumes for keywords and rank them based on relevance to the job description, meaning your resume needs to be optimized to pass through these filters and land in front of a hiring manager.
Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS) often use AI (Artificial Intelligence) and machine learning algorithms to enhance their functionality. These technologies help ATS analyze and rank resumes more efficiently by:
- Keyword Matching: AI helps ATS identify relevant keywords and phrases in resumes that match job descriptions, making it easier to filter out unqualified candidates.
- Resume Parsing: AI-powered ATS can parse and structure data from resumes, such as work experience, education, and skills, allowing for more accurate candidate screening.
- Ranking and Scoring: AI algorithms can rank and score resumes based on how well they match the job criteria, helping recruiters quickly identify top candidates.
- Bias Reduction: Some AI-driven ATS aim to reduce unconscious bias by focusing on skills and qualifications rather than names, gender, or other personal information.
- Automated Communication: AI can also automate communication with candidates, such as sending acknowledgment emails or scheduling interviews.
Before starting to update your resume, make sure you define precisely the role or title you want to apply for. Once you are clear on the role you want, optimize your resume for ATS to increase your chances of getting more interviews.
1. Use Relevant Keywords
One of the most important aspects of optimizing your resume for ATS is incorporating the right keywords that match the job description and the skills, qualifications, and experiences the employer is looking for. Carefully read the job posting and highlight the key skills, qualifications, and responsibilities mentioned. These are the keywords you should include in your resume.
2. Use a Simple and Clean Format
ATS can have difficulty reading complex resume formats. Use clear section headings like "Experience," "Education," "Skills," and "Certifications." Avoid creative section titles that might confuse the ATS. Use a standard font, like Arial, Calibri, or Times New Roman. Avoid using script or decorative fonts, images or tables.
Use bullet points and quantify your achievements by including numbers demonstrating your impact, such as "increased sales by 20%" or "managed a team of 15."
3. Do Not Include A Picture On Your Resume
Including a picture on your resume is generally not recommended, especially in the U.S., Canada, and other countries where anti-discrimination laws are strict. Adding a photo can inadvertently introduce bias into the hiring process.
4. Choose the Right File Type
The file type you choose can affect how the ATS reads your resume. Use Word Documents or PDFs. Some ATS may have trouble reading text in headers and footers, so keep important information out of these areas.
5. Taylor your resume for every job application
Customize your resume for each job application to match the specific requirements and keywords of the job posting. according to FlexJobs’ Career Experts, “Resumes have evolved over the years, moving away from a generalized document to a single tailored document for each individual job application.”
This may sound time-consuming, but focus on customizing particularly the title and the summary section or BIO to match every job application.
6. Include a Core Competencies Section
When creating your resume, including a core skills section can improve the chances of your resume being recognized by Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS). In this section, list your most relevant skills, ideally aligning them with the keywords from the job description. If you aim for a one-page resume, consider dividing it into two halves: use the left half for skills and personal information and the right half for experience, education, and awards.
7. Check Your Resume with ATS Tools
Before submitting your resume, you can use online tools to check how it will perform in an ATS..
8. Focus on Relevancy
Finally, trim unnecessary details or irrelevant past experience. Remove outdated or irrelevant information that doesn’t align with the job you’re applying for. Your resume should highlight your most recent and pertinent experiences.
Optimizing your resume for ATS is a critical step in the job application process. By using relevant keywords, maintaining a clean format, choosing the right file type, and balancing ATS optimization with readability for human eyes, you can significantly increase your chances of getting noticed and landing more interviews.
Start implementing these strategies today to make your resume stand out in a crowded job market.

title: Council Post: AI-Powered Cyberattacks: How Businesses Can Prepare And Defend
text:
Vaibhav Malik, Global Partner Solution Architect Leader, expert in Zero Trust Security and enterprise cybersecurity.
Your cybersecurity strategy needs to be updated.
As you read this, AI-powered cyberattacks are evolving faster than traditional security measures can keep up. These aren't just incremental improvements to existing threats—they represent a paradigm shift in the cybercrime landscape. Attacks that once required teams of skilled hackers can now be automated, scaled and executed with unprecedented speed and precision.
For businesses, the implications are stark. The question isn't if you'll face an AI-driven attack but when. And when that attack comes, will your defenses be ready?
This article isn't about fearmongering. It's a wake-up call and a road map. We'll explore how AI transforms cyber threats and, more importantly, how your business can harness the same technology to build a robust, adaptive defense strategy.
The Evolution Of AI In Cybersecurity
Traditional cyberattacks rely on known vulnerabilities, social engineering tactics or brute-force methods. While these remain relevant, AI-powered attacks represent a significant leap in sophistication and potential impact. AI brings several key capabilities to the table that make it a game changer in the realm of cyber threats:
• Automation and Scalability: AI can automate complex attack processes, allowing cybercriminals to launch and manage attacks at an unprecedented scale.
• Adaptive Learning: AI systems can learn from past attempts, continuously improving their effectiveness and evading detection.
• Pattern Recognition: Advanced AI can analyze vast amounts of data to identify vulnerabilities and patterns in target systems more efficiently than human attackers.
• Natural Language Processing: This enables more convincing phishing attempts and social engineering attacks.
Understanding these capabilities is crucial for businesses to grasp the full scope of their current threat landscape.
Types Of AI-Powered Cyberattacks
To effectively defend against AI-powered threats, it's essential to understand the various forms they can take:
Advanced Phishing and Social Engineering: AI can create highly personalized and convincing phishing emails or messages, making them much more challenging to detect. These attacks can analyze a target's writing style, preferences and behavior to craft messages that are more likely to succeed.
Automated Vulnerability Discovery and Exploitation: AI systems can scan networks and applications for vulnerabilities much faster and more thoroughly than traditional methods. They can also automatically exploit these vulnerabilities, potentially compromising systems before human defenders react.
AI-Driven Malware and Ransomware: These next-generation threats can adapt to their environment, evade detection and spread more efficiently. They might alter their behavior based on the security measures they encounter, making them incredibly challenging to detect and eliminate.
Adversarial Attacks on Machine Learning Systems: As more businesses rely on AI for their security, attackers are developing ways to fool these systems. By manipulating input data, they can cause AI security systems to misclassify threats or miss them entirely.
Preparing Your Business For AI-Powered Threats
As AI-driven attacks become more prevalent, businesses must adapt their cybersecurity strategies. Here are vital steps to prepare:
Enhancing Employee Training and Awareness: Human error remains a significant vulnerability. Train employees to recognize sophisticated phishing attempts and social engineering tactics empowered by AI. Regular simulations and updates can keep staff vigilant against evolving threats.
Implementing AI-Powered Defense Systems: Fight fire with fire by deploying AI-enhanced security solutions. These can include advanced threat detection systems, automated patch management and AI-driven network monitoring tools that can identify and respond to anomalies in real time.
Regular Security Audits and Penetration Testing: Conduct frequent assessments of your systems, including AI-powered penetration tests. These can help identify vulnerabilities that traditional methods might miss and provide insights into how AI might be used to exploit your systems.
Developing an AI-Specific Incident Response Plan: Update your incident response strategies to account for the speed and complexity of AI-driven attacks. This may include automated response protocols and specialized teams trained in AI forensics.
Defensive Strategies Against AI-Powered Attacks
To effectively counter AI-driven threats, consider implementing these advanced defensive strategies:
Leveraging Explainable AI in Cybersecurity: Adopt AI systems that explain their decisions clearly. This "explainable AI" approach allows security teams to understand and trust the AI's recommendations, facilitating quicker and more accurate responses to threats.
Implementing Zero-Trust Architecture: Assume no user or system is trustworthy by default. This approach, which requires continuous verification for all users and devices, can significantly reduce the attack surface that AI-powered threats can exploit.
Using Deception Technologies: Deploy decoy systems and fake data to confuse and misdirect AI-powered attacks. These technologies can help detect threats early and gather valuable intelligence on attacker tactics.
Collaborative Threat Intelligence Sharing: Participate in industrywide threat-sharing networks. By pooling knowledge about AI-driven attacks, businesses can stay ahead of emerging threats and benefit from collective defense strategies.
A Call To Action
The rise of AI-powered cyberattacks marks a pivotal shift in the cybersecurity landscape. While these threats are formidable, businesses can significantly enhance their resilience through proactive preparation and advanced defensive strategies.
To stay ahead, companies must invest in AI-powered security solutions and employee training, regularly assess and update their cybersecurity strategies, embrace emerging technologies like explainable AI and deception tech, and collaborate with industry peers to share threat intelligence. The time to act is now.
By staying informed and adaptable, businesses can defend against AI-powered threats and harness AI's power to create more robust, responsive cybersecurity ecosystems. In this new era of digital security, preparedness and innovation are the keys to staying one step ahead of AI-empowered adversaries. Those who act swiftly and decisively will be best positioned to protect their assets, reputation and future in an increasingly AI-driven threat landscape.

title: Council Post: Uncovering The Real Value In The E-Commerce AI Gold Rush
text:
Zohar Gilad is cofounder and CEO of Fast Simon.
The AI gold rush is underway. This year, the largest e-commerce retailers deployed their first wave of customer-facing generative AI (GenAI) tools. So far, e-commerce merchants and consumers are all hopeful for what AI might bring. More than half of shoppers would use GenAI to help with clothing purchases, and they believe AI has already improved shopping.
Amid all the hype and excitement, it can be challenging for merchants, especially those without the vast resources and engineering teams of e-commerce giants, to quickly extract value from AI. So, what’s realistically achievable for most merchants today? What can offer some of the quickest and most significant returns on investment for your business? And what benefits your customers the most without adding extra effort for them—or overwhelming you?
Here’s a look at how AI can impact fundamental aspects of e-commerce, helping to deliver some of the most substantial and immediate benefits.
The "I" In AI Stands For Shopper Intent
Personalization—matching a shopper’s intent and experience—remains one of the cornerstones of successful e-commerce. Historically, companies with excellent personalization drive 40% more revenue than those that don’t. Customers demand personalization, but more importantly, 73% of them expect better personalization as technology (like AI) advances.
At the simplest level, companies can use AI to collect more data for better personalization and recommendations. One way is by leveraging AI embeddings. Embeddings transform real-world objects (such as photos, text, videos and more) into numbers—essentially math that algorithms can digest and use to create better processing models.
Putting this additional data to work in these models within the shopper clickstream can help better predict intent (as well as other things). When powering popular and proven revenue generators, like "Shop the Look" or complementary product suggestions, this application of AI helps deliver improved matches to the shopper's intent. It also doesn’t require any more effort on the part of the customer (in other words, they don’t have to learn or use a new widget) to get the benefits of AI. You’re just benefiting your company and the shopper.
Eliminating The "No Results" Search Result
Another way AI can help deliver results by zeroing in on intent is by using more data to tackle search abandonment. Most users—especially buyers with high intent—flock to a site’s search function. And those buyers historically convert three to five times more than others.
Today, most on-site searches are limited to keyword data and inputs, a single source (or mode) of data that can deliver poor results that can frustrate and drive high-intent shoppers away. By adding vector search AI technology, merchants can expand beyond a single mode of data (keywords) into multiple modes of data, adding text, images and other unstructured data. We've found that some early adopters of this multi-modal search approach are already seeing double-digit conversion increases simply by decreasing a "no results" search result.
Merchandising Productivity Gains
Effective merchandising—presenting items in the most favorable way to drive sales and profit—can be difficult to achieve as technology spreads and shopper patience decreases. It’s also a craft that isn’t going to be replaced by algorithms any time soon.
AI can help merchandisers make better decisions and boost their productivity, freeing them up for more human endeavors like developing brand, creativity and design. AI assistants can take instructional prompts like "move this product" or "promote these products" and implement the changes. Over time, when applied to your data, AI can deliver insights that help merchandisers balance the brand’s creative endeavors with what’s best for the business.
From Chatbots To Conversational Commerce
As technology advances, virtually all customers expect faster service and often turn to messages and chatbots to speed up interactions. Chatbots have been historically frustrating for brands and customers, but that’s changing to uncover what could be the largest AI-powered shopping opportunity—conversational commerce.
Conversational commerce helps brands interact with (and sell to) customers right where they are through social media, messaging apps, voice assistants like Siri and more. The customer journey is now fairly fragmented, and customers appreciate conversational commerce because it meets them where they are in real time. Fifty-five percent of shoppers turn to chatbots for support, and 36% of shoppers made a purchase via a messaging app last year—a 227% increase since 2021.
AI is greatly speeding up and improving the quality of chatbots and other forms of conversational commerce. Social media platforms are investing tens of billions of dollars in AI and more immersive experiences that are ripe for improving and better facilitating shopping and self-service. Merchants can capitalize on this investment without building their own expensive AI technology stacks.
And, of course, chatbots, messaging and other such tools often serve as launchpads for human interaction. AI can really shine if it can speed up the time it takes to reach the agent or the speed of that agent’s response to inquiries by providing fast, timely information.
Balancing AI Market Pressures And Customer Trust
As AI challenges and empowers businesses and public markets reward it, there’s great pressure to speed up the process and find shortcuts. Combined with a lot of experimentation, that can raise your risk. But in the race to improve customer support, the one guardrail that customers remain adamant about is that businesses must maintain transparency and trust. Most (77%) of consumers want companies to identify when GenAI is used, and 81% want humans to regularly check on the accuracy of when GenAI is used.
Just like employees, your algorithms represent your brand and business. You need to manage AI, train it properly and enforce your brand standards. Be transparent when AI is used in the appropriate ways. And most importantly, ensure that AI doesn’t clash with your values or industry best practices. Follow the growing list of industry best practices, like the National Retail Federation’s core principles for AI adoption, to make sure you’re just not getting caught up in the hype.

title: Council Post: When It Comes To AI For Supply Chains, Reaching The Promised Land Requires More Strategy, Less FOMO
text:
Matt Elenjickal is the founder and chief executive officer of FourKites.
FOMO—"fear of missing out"—is driving too much unproductive spinning in many supply chain organizations looking to implement AI. (And they are all looking to implement AI.)
Companies across every industry see AI and machine learning (ML) as key to reaching the "supply chain promised land"—a future state where supply chain disruptions are anticipated and nimbly sidestepped, where complex processes are automated and where happy, empowered teams make smart, data-based decisions in real time.
As of today, however, many chief supply chain officers (CSCOs) are still trying to find their way out of the wilderness.
CSCOs know they want to do something with AI. They've all set aside a budget. Many have spun up various councils, experiments and even robust projects to leverage AI in their supply chain operations. However, while many are making real progress, others are lagging behind.
In my conversations with CSCOs, CIOs and other company leaders, I'm finding that the laggards are often being driven by "AI FOMO" rather than a cogent strategy and disciplined approach. Here's my advice for how to move forward in a way that promises real returns.
Problem Definition
"If I were given one hour to save the planet, I would spend 59 minutes defining the problem and one minute resolving it."
That pearl of wisdom has been attributed to none other than Albert Einstein, and CSCOs would do well to follow a similar approach when formulating AI strategies and programs.
AI has great potential to transform a plethora of supply chain processes—demand forecasting, order management and fulfillment, supply planning, logistics and distribution, sales and operations planning, to name a few. Companies need to be deliberate and specific about the problem they're trying to solve and weigh the estimated effort versus anticipated returns.
Start Small But Dive Deep
Start with one problem and its associated processes. That said, dive deep into the process, paying particular attention to where the handoffs occur between different internal teams, trading partners and systems. These are where problems often manifest.
Many companies are starting with customer service processes, where the potential positive impact is high and they tend to have plenty of historical data within the four walls of the company.
Get Specific On Automation Opportunities
Diving deep into the process makes it possible to proceed to the next critical step—determining which parts of the process you intend to automate with AI. This is not a trivial step. In fact, it's hard work to determine what can be automated and what should be automated. What's technically possible? Where do you need to ensure humans are actively involved or providing oversight? Do you have a plan for redeploying people when time has been freed up due to the automation of certain tasks?
My company's approach with customers and prospects is to workshop all of this in a dedicated, one-day session. It's well worth this minimal upfront time investment to get clarity on the problem you're trying to solve and the path forward.
Don't Go It Alone
It's early innings in the AI implementation game, and let's not kid ourselves—there's a lot we don't know.
That makes it all the more important that companies put their heads together with trusted technology partners. I advise companies to carefully evaluate partners based on three criteria:
1. Rich, varied information sources. AI thrives on high-quality, diverse data. Make sure your chosen AI collaborators have access to a wealth of information across industries.
2. Operational overhaul. Embracing AI isn't just about new gadgets; it's about transforming how you work. Look for partners who can adapt to your workflows and business practices.
3. Connected ecosystems. It's important that your technology stack can play well with others. Prioritize partners who've built robust networks that can tap into and share insights across different systems and organizations. This connectivity enables a bird's-eye view and allows for tweaks at every stage.
I genuinely believe there's a supply chain promised land on the horizon that most companies will be able to reach, but we have work ahead of us. Part of that includes serious change management to help supply chain professionals navigate this massive transition.
There are no easy answers here. Leadership has to listen to employee concerns and dedicate time and resources to training, upskilling, education and support. Leaders also need to really harness the creativity and energy of employees who are excited about AI because many are. A February 2024 Epicor survey of hundreds of U.S. manufacturing workers found that more than half want to work for tech-driven companies, and more than eight out of 10 felt new tools and tech made them more efficient. My sense is that supply chain professionals are no different.
Lastly, the supply chain industry has to get over its exaggerated anxiety about data sharing and training AI on big, shared datasets. Yes, best-in-class security and data privacy are absolutes, but we can navigate both the technical issues and the competitive/intellectual property concerns.
When I hear hesitation or concern from supply chain professionals, I say: "Look, we have two options. One, we can give you basic, simple output that will not have a lot of intelligence built into it because you're limiting yourselves to just your data. Or we can give you advanced, intelligent outputs that utilize data from a broader ecosystem. But for you to get it, you have to share your data as well."
There is a supply chain promised land—and the best and fastest way to get there is together.

title: Council Post: Five Ways AI Could Change How Businesses Think About Data
text:
Glenn Mathis is President and Chief Operating Officer of Integris, a national managed IT service provider.
Moore’s Law is the time-tested prediction that computer chip speeds and capabilities will continue to double with time. For most of our computing history, that “doubling” time usually took about one to two years. But, according to Microsoft Chairman and CEO Satya Nadella’s recent speech at the Microsoft Build conference, AI has helped cut “Moore’s Law,” doubling from 15 to 18 months down to six months.
Buckle up, everyone. We’re about to enter the golden age of AI computing, where everything from our documents to our meetings to our images and search preferences can be infinitely parsed by our intelligent AI assistants. From the AI-powered Copilot being built into Microsoft 365’s platform to the free AI network being built by giants like Google, I believe the next few years will see an explosion of AI-driven productivity and innovation unlike anything we’ve ever seen.
As promising as all of this is, I think the biggest shift we’ll see in the next few years won’t necessarily be in chips and processing speed; it will be in how we think about our data—how we share it, how we analyze it and how we harness it to power our growth.
The Big AI Rethink And What You Can Do To Prepare For It Now
Tools like Copilot for Microsoft 365 will take our files out of siloed storage, making all the information in your documents easily searched and summarized. It will make it easier to work interchangeably between programs as well. This will soon change the way we store, search and think about our information. Here’s how I believe that will play out in the next few years:
1. Every word said in your meetings will become part of a mission-critical archive.
Will AI kill endless, unproductive meetings? Maybe. With recording, transcription and lightning-fast translation services baked in, companies could soon make recorded meetings mandatory. Then, they’ll automatically store these meetings in searchable archives so that the organization at large can follow the thread of decision-making and progress.
With AI, your team members can quickly summon facts from your discussions, watch real-time summaries being produced during your meetings and quickly get up to date even if they weren't able to attend. Smart companies will be preparing for this shift now by creating protocols around efficient meetings, transcript storage and levels of access.
2. Your files will become part of the organization’s collective wisdom.
Your files may be on SharePoint now, but your coworkers must know which information is in which file to access it. Soon, that won’t be necessary. With one prompt, AI can search the information inside all your organization’s documents and craft a simple answer to that colleague’s question. It can even summarize documents, rewrite marketing materials and draw conclusions based on the data in your systems.
If you want to work smart with AI, you’ll need to determine which information is searchable, when and by whom. More importantly, you’ll need to develop a protocol around cleaning out old information, trashing first drafts and creating levels of access for restricted information.
3. Your customers will expect a highly personalized experience on your website.
AI will soon be able to reason across text, sound and images. One of the first places this will show up is in chatbots. With AI online assistants, your website could be capable of interacting with your customers in a more meaningful way, conversing with them much like a real salesperson might.
Imagine a customer holding up a past item they'd purchased to their computer's camera, and your chatbot instantly identifying the product, its availability and similar products you offer. Start thinking about how that kind of machine-driven service power could change the way you present and talk about your products. How could it change the way you access your client's purchase data?
4. Language barriers will be broken down.
With real-time translation, you'll be able to get AI-generated captions and audio overdubs. Before long, we could be able to converse with customers around the world, exchange documents that are instantly converted to our language and more. With this kind of power at your fingertips, what new markets could you pursue? How could this open your hiring processes to top talent from around the world?
5. Information will be more available, but also more unreliable and vulnerable to attack.
Innovations abound, but so do AI hallucinations, data handling risks and, of course, the hype that often comes with new tech. The job of securing AI has only just begun, and no one has this fully figured out. We are all going to be learning this as we go. Until then, trust, but verify.
With the advent of AI coding, technology has effectively kicked down the barrier to entry for hackers. Conversely, AI has also given us the ability to create more powerful detection, monitoring and remediation tools for our cybersecurity. The future will be a continuing battle for the integrity of our information and our platforms. Prepare your budgets to invest and stay watchful. Now is the time to start thinking critically about the information we accept, the way we access our networks and the reliability of our datasets.
We are about to see one of the biggest technological shifts in computing history. There will be hits and misses. Just because you can do something with AI does not always mean that you should use it. Still, in the years to come, AI will demand we change our thinking around the nature of work, while also developing a set of tools to help us accurately assess these new opportunities. It’s a big job, and enormous opportunities await. Those who commit to the journey early will get there the fastest. I hope to see you on the road ahead.

title: Council Post: How Open Benchmarking Ensures AI Development Is Reliable And Safe
text:
Jairam Ranganathan is the Chief Product Officer at Motive.
Artificial intelligence (AI) is essential to our daily lives. It influences everything from the way we drive and secure our homes to how we manage our money and receive medical care.
However, the rush to innovate and deploy cutting-edge AI has outpaced the critical process of establishing reliable benchmarks that ensure customers know the truth about what they are buying and how safe those AI-dependent products are. You wouldn’t dream of getting behind the wheel of a car that had failed a basic operational safety test. Should you take that same gamble with AI?
Business leaders must balance rapid innovation with developing customer trust by participating in transparent AI benchmarking for the most high-risk and consequential areas. This is particularly true when it relates to safeguarding public health, ensuring the safety of our communities and protecting our health and well-being.
AI benchmarking is the process of evaluating AI models and systems against specific tasks using defined parameters and datasets. This verification ensures that a product performs as claimed. Companies that avoid benchmarks or comparisons undermine the market, other AI providers and, most importantly, their customers. To establish meaningful open benchmarking, three critical components are necessary:
• Companies must commit to transparency and embrace evaluation for the benefit of the industry and consumers.
• A consortium of industry leaders, technologists and research institutions should develop the essential tools for testing outcomes, verifying claims and setting standards.
• An independent environment is needed where simulations can be replicated, allowing AI technologies to be tested on an equal footing, ensuring unbiased results.
Setting Industry Standards
Benchmarking services are an important way for consumers to get reliable information and make informed purchasing decisions. We want verifiable proof that we can trust the food we eat, the medicine we take, the cars we drive and the technology that is shaping our lives in new ways.
Consumer Reports, for instance, is a nonprofit organization that provides unbiased product testing, research, ratings and recommendations to consumers. The company tests and evaluates a wide range of products, including appliances, electronics, household items and more, based on various criteria such as performance, reliability, safety and value for money.
Similarly, Kelley Blue Book provides trusted information about the value of new and used vehicles. Edmunds, too, is an essential service for a car buyer. It provides a wide range of services related to cars, including reviews, pricing information, vehicle specifications and comparison tools.
AI, however, presents unique challenges that make benchmarking more complex. The dynamic nature of AI systems, their capacity for continuous learning and the opaque mechanisms by which they often operate call for a new approach to benchmarking—one that is as adaptive and nuanced as the technologies it seeks to evaluate.
A years-long process of government regulators setting up industry oversight committees won’t work for AI. Unbiased parties familiar with the industry, like academics or commercial researchers, need to partner with companies to set benchmarks and create real-life operating scenarios that give customers a view into how a vendor’s product works and ensure they are meeting industry standards.
Commitment To Open And Transparent Benchmarking
However, it’s on business leaders to partner with these third-party organizations and give them access to products so we can increase trust and transparency, and better the entire industry. Many of the companies building large-language-model (LLM) foundation models are benchmarking and doing it openly and transparently.
Meta, for example, used two popular coding benchmarks to test Code Llama’s effectiveness against its competitors and published the results. Meta also stated that "the entire community can evaluate their capabilities, identify issues, and fix vulnerabilities" to ensure that Meta is building its AI models responsibly and transparently.
Open Testing For Unbiased Outcomes
The importance of benchmarks and their impact on consumer perception and decision-making is recognized in various legal frameworks. The United States Federal Trade Commission (FTC) encourages truthful and non-deceptive product comparisons because they provide important information to buyers to assist them in making rational purchase decisions.
Having unbiased parties set benchmarking standards and getting companies to commit to benchmarking isn’t enough if we don’t have the tools to effectively test our AI against benchmarks. Testing AI technologies before they’re deployed in the real world is crucial for safety, reducing development costs and accelerating time-to-market.
Some industries have this. Foretellix, for example, develops verification and validation tools for automated driving systems that can generate, orchestrate, monitor and analyze the hundreds of millions of driving tests required to ensure the safety of autonomous vehicles (AVs). Foretellix’s platform is utilized by original equipment manufacturers (OEMs), AV providers and other suppliers to ensure fast and safe deployment of automated driving technologies.
We have to develop these benchmarking tools across every industry. But where do we start?
Prioritizing Vigorous Benchmarking In The Most Consequential Areas
There are now many areas where the implications of AI errors or inaccuracies are not merely inconvenient but could have grave consequences (paywall). Companies need to be open to evaluation. It’s critical for the industry's and consumers' benefit. The methodology behind benchmarking must prioritize consumer risk, addressing both direct and indirect impacts on consumers.
With AI integration accelerating, claims about AI enhancing safety or quality of life are increasing without substantial verification. This creates a dangerous illusion of consumer security, underscoring the urgent need for rigorous benchmarking in critical areas like autonomous or AI-assisted driving, medical AI and children's interaction with technology.
For benchmarking to work, it requires a concerted demand from consumers for evidence of excellence and efficacy, and an openness from companies to benchmark and consistently improve. By setting clear standards, testing and making information accessible, benchmarks empower consumers to make safer, more informed choices, driving product safety and quality improvements.

title: Are Organizations Ready For The Full Integration Of AI?
text:
Business and IT leaders are ready and willing to make artificial intelligence a core component of their business operations. The question is whether they are able to fully integrate AI across the enterprise in a way the delivers all of AI’s potential benefits while ensuring security and meeting compliance requirements.
While organizations are embracing AI, there remain some lingering concerns. According to a recent Prosper Insights & Analytics survey, 34% of business owners and professional managers believe that AI implementations require human oversight while a significant percentage feel that AI needs more disclosure and transparency on the data it uses.
Furthermore, 36% of business owners and 27% of managers are extremely concerned about their privacy being violated from AI using their data. Fortunately, organizations are finding ways to mitigate those issues by investing in proper security and IT governance.
Nearly every IT and Operations leader surveyed in the recent Celigo AI Trends and Operations Report 2024 said their organizations have implemented AI solutions, and 97% said AI is critical to improving operations in the coming year. Having already seen improvements in areas such as productivity, optimized operations, and customer experiences, they are enthusiastically investing in AI, with most planning to increase spending on AI in 2025 by between 25% and 50%.
But fully implementing AI in a complex, cloud-based enterprise is not a simple task. A successful AI implementation requires optimized data collection and the full integration of SaaS applications, yet 52% of respondents cited connecting data across applications as the biggest barriers to AI training and workflows. Another 45% identified overall implementation as a significant challenge.
They also cited other barriers to enterprise-wide adoption, with 56% identifying security concerns, 47% citing a lack of understanding within the organization about AI’s capabilities, 46% needing to address employees’ fears of being replaced by AI and 33% maintaining that other IT priorities should take precedence over AI.
On top of that, IT and Operations leaders are aware that overworked IT departments—a common theme in most organizations—are already spread too thin to oversee a full range of AI implementations. That’s prompted companies to support the idea of the “Citizen Developer,” allowing business users to manage their own AI applications. Sixty-eight percent favor a Citizen Developer mindset, and 53% are already allowing business users to implement their own applications.
To help Citizen Developers succeed with AI, training is critical but only 14% of organizations have training in place for the effective use of AI, and even fewer have training programs to reskill workers that may be impacted by AI-driven automation, according to Valoir Research CEO and Principal Analyst Rebecca Wettemann.
“Investing in training drives effective use of AI and ensures employees feel comfortable taking advantage of it. We're seeing a real focus on a more skills-based - rather than role-based - training strategy that helps companies identify skills gaps as well as identify growth opportunities for those who may find part of their jobs being automated by AI,” said Wettemann.
But that approach still requires that those users have proper IT governance. Organizations may be making effective use of AI now, but they are unlikely to gain full integration on their own.
An In-house Approach May Not Be Enough
For all of AI’s promise and proven effectiveness, organizations need a comprehensive strategy for AI that includes full integration while providing governance, security, and guardrails to guide Citizen Developers and protect against misuse of a powerful technology that is still being developed. Organizations will likely need help to make it all work.
“AI is game changing and can help improve business operations in a variety of ways. However, I haven’t seen a wave of new technology over the last 25 years where it has been more critical to partner with experts on implementation,” said Jotham Ty, founder and CEO of Gappify. “Not only is the technology still evolving, but the governance and compliance implications may be too high to manage in-house.”
An AI integration must align with business goals, setting timelines for implementation, establishing an AI policy that accounts for both IT and business users, and one that’s fully integrating AI tools into business processes. Organizations need to establish learning programs to train all users, allowing for two-way communications via feedback loops and knowledge-sharing lunches or other sessions. You must be sure to choose AI tools that clearly benefit the organization, automating tasks and workflows that boost productivity and efficiency. And regularly monitoring progress can identify areas in need of improvement and help optimize operations.
While 82% of survey respondents said they are following a strategy or roadmap for AI adoption, those barriers remain, which is where expert guidance can come into play.
Building on AI’s Capabilities
Full integration of AI is a challenge, but companies should not let that deter them.
"Organizational leaders cannot ignore AI, nor should they be afraid of it," said Josh Meiri, CTO and CIO at AppWrap. "They should embrace AI because it has tangible, real-world benefits. AI enables our team to focus on critical tasks and elevates roles throughout the organization by handling the mundane work that often consumes the most time and resources."
AI already has a good foothold in many organizations, with 53% using it for data analysis and to gain insights across their business. Another 39% are applying AI to training and simulation, while 38% say they use AI to streamline operations. Looking ahead to 2025, a full 59% plan to prioritize IT services, 52% will focus on analytics, 51% will look at data processing and 32% will concentrate on using AI for marketing automation.
The key to all that success is a strategy that accounts for every aspect of AI, which organizations may not have the resources to do on their own. “Enterprises should consider prioritizing investments in AI with proven solution providers to achieve quicker time to value and ensure their AI implementations have a solid foundation,” Gappify’s Jotham Ty said. For most organizations, getting the most out of AI for their operations will require solid partnerships with reliable AI experts who can help them get the most out of this fascinating and powerful new technology.

title: The President Of Verizon Global Services Has A Game Plan For Gen AI
text:
Verizon Communications Inc. is a global telecommunications and media giant, boasting more than $133.6 billion in revenue in 2023. The company has a subscriber base of over 140 million people. The company’s extensive infrastructure, combined with its cutting-edge technological advancements, positions it at the forefront of global connectivity and innovation.
Arumugavelu Arumugavelu's New Role and Vision
In July of this year, Shankar Arumugavelu was promoted to Executive Vice President and President of Verizon Global Services. For nearly seven years prior, he was the global CIO of the company, and he joined Verizon through a predecessor company, GTE, in 1999. As such, for the past 25 years, he has been involved in numerous technological innovations that the company has brought to bear. In his current role, Arumugavelu has taken the helm of a vast portfolio that includes not only information technology, data and analytics, but also supply chain, real estate and broader shared services. He is now responsible for overseeing global technology, commercial and corporate functions, and the infrastructure that supports Verizon’s operations worldwide.
Arumugavalu’s leadership is marked by a keen focus on leveraging advanced technologies to drive business transformation. Central to this has been his emphasis on predictive AI and generative AI, which he views as pivotal to Verizon’s future growth. "Our mission is to industrialize AI across multiple parts of the business," Arumugavelu explained, highlighting the significant strides Verizon has made in integrating AI into its operations.
Predictive AI: Enhancing Customer Experience and Operational Efficiency
Predictive AI plays a crucial role in Verizon’s strategy, particularly in managing its vast customer base. With a subscriber count exceeding 140 million, Verizon relies on predictive AI to analyze customer behavior, anticipate needs, and reduce churn. “We’ve developed models that can predict which customers are likely to leave, allowing us to intervene proactively,” Arumugavelu noted. “This has become a crucial part of our base management.”
These AI-driven insights enable Verizon to segment its customer base effectively, targeting specific groups with personalized offers and communications. Arumugavelu pointed out that predictive AI has excelled in making these decisions, helping Verizon not only retain customers but also enhance the overall customer experience. “Data is abundant but converting it into actionable insights is where the real value lies,” he underscored.
Generative AI: Revolutionizing Customer Interactions and Internal Processes
While predictive AI has been instrumental in decision-making, Arumugavelu is particularly excited about the potential of generative AI to transform both customer interactions and internal processes. In 2023, Verizon embarked on an aggressive experimentation phase with generative AI, which has now evolved into a phase of thoughtful implementation across the company.
One of the most impactful use cases has been the deployment of a generative AI-powered personal research assistant for Verizon’s customer success agents. “This tool helps reduce the cognitive load for our agents by providing quick access to the information they need, which in turn builds a stronger emotional connection with our customers,” Arumugavelu said. By rolling out this capability to 40,000 agents, Verizon has significantly reduced the time customers are placed on hold, improving both employee experience and customer satisfaction. “We’ve seen a 20% reduction in hold times, which pays due respect to our customers’ time and increases their satisfaction,” he added.
Verizon is also extending the use of generative AI beyond customer service. Arumugavelu shared plans to integrate this technology across different personas within the company, including network agents and the developer community. “Generative AI is becoming a great pair programmer, allowing our developers to be more productive and deliver higher quality code,” he explained.
Strategic Implementation and Future Outlook
Arumugavelu’s approach to AI is not just about experimentation but also about ensuring that these technologies are implemented at scale, delivering measurable value. He emphasized the importance of collaboration between business and technology teams, noting, “It’s about purposeful innovation. We need to bring in business leaders early on to ensure we’re solving the right problems.”
Looking ahead, Arumugavelu is excited about the convergence of AI and connectivity, particularly the rise of edge AI. “The low latency of our networks, combined with the capabilities of AI, will enable more edge AI solutions,” he said. “This is a big opportunity for us.” He also believes that natural language interfaces, powered by generative AI, will increasingly become the norm, bridging the digital divide and making technology more accessible to all.
As Arumugavelu continues to lead Verizon Global Services, his focus on AI and innovation is set to drive the company forward, while providing examples for others to note as they think about the value that generative AI might drive for their companies.
Peter High is President of Metis Strategy, a business and IT advisory firm. He has written three bestselling books, including his latest Getting to Nimble. He also moderates the Technovation podcast series and speaks at conferences around the world. Follow him on Twitter @PeterAHigh.

title: When Building Winning Teams, Take Your Cue From Hollywood And The Olympics
text:
The need for building high-impact teams in the age of generative artificial intelligence has never been more critical, taking center stage in boardroom conversations and company strategies. Ask any recruiter or hiring manager in the market, and they might say that hiring today feels oddly like the opening line in Charles Dickens’ Tale of Two Cities: “It was the best of times, it was the worst of times.” We’ve entered an era where AI is simultaneously revolutionizing and complicating the future of work, making the need for building high-impact teams a top priority in one of the toughest candidate markets for knowledge workers. However, most practitioners and seasoned leaders know that the secret to true success isn’t found solely in algorithms or data points but in the art of blending diverse talents—a process that mirrors the intricate craft of casting a Hollywood blockbuster or selecting the starting lineup for an Olympic basketball team.
The Art of Casting: Building Teams Like a Hollywood Production
At a summer gathering of industry leaders in Talent Acquisition in New York, I had the opportunity to join a panel with Jessica Zwan, who shared a compelling analogy: hiring is like producing a major motion picture, and there’s much that talent leaders can learn from this framework. Her analogy resonated with me because it captures the essence of what the recruiting industry values while adding the urgency of creating a masterpiece that shapes culture and drives extraordinary returns.
Imagine you're casting a Hollywood film, maybeifically the next installment in the Avengers franchise—a series that has grossed over $7 billion worldwide. You wouldn’t just select the most famous actors or those with the highest box office earnings. Instead, you’d focus on the chemistry between the actors, their ability to bring unique characters to life, and how their individual talents contribute to the overall narrative. This approach is strikingly similar to the “war for talent” that corporations face every day. In my experience, building a high-impact team isn’t just about filling roles; it’s about selecting individuals who complement each other, bring diverse skills to the table, and align with the team’s mission.
This summer offered a powerful, real-time demonstration of the impact a well-crafted team can make in just a few moments. I'm referring to the 2024 Summer Olympics, where the concept of high-impact teams was vividly illustrated through the assembly of the U.S. Men's Basketball team. Featuring NBA legends like Stephen Curry, LeBron James, and Kevin Durant, this team wasn’t just about bringing together the biggest names in the sport—it was about crafting a lineup that functioned as a cohesive unit, with each player enhancing the strengths of the others. This approach mirrors how top companies like Apple, Google, Netflix, and innovative startups strategically hire talent, not just for individual brilliance but for their ability to work seamlessly within a high-performing team.
In the tech world, top talent teams don't simply seek out the brightest minds from prestigious brands. Their focus is on how these individuals will collaborate, how their diverse experiences will integrate, and how they will collectively drive innovation and growth. Much like the 2024 Olympic basketball team, which had to mold its star players into a cohesive unit, companies and leaders should draw inspiration from this approach. By blending talent from varied backgrounds, they can create high-performing teams where the cross-pollination of mindsets, skill sets, and toolsets leads to extraordinary results.
In both sports and business, the true measure of success lies in how well a team’s members can blend their unique talents; this principle becomes even more evident when considering the competition on the court. The U.S. team faced formidable competition from France, which included Victor Wembanyama, the NBA’s 2023 first-round draft pick and rising star with the San Antonio Spurs, as they battled for the gold medal. Much like a tech startup disrupting an industry, Wembanyama’s presence demanded that the U.S. team not only rely on individual brilliance but also on their ability to work together, adapt, and elevate each other’s performance.
The Epic Game: High-Impact Teams in Action
The 2024 NBA Olympic team delivered one of the most epic basketball games in history, a game watched by millions of people worldwide. In fact, the highest viewership number for the Paris Games was recorded during the men’s basketball gold medal game, where the U.S. secured a 98-87 victory over France in a thrilling finish against the host country. In the final moments of the gold medal match, with the score tied and the pressure mounting, the team's success hinged on their ability to blend their diverse talents into a cohesive whole. Stephen Curry’s unparalleled shooting, LeBron James’ leadership and playmaking, and Kevin Durant’s clutch scoring created a breathtaking finale that left the world in awe.
Their victory wasn't just a testament to individual talent; it was a demonstration of the power of a high-impact team. The team’s ability to come together, despite the varied playing styles and backgrounds of its members, mirrors the successful execution of a blockbuster film, where the synergy between the cast can make or break the story.
Lessons from the Court: Insights from Tech Giants and Olympians
The triumph of the 2024 NBA Olympic team, much like the magic behind Hollywood’s most successful blockbusters, provides invaluable insights for leaders and organizations aiming to build high-impact teams. Here are some practical strategies to consider when crafting your own winning lineup:
Understand the Unique Strengths of Each Team Member
Just as Curry, LeBron, and Durant each brought unique skills to the team, it’s essential to recognize and understand the individual strengths of each team member. Data from a LinkedIn report shows that while AI can automate certain hiring processes, it still falls short in assessing a candidate’s soft skills—skills that are vital for building cohesive teams. Leaders must take the time to identify what each person excels at and how their skills can be leveraged to complement those of others.
Focus on Chemistry, Not Just Talent
Talent alone isn’t enough. The chemistry between team members is critical. The 2024 NBA Olympic team’s success wasn’t just about having the best players; it was about how well they could work together. This lesson applies to business teams as well. According to a World Economic Forum survey, 92% of business leaders believe that creativity, adaptability, and collaboration are just as important as technical skills. These attributes, which foster team chemistry, are often overlooked by AI in the hiring process.
Align Team Members with the Mission
Every successful team, whether in sports or business, has a clear mission. The 2024 Olympic team was united by the goal of reclaiming the gold medal, just as a blockbuster film cast is united by a shared narrative. In your organization, ensure that each team member understands and aligns with the team’s goals. This alignment creates a sense of purpose and direction, driving the team to work cohesively toward a common objective.
Embrace Diversity for High Impact
The diversity of skills, backgrounds, and experiences creates a team capable of achieving high-impact outcomes. The 2024 NBA Olympic team, with players from varied backgrounds and playing styles, demonstrated how diversity fuels innovation and success. Research by McKinsey & Company supports this, showing that diverse teams outperform their less diverse counterparts by 35% in terms of innovation and problem-solving.
Value Differences and Recognize Super Learners
The NBA stars on the 2024 Olympic team didn’t just rely on their skills; they respected each other’s talents and learned from one another. In a successful team, it’s important to cultivate a culture where team members respect each other’s contributions, value their differences, and are open to learning from their teammates. This becomes a flywheel of mutual respect that strengthens the whole and enhances collaboration and shared outcomes.
Adapt and Evolve as a Team
Just as the NBA team adapted their play to outmaneuver their opponents, successful teams must be agile and willing to evolve. The ability to pivot and adjust strategies is key to navigating challenges and seizing opportunities in a rapidly changing environment—a lesson equally applicable on the court and in the boardroom.
Team Building in the AI Era: Where Technology Meets Human Insight
As AI continues to evolve, its role in team building is becoming increasingly sophisticated, but the human element—understanding the unique strengths and potential of each team member—remains irreplaceable. While AI can efficiently identify potential candidates and analyze vast amounts of data, the art of blending these candidates into a cohesive, high-performing team still requires a human touch. As Raphael Ouzan, founder of A.Team, states, "You can’t build the future without the builders who are empowered to make decisions." This insight underscores the limitations of AI in capturing the subtle nuances of cultural fit, team dynamics, and individual potential—critical areas where human judgment plays a pivotal role in achieving successful outcomes.
A 2022 study by the Harvard Business Review reinforces this point, revealing that while AI excels at processing data, it often falls short in recognizing the deeper aspects of team building that experienced human managers bring to the table. Leaders must go beyond resumes and job titles, delving into how individuals think, collaborate, and contribute to a shared goal.
The most successful teams are those that blend a variety of skills, perspectives, and experiences—much like the carefully crafted lineup of an Olympic team or the ensemble cast of a blockbuster film. It’s this combination of diverse talents, unified by a common purpose, that drives extraordinary impact.
Legendary Teams, Extraordinary Outcomes
In the end, building a high-impact team is much like casting or crafting your starting lineup for success—whether in Hollywood, on the basketball court, or in the boardroom. It requires a deep understanding of the unique contributions each individual can make and a strategic approach to bringing these talents together in a way that amplifies their strengths and achieves extraordinary outcomes.
As the workplace continues to evolve, embracing the art of building cohesive teams will be key to driving innovation, creativity, and impact. Just as the 2024 NBA Olympic team demonstrated the power of diverse, complementary talents, businesses can achieve greatness by carefully curating teams that blend the best of human and technological capabilities. Imagine a world where hiring is driven by a clear understanding of business outcomes, where we change the game (pun intended), and recruiters can then deliver a starting lineup of franchise-caliber talent into the boardroom to accelerate outcomes, innovation, and returns.
In the AI era, the future of team building is not just about filling roles—it's about casting for success and seeing the through-line beyond just skill sets and talent. While we relish in the newness of transforming our selves as AI takes hold, it’s nothing new, because it’s all too familiar a feeling. After AI, there will be other technologies and teams that will form to advance out comes and accelerate us. Similar to the NBA Dream Team that graced our screens in 1992, the epic performance of Curry, LeBron, and Durant on the world stage serves as a powerful reminder that when the right talents are blended together with purpose and precision, the results can be nothing short of legendary.

title: How AI Is Making Hiring More Human
text:
As the CEO of a company with over 650 employees, I delegate a lot of responsibility to other people, and automate whatever I can. But one aspect of running my business that remains a core part of my job is hiring. Why? Because making sure candidates are the right fit is extremely important to having a creative, high-functioning team.
Everyone knows that while bad hires are occasionally inevitable, they’re always painful—and expensive. One frequently cited statistic from the U.S. Department of Labor holds that a bad hire can cost a company 30% of that employees’ annual earnings. On the flipside, a series of good hires can achieve nothing short of greatness: Take Pixar, the animation studio that turned out its first commercial success in 1995 with Toy Story and has been producing hits ever since. Pixar is known for its commitment to nurturing talent and maintaining its creative culture, to amazing effect.
Hiring is an intensely personal process. That’s why I think AI is so well-suited to make it easier. Sound counterintuitive? Read on.
The Human Part of Hiring Vs. The Rest
Most people don’t want the fate of their careers to be determined by a robot. In a survey conducted by Harvard Business Review, 69% of respondents expressed concern about the use of AI to make decisions about hiring, promotions and work assignments based on its understanding of human behavior.
These concerns are valid: There’s plenty of evidence that these technologies contain disturbing biases—the Berkeley Haas Center for Equity, Gender, and Leadership, for example, reports that 44 percent of AI systems are embedded with gender bias, and around 26 percent display both gender and race bias.
But what AI can do is automate the tedious parts of an HR professional’s job, freeing up more time for what actually matters—getting to know the candidate. Some activities ideally suited for AI include scheduling interviews and screening resumes based on objective criteria—for example, the distance a candidate lives from the office or the hours they’re available to work.
For the most part, though, the most effective way to use AI is to assist with more complex tasks requiring human oversight. Take the process of writing job postings—AI tools can recommend language that attracts more diverse applicants, or mask an applicant’s gender and race. It can also actively source job-seekers across platforms like LinkedIn and job boards, pulling in a larger pool of potential hires.
The efficiency of AI makes it possible for my team and I to focus on what really matters about a candidate. Having the technical aptitude to do the job is necessary, of course, but the reason I like to be involved in hiring at Jotform is to assess a candidate’s soft skills—those interpersonal traits like emotional intelligence and adaptability. My company is built around cross-functional teams, and the ability to work well with others is crucial. Is the person sitting across from me someone who values others’ ideas, takes feedback to heart and supports the organization’s goals? AI can’t decide that for me, but it can certainly take other tasks off my plate so I can focus more on learning the answers to those questions.
How AI Can Help Candidates, Too
The jobs AI is least likely to replace are the ones that take leadership, creativity, and empathy. While not every role specifically requires those traits, it’s safe to say everyone wants employees who display them in some capacity, whether it’s core to their job description or not. For candidates, being able to demonstrate their soft skills to a fully focused hiring manager can only be beneficial.
The added efficiency of AI can also shorten the hiring process, meaning job seekers will hear about next steps sooner. These days, the average time-to-hire now includes multiple interviews and lasts around 43 days—if not longer. But 62 percent of working professionals say they lose interest in a job two weeks after their initial interview if they haven’t heard back. Hiring managers may not only be losing good candidates to bloated timelines, they may be damaging the company’s reputation by coming across as uncommunicative. Rather than leaving candidates in eternal limbo, recruiters can speed up hiring and also offer feedback to finalists who didn’t make the cut, creating a positive rapport and maybe even leave the door open for them to fill a future role.
While there are AI tools available that claim to handle the recruitment process from end-to-end, that’s not how I see it working out. After all, there’s a reason we call it “human resources.” What AI can do, however, is tackle the impersonal sides of hiring, leaving executives with the time and space to really get to know the candidates they’re talking to. There’s still a lot of work to be done to assess AI’s capabilities and shortcomings—and there are many. But by viewing it as a tool for efficiency, we can actually add a lot of the humanity back into hiring, and ensure we’re genuinely getting the best people for the job.

title: 3 High-Income Skills To Learn For Free Without A Degree In 2024
text:
If you're at a point in your career where you recognize the value of upskilling, want to make more money, and and desire to be in a career that has enormous potential, then you need to learn about high-income skills.
High-income skills are skills that you can learn which are highly specialized and provide tremendous value to employers (in your job) and to corporate clients (as a freelancer). While there are many high-income skills to choose from, here are three that stand out as having exceptional potential this year:

If there was ever a skill that is of utmost importance to learn this year, it would be AI. Artificial intelligence can boost your salary by as much as 40%, according to the University of Oxford.
